The University of California, Los Angeles won the 23rd Annual National College Fed Challenge.

The University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) won the 23rd annual national College Fed Challenge on Friday, a team competition that encourages undergraduate students to learn about the U.S. economy, monetary policymaking, and the role of the Federal Reserve System. Teams analyze economic and financial conditions and formulate a monetary policy recommendation, modeling the Federal Open Market Committee. The team, from Los Angeles, California, represented the San Francisco District and included Aarushi Maheshwari, Annika Chan, Atul Prasanth, Caitlyn Cox, Finn Karish, Eli Brooks (alternate), Kennedy Yang (alternate), Manasi Vartak (alternate), Ronojoy Borpujari (alternate), and Sahil Sudani (alternate). The team's advisers were Chris Surro and Ali Haider Ismail.

"I am very happy to congratulate the students who competed in this year's College Fed Challenge, especially the winners and finalists," said Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh. "They took on the same big questions we policymakers face. I'm impressed by their talent, their rigor, and their eagerness to think hard about monetary policy and the economy."

This year's College Fed Challenge included 141 schools from 34 states across the nation, the most in the competition's history. Teams submitted video presentations or participated in local competitions last month. Twenty-one semi-finalist teams then participated in question-and-answer sessions held earlier this month, and seven finalists were invited to the Federal Reserve Board for the national finals. The other national finalists were the University of Chicago in second place and the University of Maryland, College Park in third place. Teams with honorable mentions include Cleveland State University, Harvard College, Pennsylvania State University, and St. Lawrence University.

Teams were evaluated on their economic analysis, responses to the judges' questions, teamwork, and presentations.

#2855. Cowboys turn into turkeys during epic Thanksgiving Day meltdown | Opinion

ARLINGTON, TX – Give the people what they want, Dallas Cowboys. Or not.

Points. More points. Drama. And a holiday meltdown for the ages.

Hail to the depleted Philadelphia Eagles, capping a wild rally from a 21-point deficit with a 59-yard field goal from Jake Elliott with two seconds left that lifted them to a 39-38 victory – the largest Thanksgiving comeback in NFL history.

Joe Milton, the Eagles' fill-in quarterback signed off the Cowboys' practice squad in mid-October, got some serious revenge on the team that didn't keep him again as Dak Prescott's backup. Milton passed for a career-high 331 yards and three TDs. And boy did he live up to his "Bazooka Joe" moniker, using that cannon arm to connect with DeVonta Smith for a 50-yard touchdown in the first half and a 45-yard scoring strike in the second half.

Yet Milton's big day was only a part of the stain and shame left with the Cowboys.

They blew it again. Wasn't this the team that collapsed in crunch time in Week 8 against Arizona?

Indeed. Only this might have been even worse.

"Pretty stunning," said Cowboys quarterback Dak Prescott, a man who has way too much practice in trying to explain these embarrassing losses. "I guess I said it a couple weeks ago after the Arizona game, how stunning that was. This definitely takes the cake."

And the turkey, stuffing and sweet potato pies, too.

"Numbing is the word," Cowboys owner Jerry Jones offered.

He, too, has seen this season of promise for the Cowboys dissipate into disaster. Again. They are 5-7 and with road games against the Seahawks and Rams up next on the docket, this does not have the look of getting better. Yet, when Jones went on to hype the skill level of his coaching staff as he held court during his typical postgame briefing outside of the locker room, it was like the spin cycle repeating itself.

Which brings us to Brian Schottenheimer, in his second season as just the second coach in franchise history with a losing record (12-16-1), and a man losing, too, is trying to explain it.

"Every situation is different, each game is different," Schottenheimer said.

Maybe so, but there are common denominators. They lost to the Cardinals when Gardner Minshew came off the bench in the fourth quarter to throw his only three touchdowns of the season. They were upset by the Bucs, starting undrafted rookie quarterback Jalon Daniels on a night that started with the defense getting pushed around on a game-opening, 15-play touchdown drive. They lost in Week 3 in Rio with bone-headed blunders in crunch time, as the Ravens scored 10 points in the final 90 seconds.

Different situations, yet early or late in games, Dallas finds ways to lose.

Week 3: Indianapolis Colts kicker Spencer Shrader (3) celebrates with long snapper Luke Rhodes (46) after Shrader kicked a 58-yard field goal against the Houston Texans at Lucas Oil Stadium. The Colts debuted their "Anvil Strike" uniform - featuring an unfamiliar gray uniform and glossy, metallic blue helmet with the familiar horseshoe logo in white. The Colts won, 19-17, for their first win of the season.

Week 3: Buffalo Bills quarterback Josh Allen (17) hands off to running back James Cook III against the Los Angeles Chargers at New Highmark Stadium. For the game, the Bills debuted their "Nickel City" alternate uniforms - the most striking element being the blue "Charge Helmet," adorned simply with an oversized cutout of the team's familiar logo. The Bills won the game, 24-16.

Week 2: Los Angeles Rams quarterback Matthew Stafford (9) hands the ball to running back Kyren Williams (23) during a 28-6 win on "Monday Night Football" against the New York Giants at SoFi Stadium. The Rams debuted their new "Classic Sol" uniforms, an homage to the team's look during its 1951 championship season.

Week 2: Arizona Cardinals quarterback Jacoby Brissett (7) hands off to running back Jeremiyah Love against the Seattle Seahawks at State Farm Stadium. The Cardinals wore their desert-themed "Rivalries" uniforms in the 31-7 loss to the Seahawks. Arizona's "Rivalries" look was one of the best to debut in 2025.

Week 2: The Baltimore Ravens' Trey Hendrickson (91) reacts after a sack against the New Orleans Saints at M&T Bank Stadium. The Ravens wore their "White Noise" uniforms, just one of the team's new uniform combinations that will debut during the 2026 season. The Ravens lost the game, 24-17.

Week 2: New York Jets wide receiver Garrett Wilson (5) celebrates after scoring a touchdown against the Green Bay Packers at MetLife Stadium. The Jets debuted their "White Out" uniforms for their home opener, which ended in a 20-17 overtime loss.

Week 3: Indianapolis Colts kicker Spencer Shrader (3) celebrates with long snapper Luke Rhodes (46) after Shrader kicked a 58-yard field goal against the Houston Texans at Lucas Oil Stadium. The Colts debuted their "Anvil Strike" uniform - featuring an unfamiliar gray uniform and glossy, metallic blue helmet with the familiar horseshoe logo in white. The Colts won, 19-17, for their first win of the season.

Week 3: Buffalo Bills quarterback Josh Allen (17) hands off to running back James Cook III against the Los Angeles Chargers at New Highmark Stadium. For the game, the Bills debuted their "Nickel City" alternate uniforms - the most striking element being the blue "Charge Helmet," adorned simply with an oversized cutout of the team's familiar logo. The Bills won the game, 24-16.

Week 2: Los Angeles Rams quarterback Matthew Stafford (9) hands the ball to running back Kyren Williams (23) during a 28-6 win on "Monday Night Football" against the New York Giants at SoFi Stadium. The Rams debuted their new "Classic Sol" uniforms, an homage to the team's look during its 1951 championship season.

Week 2: Arizona Cardinals quarterback Jacoby Brissett (7) hands off to running back Jeremiyah Love against the Seattle Seahawks at State Farm Stadium. The Cardinals wore their desert-themed "Rivalries" uniforms in the 31-7 loss to the Seahawks. Arizona's "Rivalries" look was one of the best to debut in 2025.

Week 2: The Baltimore Ravens' Trey Hendrickson (91) reacts after a sack against the New Orleans Saints at M&T Bank Stadium. The Ravens wore their "White Noise" uniforms, just one of the team's new uniform combinations that will debut during the 2026 season. The Ravens lost the game, 24-17.

Week 2: New York Jets wide receiver Garrett Wilson (5) celebrates after scoring a touchdown against the Green Bay Packers at MetLife Stadium. The Jets debuted their "White Out" uniforms for their home opener, which ended in a 20-17 overtime loss.

This time, it started with a bang. The Cowboys had five possessions in the first half and scored four touchdowns. This flowed with recent trend. A few days earlier, when the Tennessee Titans came to town, Dallas had eight drives and seven TDs. And the week before that, in losing a shootout against the mighty Niners, they scored touchdowns on four of the last five possessions. In Cowboys math, that's 15 TDs over 18 drives during the three-game homestand (until country music star Miranda Lambert's halftime concert), which was nothing less than a certified roll.

Then poof. For all the feel-good flow of a 28-10 halftime lead enabled by Javonte Williams' 3 TDs, Dallas gagged against an injury-depleted team that used Aaron Rodgers earlier in the week to snap a seven-game losing streak.

MORE: Catch rule, Aaron Rodgers, Bears stars among winners and losers from NFL's Thanksgiving trifecta

The Eagles, fighting on for weeks after losing Jalen Hurts to blood clots, had one setback after another on Thursday. Star cornerback Cooper DeJean suffered a concussion on the game's first snap. Saquon Barkley had just five carries before getting sidelined by a stinger. Tight end Dallas Goedert was knocked out with a shoulder injury.

And Philadelphia (4-7) was still game enough to lay it on Dallas. Besides a huge, career-high 200-yard game from Smith, who torched Dallas on 11 catches as Milton's go-to man, the Eagles got a blocked punt from Ty Robinson early in the fourth quarter that Kenny Moore scooped and returned 3 yards for a touchdown. And then a 55-yard kickoff return by Britain Covey set up a 15-yard TD run for Milton. Throw in a 40-yard missed field goal by usually reliable Cowboys kicker Brandon Aubrey and yeah, words like stunning and numbing surely apply.

Reality check: The Cowboys, with all that explosive offense, still have a defense capable of imploding, of giving up huge chunks of yards, of allowing quick scores, of allowing opponents to stay in the game.

Of, well, allowing a castoff come back to haunt you.

"You never know when your opportunity is going to come," Milton said. "You never know when, where, how. The only thing you can is prepare yourself."

And if you're a quarterback, pray that the opportunity comes against the Dallas defense.

Remember when the Cowboys stripped first-year defensive coordinator Christian Parker of his play-calling duties? Like two weeks ago. They gave the reins to recently hired consultant Mike Pettine. Well, look at where that got them.

Still, for all of that, the Cowboys, with that red-hot, star-studded offense that produced 416 yards, could have bagged a victory by gaining 1 more yard.

The Eagles would have never had a chance for Elliott's big kick if Dallas had converted on fourth-and-1 from the Philadelphia 39-yard line with 55 seconds remaining. One yard.

Prescott was sacked for a 9-yard loss as he looked for CeeDee Lamb. Then it was left for Dallas' defense to protect the slim lead. And you know where that has gotten them.

Schottenheimer said he went for it because he trusted his offense to get a yard. Of course, there was no reason to trust the defense. And as it turned out, he couldn't trust the offense, despite a 100-yard game from Williams, to pound it inside to move the chains. Prescott took a shotgun snap. Then was eaten alive.

"You can't put the game on one play," Prescott said.

Yet sometimes, all it takes is one more play. Prescott acknowledged that part of his frustration was that his unit scored just 10 points after halftime. No, the defense's lapses and the special teams blunders could not be pinned on the quarterback, who has been on a tear with an 11-2 TD-to-INT ratio during the homestand.

Someone asked Prescott, fairly and pointedly, whether he'd expect to win after putting up 38 points.

"I'm not going to be the guy that's going to put things on other people," he said. "And I shoulder this one because of that last play."

Rest assured, there's plenty of embarrassment and shame to go around for the Cowboys. And little hope that this will be the season for a different type of finish.

This article originally appeared on USA TODAY: Cowboys turn into turkeys during epic Thanksgiving Day meltdown | Opinion

#2854. Knicks’ Pacome Dadiet has big night after Mike Brown calls him out

Mike Brown sent a warning to Pacôme Dadiet:

Dadiet responded with his best game of the season Wednesday, dropping seven points in 14 minutes of the Knicks' 121-102 win over the Cavaliers — including a couple of big buckets in the fourth quarter.

Pacome Dadiet, who scored seven points off the bench, goes up for a layup during the Knicks' 121-102 win over the Cavaliers on Nov. 25, 2026, at Madison Square Garden. Vincent Carchietta-Imagn Images

"I didn't think he played hard in the game before," Brown said. "And I actually called him into my office and showed him some film. I told him, 'As a young guy, if you don't play hard, I can't play you.'

"And I said, 'Believe me, I got a lot of guys I can go to. I'm not afraid to go to somebody else. So the least you could do is play hard.' And I showed him how he wasn't. And I thought [Wednesday], he played hard."

OG Anunoby, who is recovering from a calf strain, progressed to individual on-court work Wednesday morning, according to Brown.

Anunoby missed his third straight game with the injury, sitting out Wednesday's game.

The Knicks are classifying Anunoby's recovery as "day to day." Calf strains have become dangerous injuries in the NBA because they've developed into Achilles tears. But Brown said he's blissfully unaware of that risk for Anunoby.

"There are a lot of medical terms that are above my head," Brown said. "They tell me and I don't really pick up on the injury. If he's out, I change my minutes sheet. And then I'll just wait for them to tell me when he's back. [Wednesday], OG's individual work happened before shootaround and I didn't even know he had individual work until his player development guy told me later on. You never want a guy to hurt himself more. But I don't think about it."

Jalen Brunson (illness), Karl-Anthony Towns (knee soreness) and Josh Hart (sprained shoulder) all played despite being on the injury report.

Miles McBride (left adductor tightness) sat out his second straight game.

"Tightness and just being smart," the Knicks said.

McBride had surgery around that area last season.

Andre Drummond suffered a head injury in the first half Wednesday and played just eight minutes.

Lead assistant Chris Jent returned to the sideline Wednesday after missing nearly a month for personal reasons.

Jent is the Knicks' offensive coordinator and was recently lauded by LeBron James for developing the future Hall of Famer's jumper.

"I used to watch [Jent] shoot in practice," said James, who was with the Cavaliers when Jent was an assistant under Brown. "And I just started to work with him a lot.

"I would be like, 'Yo, CJ, I need you to come with me. We need to work.' And he was kind enough to join me. So I give a lot of credit to where my shot is today from where it was to Chris Jent."

Assistant TJ Saint served as Jent's replacement over the past month.

The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, the Federal Reserve Board, and the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency today announced that the 2027 threshold for higher-priced mortgage loans that are subject to special appraisal requirements will increase from $34,200 to $35,500.

The threshold amount will be effective January 1, 2027, and is based on the 3.9 percent annual percentage increase in the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers, known as CPI-W, as of June 1, 2026.

The Dodd-Frank Act added special appraisal requirements for higher-priced mortgage loans to the Truth in Lending Act, including that creditors obtain a written appraisal based on a physical visit to the interior of the home before making a higher-priced mortgage loan. The rules implementing these requirements contain an exemption for loans at or below a threshold amount that is adjusted annually to reflect CPI-W increases.

The Federal Reserve Board and the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau today announced the dollar thresholds used to determine whether certain consumer credit and lease transactions in 2027 are subject to certain protections under Regulation Z (Truth in Lending) and Regulation M (Consumer Leasing).

By law, the agencies are required to adjust the thresholds annually based on the annual percentage increase in the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers, known as CPI-W. Transactions at or below the thresholds are subject to the protections of the regulations.

Specifically, based on the 3.9 percent annual percentage increase in the CPI-W as of June 1, 2026, Regulation Z and Regulation M generally will apply to consumer credit transactions and consumer leases of $76,300 or less in 2027. However, private education loans and loans secured by real property, such as mortgages, are subject to Regulation Z regardless of the amount of the loan.

#2846. There’s something to like about the way the Suns lost in Houston

The Phoenix Suns went to Space City to battle the team whose logo resembles one of those silly little patches that go on astronaut suits, ultimately losing by 12. What that final score doesn't tell you is that with 4:45 remaining, the Suns were down three points. What killed them down the stretch is what killed them throughout the game, and it shouldn't come as a surprise to any of us. Rebounding was the culprit. Or, more specifically, their inability to rebound.

Phoenix was outrebounded 51-38 overall and 20-13 on the offensive glass, but it was the 27 second-chance points they surrendered that ultimately sunk them. When Alperen Sengun pulls down 11 rebounds, and seven of them are of the offensive variety, you know you've done something wrong.

But my takeaway from this game? The impressively physical brand of basketball the Suns played. They stood up to a Rockets team that clearly had revenge on its mind as they ran up and down that bright red clowny court. After all, Phoenix had already beaten Houston earlier this season. When the Rockets came out with a chip on their shoulder, the Suns rose to the challenge and battled them throughout.

The final result comes down to two things. Houston possesses a more talented roster, and they're bigger, badder, and better on the boards. The attitude with which the Suns played, however, was something I thoroughly enjoyed watching. That's who this team was a season ago, and perhaps they needed a team like Houston to push them around a little, to jostle them enough to draw a line in the sand and say, "We're done with this."

The hope is that they carry that attitude forward. Because if they can bring that level of intensity and fight night in and night out, nobody is going to want to play that version of the Phoenix Suns. We know that because we saw it last year.

The rebounding issues aren't going away, and there will be nights when Phoenix simply doesn't possess the personnel to overcome them. But physicality and effort are things this team can control regardless of the opponent. What we witnessed in Houston was a willingness to compete on somebody else's terms without being intimidated by them. The Suns lost the basketball game, but somewhere on that obnoxiously red court, they rediscovered a little bit of their swagger.

#2843. S&P warns Nvidia credit rating could be cut over 'rising' management and governance risk

Nvidia's credit rating could be cut by one notch over the next 90 days if the company continues to have "deficiencies" in its management and governance framework, S&P Global Ratings said in the wake of the Jensen Huang's ouster and reinstatement as Nvidia CEO.

"News regarding the CEO and questions regarding potential export control violations have exposed vulnerabilities in Nvidia's management and governance framework, especially in regard to its board structure, composition, and effectiveness," S&P said in a Wednesday note.

Nvidia currently holds an AA rating, the third-highest level.

S&P has placed the chipmaker on "CreditWatch with negative implications," though any potential downgrade would be limited to one notch, to AA-, unless investigations or disclosures lead the agency to conclude that Nvidia's reputation or future prospects have also been harmed.

A downgrade can pressure bond prices, push yields higher and raise borrowing costs. Nvidia priced $25 billion of investment-grade senior notes in June, with maturities from 2028 through 2056, shortly after S&P upgraded the company from AA- to AA.

Nvidia has about $32.5 billion of bonds in the U.S. high-grade corporate bond index, according to Bloomberg.

S&P's Wednesday note follows Moody's Ratings changing its outlook on Nvidia to stable from positive on Nov. 18, citing governance concerns, and leaving that outlook unchanged after Huang's return on Monday.

In its note, S&P cited the "long tenure" of certain board members as a reason their independence may be "compromised" and said Nvidia's management and governance risk was "rising."

The ratings agency added that it remained unaware of any remedial action taken by the board to address what could be "meaningful" management and governance deficiencies.

Chairman Harvey Jones and early investor Tench Coxe have served on Nvidia's board since 1993, while Brooke Seawell joined in 1997. Mark Stevens served from 1993 to 2006 and rejoined the board in 2008.

S&P also flagged questions around geopolitical risk management and internal controls arising from Nvidia's exposure to China.

"While Nvidia management has delivered significant returns for its stakeholders over decades, weak executive oversight and lack of succession planning have brought questions around the "key man" risk to the forefront," S&P's Andrew Chang and David Tsui said.

Chang and Tsui noted that Huang's resignation and subsequent reinstatement did not resolve questions about the board's oversight of executive conduct.

The agency also intends to meet with Nvidia's board and management to discuss plans to address those deficiencies, particularly around "board independence, effective management oversight and a credible leadership succession plan."

Huang returned less than two weeks after Jones said Nvidia's directors did not intend to reinstate him. The board later voted unanimously to bring Huang back, sending Nvidia shares up as much as 36% during Monday's session.

Nvidia shares are down about 12.5% since Monday's close.

#2840. Tokenization platform Securitize gains 10% postmarket on Q3 results, move into asset-backed finance

Tokenization platform Securitize climbed about 10% postmarket after reporting third quarter growth alongside increased operating expenses, and announcing an expansion into asset-backed finance through a strategic acquisition.

Miami-based Securitize, which made its public market debut in July, operates in the relatively new corner of the crypto equity universe involved in institutional tokenization infrastructure. Tokenized assets on the platform grew 9% in the third quarter, to $4.8 billion, from the same period a year ago. Aggregate transaction volume rose 20% from a year ago, to $4.3 billion. Revenue of $11.5 million was up 28% from last year.

The growth came as bullish sentiment around tokenization gained traction throughout the third quarter, ahead of the Security and Exchange Commission formalizing the long awaited Innovation Exemption on Sept. 17, which created a temporary pathway for trading of certain tokenized stocks and strengthened the regulatory outlook.

Profitability is still meaningfully below year-ago levels, due in part to costs associated with going public over the summer, as well as the scaling up of the tokenization business at an active time for the entire sector, Securitize CEO Carlos Domingo told CNBC in an exclusive interview.

Securitize reinforced "certain areas of the company like finance, compliance, legal [and] cybersecurity," which increased corporate costs "compared to a year ago when we were privately held," Domingo said. "We're in in a very good position. The adjusted EBITDA … is improving significantly from previous quarters."

Securitize reported an adjusted EBITDA loss of $2 million, compared with positive adjusted EBITDA of $3.6 million a year ago, better than a $5.5 million loss in the second quarter. The company posted a 183% increase in operating costs and expenses.

Also on Monday, the Securitize board authorized a $50 million share buyback and announced the acquisition of River One, an institutional asset-backed financing platform developing technology to connect stablecoin capital with traditional lending markets. Terms were not disclosed.

Securitize sees an opportunity to modernize the $9 trillion market for asset backed finance by using stablecoins to finance real world assets, generate yield and tokenize investment positions and credit products, Domingo said.The acquisition also marks an expansion beyond Securitize's core niche markets at a time when tokenization's competitive landscape is growing, with traditional asset managers like BlackRock and Franklin Templeton, and established financial market infrastructure providers like DTCC and Broadridge, entering the industry.

"We have been very active in tokenized funds, treasuries [and] yield … And we've been obviously recently very active in tokenized stocks, so this adds another piece of the puzzle in the emerging tokenization space for us to capture revenue growth."

#2839. Grading the Mavericks: Dallas’ accountability helped prevent a serious fall

The Mavericks went 4-2 over the last two weeks and sit at 11-7, in eighth place in the West. They lost back-to-back road games to Cleveland (127-117) and Boston (131-94), but rebounded with four straight wins against Golden State (116-94), the Clippers (110-100), Utah (116-114), and Denver (120-101). Cooper Flagg led the team in scoring with 23.7 points per game.

The Mavericks did not start the last two weeks well. Losing back-to-back road games in embarrassing fashion, then giving a suboptimal performance against a really hurt Golden State team was pretty dire, despite the large margin of victory. The three games since have been pretty convincing; the Mavericks are a good team somewhere in the realm of "better than bad, not elite, but can win on any night".

We have seen the emergence, or more accurately, the rebirth of Caleb Martin in the last six games. He is scoring over 10 points per game, shooting 56.5 percent from three, and grabbing 2.3 steals per game over that stretch. Martin is the true definition of a glue guy and has held the team together in their four-game win streak.

The win against Denver was incredible. It was an utterly dominant defensive performance. It is the type of win you have to build off of and refuse to let the train slow down. It was also Dallas' third NBA Cup victory, meaning if they beat Phoenix on Friday, they will win their group.

Dallas' two losses that applied to this round's grades were part of a three-game skid that lacked effort in every sense of the word. Losing to a Cleveland team that sat all of their starters after travel issues was bad, but going into Boston the next day and losing the game in roughly six minutes (after Dallas went down 24-4) was a true wake-up call. Cooper Flagg said after the loss: "I don't think we competed at a high enough level, you know, throughout the three games".

Every viewer noticed that, but having a guy in the fire acknowledge their shortcomings showed they could get through the adversity. And they did, to the tune of four straight wins. Even after the third victory in Utah, where they squandered a 17-point lead in three-and-a-half minutes, Kyrie Irving held the team, including the coaches, after practice to run in preparation for their game in Denver's altitude. It paid off with a 19-point road victory.

That is the sign of a good team. Being able to have honest conversations about your play and notice when things need to change is a key component of success. The Mavericks clearly have that. There will be more adversity and plenty more losses to come this season. If the Mavericks can lean on this framework, they will be solid, no matter what happens.

The Mavericks already have a weird roster, but the player that sticks out the most is Naji Marshall. He is not a good enough defender to justify the offensive dominance, and he turns the ball over far too much to be handling the ball at the rate he does. Part of his 20 percent usage rate is the fact that the roster is lacking ball handlers, but some of it, and perhaps the most frustrating part, is that he simply chooses to play hero ball far too often.

It's not clear when you look at his 10.9 points in 24.1 minutes per game. And sometimes he does play well enough to matter. But it's the choice to keep a dribble handoff, or the pass that he forces in transition, or the insistence on taking floaters and shrinking the floor that really hurts the team. The extension Dallas signed him to already feels cumbersome, and I expect the best version of this team to not have him on the floor. Whether that is because he is benched or traded away, I am not sure.

Maybe we have been spoiled by the likes of Luka Doncic and Cooper Flagg, or it's the guys picked behind him playing well, but Johnson Jr., the ninth overall pick in this past draft, has felt overwhelmingly underwhelming. His athleticism does not jump off the screen a lot of the time, his offensive awareness is sketchy, and he fouls a bit too much to stay in the game consistently. That being said, he has shown flashes of being a really good glue piece to a great defensive team.

One of these came against Dallas' statement win in Denver, where he scored nine points and had a team-high 10 rebounds. He played excellent defense, had a monster dunk, moved his feet incredibly well, and impacted winning on all fronts. It is this type of game that makes you wonder why he can't do this all the time. Some of it may be physical, with the shin splints still affecting him. A lot of it is probably mental. But either way, although the consistency isn't there yet, you can see the vision finally.

#2837. Wealthy Europeans look beyond stocks amid AI selloff. Here’s where they’re investing

Wealthy Europeans are looking to alternative asset classes to build exposure to artificial intelligence themes amid turbulence in public markets.

Goldman Sachs Alternatives' inaugural survey of high-net-worth and ultra-high-net-worth investors found 47% of European respondents saw alternatives as the best way to gain exposure to AI and future tech growth, compared to just 24% of U.S. investors.

The survey found a significant gap between the U.S. and Europe in terms of investor knowledge of alternatives, which include assets like private equity, property and infrastructure. Goldman said 82% of European respondents are familiar with the alternative investments market — compared to 50% of U.S. investors.

Goldman polled 1,000 investors with at least 1 million in investable assets in their local currency across the U.K., France, Germany, Italy and Switzerland. The survey was carried out between June 29 and Aug. 18 this year.

The report on the findings, published Wednesday, did not specify the proportion of respondents who already have a stake in some kind of alternative investment — but wealthy Europeans appeared particularly bullish on the space.

Private equity made up the largest proportion of current alternatives holdings. Among wealthy Europeans with alternatives exposure, 62% said they invested in private equity. The second most commonly held asset class was private real estate, which was backed by 51% of European alternatives investors. Hedge funds were held by 37% of European alternatives owners, and private infrastructure was held by 30%.

One in four respondents who did not already own an alternative investment said they were likely to invest in the market in the coming 12 months. Among those already in the space, 26% said they were likely to increase their allocations over the next year, while just 5% said they planned to decrease their exposure.

Of the European investors who already owned alternatives, 54% said their assets had performed as expected, while 44% said their assets had exceeded their expectations to the upside. Only 2% said their alternative investments had performed worse than expected.

"Recent reforms gave individual investors unprecedented access to alternative asset classes like private equity, venture capital, and private credit," Kyle Kniffen, global head of alternatives for third-party wealth at Goldman Sachs Asset Management, said in Wednesday's report.

He added that wealthy investors "look ready to jump at the opportunity."

"Our survey shows satisfaction among current alts owners is high and adoption looks set to increase," Kniffen said.

Alternative investments have increasingly become a staple of high-net-worth individuals' investment portfolios.

Over the past year, JPMorgan Asset Management's private wealth alternative assets in the Asia-Pacific region have jumped 40%, while BNY Wealth says alternative investments now account for 60% of single-family office portfolios — recently surpassing traditional assets for the first time.

But investing in alternatives carries risks. Private equity, for example, can lock up capital for long periods, and although the number of exits ticked slightly higher last year, the value of those deals fell.

Concerns about private credit, meanwhile, have dominated headlines, with JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon warning on Oct. 14, 2025, that "cockroaches" were likely to be lurking in private markets.

— CNBC's Lee Ying Shan contributed to this article.

Veteran quarterback Aaron Rodgers passed through waivers Thursday and was not claimed. He is now officially a free agent after going unclaimed on waivers and is free to sign with any team.

The soon-to-be 43-year-old is now a free agent. Rodgers could land with a team that has quarterback injury problems or is right on the playoff bubble, but his conduct on Wednesday reportedly means that his options might be even more limited.

Rodgers may have played the final game of his illustrious career, but his tenure with the Steelers will almost assuredly be remembered for his rant on Wednesday.

#2833. ‘Ready for any storm’: UAE minister optimistic on economy as IMF lifts forecast

The UAE is "very optimistic" about achieving 7%-8% growth next year, the country's economy and tourism minister Abdulla bin Touq Al Marri told CNBC after the latest data from the International Monetary Fund showed the country would avoid a recession in 2026.

The IMF last week revised the UAE's real GDP forecast to 0.2% growth in 2026 from a 3.9% contraction predicted a month ago. "The UAE is coming back, and that adjustment within one month shows that there is a huge potential aspect when it comes towards the end of the year," the minister told CNBC's Dan Murphy.

He said the tourism industry was already picking up with occupancy rates returning to "almost near normal" and international carriers including British Airways and Air France rerouting flights to the UAE. The minister expects economic growth to be higher than 0.2% this year.

The Iran war has disrupted economic activity in the UAE, with missile and drone attacks from Tehran and maritime disruptions weighing on energy trade, tourism, aviation and private-sector confidence.

Earlier this month, U.S. President Donald Trump said that renewed attacks on Iran were "highly unlikely" if negotiations produce a "very strong agreement." However, on Monday, Trump threatened that Tehran could face fresh U.S. strikes next year if the two countries failed to strike a deal, as per Fox News.

"We can we cannot promise the world for any storms that will land on our shore, but we can always promise that the UAE's economy is ready for any storm," Al Marri said.

He added that next year the UAE's economy will have a "different" model than the one before the conflict and investments will be focused on building factories and "things that we really need in times of crisis."

The World Bank in October said it expects the UAE's economy to recover next year, driven by rising oil production and exports and a rebound in tourism, trade, transportation, financial services, and construction.

It warned that the improvement in economic activity in the UAE largely depends on the duration and intensity of the Iran war, with a faster de-escalation likely to accelerate the recovery in services exports and private-sector activity.

#2830. Norse Atlantic suspends all flights, warns it may file for bankruptcy after share price collapse

Norse Atlantic suspended all of its flights on Thursday and warned it may have to file for bankruptcy after its stock collapsed on Wednesday following its warning about its "critical" financial situation.

Oslo-listed shares of Norse closed 85% lower on Wednesday.

"The board of directors continues to consider options to secure short-term financing," Norse said in a Thursday statement. "If a short-term financing solution is not secured urgently, it is the board's intention to file for bankruptcy."

The airline added that "there can be no assurance that a viable solution will be found."

Checks by CNBC showed the airline was still selling tickets for flights on Friday and beyond as of 9 a.m. Oslo time on Thursday.

Warning signs first popped up when PK786 from London to Islamabad and PK710 from Manchester to Lahore were cancelled because of "an unexpected operational suspension," the Pakistani flag carrier said on X.

The airline had been set to operate two Pakistan International Airlines flights Wednesday under a wet-lease agreement, in which one airline provides the aircraft and crew to another. The agreement had only been signed in early October.

PIA said it would operate the routes using its own Boeing 777 aircraft from the next day.

Norse's own flight Z0 783 from London Gatwick to Orlando was also shown as canceled Wednesday on live air traffic website Flightradar24. London Gatwick's website listed the flight's status for Thursday as "enquire airline."

In a bid to stave off financial troubles, Norse cut 75 jobs in May as part of an effort to reduce costs by $50 million, after Eivind Roald replaced founder Bjorn Tore Larsen as CEO in November last year.

The Norwegian carrier said Wednesday that its situation depended on securing financing for short-term liquidity needs and that it was in discussions about a potential strategic takeover.

"Norse is also engaged in discussions with selected parties on short term financing, however, there can be no assurances that such discussions will result in a viable solution," the airline said.

The Norwegian carrier has come under strain due to soaring jet fuel costs since the onset of the Iran war.

India's largest airline, low-cost carrier IndiGo, entered an agreement with Norse Atlantic in early 2025 to lease six 787-9 aircraft as it launched flights to Europe and Britain ahead of the arrival of its own widebody planes.

The agreement concluded at the end of October this year, with IndiGo citing airspace constraints, elevated fuel costs and currency pressures.

At its peak in 2024, Norse Atlantic had 4,822 scheduled flights. That number dipped to 4,695 in 2025 and 2,565 in 2026, according to aviation analytics company Cirium. The airline had 122 flights scheduled for November this year.

Norse Atlantic CEO Roald told CNBC in May that he was not "overly concerned" about access to fuel and said the airline had no indication at the time that the crisis would have an immediate impact. The airline said in October that it was continuing to operate at reduced capacity because of "prolonged high fuel prices."

#2829. ‘Your booth is waiting’: Denny’s welcomes Jensen Huang back as Nvidia CEO

Jensen Huang is back at the helm of Nvidia — and Denny's has a booth waiting for him.

The American diner chain welcomed the billionaire's return as Nvidia CEO by revealing that it had reinstated a commemorative plaque marking the birthplace of the artificial intelligence chip giant after learning of its removal on Nov. 13.

"Some things you just don't take off the menu. Jensen Huang is one of them," Denny's said in a post on X.

The plaque marks the booth at a Denny's restaurant in Silicon Valley, California, where Huang and his co-founders discussed the idea for Nvidia, which was founded in 1993.

The restaurant chain said it learned on Nov. 13, a day after Huang's resignation, that the plaque had been removed.

"We put the plaque right back up where it belongs," Denny's said, without specifying who had removed it or why.

Huang's ties to the diner chain, however, stretch back well before Nvidia's founding. He worked at Denny's as a teenager, washing dishes and serving customers before going on to build one of the world's most valuable companies.

The restaurant chain also disclosed that it had contacted Nvidia's communications team on Nov. 10 to express its pride in their shared history.

Huang's return came less than two weeks after his sudden resignation rattled investors and raised questions about corporate governance and succession planning at the chipmaker.

While his return has put those issues in the spotlight, Denny's offered a simpler message to its former employee.

"Jensen, your booth is waiting and the coffee's on. We're always open, 24/7," the restaurant chain said.

#2828. Hull City unlikely to keep Vaz beyond January

From a future investment to a potential transfer problem: Robinio Vaz's time away from Roma risks ending sooner than expected.

The French striker, who moved to Hull City during the final days of the summer transfer window, has failed to establish a significant role in the English side.

According to Tuttomercatoweb.com, the Premier League club is even considering terminating his loan deal early.

Roma acquired Robinio Vaz from Marseille last January for approximately €25 million, banking on the qualities of the 2007-born striker, considered an interesting prospect.

The deal was designed with the player's future development in mind, but the size of the investment also suggested a potential immediate contribution.

In the second half of the season, however, the Frenchman failed to convince Gian Piero Gasperini, finding very few opportunities to shine. After spending the summer in Rome, the club therefore chose to send him out on loan to help him develop through increased use.

The agreement with Hull City included a €2 million loan with a €30 million option to buy, a deal that could have guaranteed Roma a significant financial return in the event of positive performances. However, things aren't going as expected.

Vaz continues to find little playing time, and the English club isn't reportedly considering a permanent purchase of the player.

Instead, the possibility of terminating the deal during the next transfer window has emerged, potentially returning the striker to the Giallorossi early.

Roma is also reportedly dissatisfied with the situation, especially since the lack of playing time risks further slowing the young Frenchman's development and compromising his value.

The initial goal of the loan was to allow Vaz to gain experience and demonstrate his qualities more consistently, but so far the move to England hasn't yielded the desired results.

#2827. James Cook touchdown gives Bills 7-0 lead over Chiefs

There is some nasty weather in Western New York on Thanksgiving night.

The Bills have at least scored one early in the second quarter, with James Cook going in for a 5-yard score.

It took Buffalo 11 plays to go 49 yards, with the team getting great field positions as a result of one play on special teams.

Chiefs returner Josh Downs let a punt fall and roll instead of fielding it in his team's territory, which led the offense to start its second drive at the 4-yard line. Kansas City then went three-and-out, and the punt went out of bounds at the Kansas City 49.

The Bills only needed to convert one third down on their ensuing drive, with Josh Allen hitting Khaliil Shakir for a 17-yard pass on third-and-6.

While Buffalo got down to the 1-yard line, a false start backed them up. but Cook then erased that with his touchdown run.

In three drives, Cook has 42 yards on 13 carries with one touchdown. Allen is just 3-of-6 passing for 30 yards.

#2826. 'All about giving': Why the Lakers' Ziaire Williams enjoys giving back

As the gathering of kids began, their eyes grew wide and several of them said "oooh" when they saw the tall, slender young man with the stylish dreads approach the microphone and introduce himself as Lakers forward Ziaire Williams.

Williams had come to Inglewood High to provide meals and fellowship with about 150 kids from the Boys & Girls Clubs of Metro Los Angeles, an event he has done for his entire six-year NBA career.

Having grown up in Lancaster and attended Sierra Canyon, where he was a high school teammate of Bronny James, Williams saw himself in those kids. He, too, went to the Boys & Girls Club while a youth. He remembers the influence it made on his life and how his parents, Ziaire Williams Sr. and Marquita Fields-Williams, felt at ease because their son was safe.

Williams, who held the event last week, believes it is important to be active in the community.

"Being a part of a Thanksgiving event like this means a lot to me," he told the kids. "I appreciate all of you guys coming out to support the event. This is a time of giving and Thanksgiving. It's just all about giving back and being appreciative for your loved ones and all the small things in life.

"So, I hope you guys can meet some new friends, eat some good food, and just appreciate the small things in life. That's what it's all about."

Williams then helped to serve the food, a smile on his face, "joy" in his heart to see the kids enjoying the moment and each other, all of them relishing the opportunity to meet a Laker in person.

"I've actually been doing this every year since I've been in the NBA," Williams said. "Growing up, I was in the Boys & Girls Club. My parents were always at work. The Boys & Girls Club, it was almost like my second home growing up. It's just a great safe place after school just to hang out, do your homework, meet some new friends and occasionally Christmas, Thanksgiving, hopefully have a good meal, maybe a pizza party or something.

"So, since I've been in the NBA, I always try to just find different Boys & Girls Clubs I can partner with for just the holidays and seasons of giving. Now, just do my part to give back, give them something to smile about and, you can't go wrong with a good meal."

Initially, some of the kids looked nervous and shy when they walked by Williams.

But he greeted them all, shook hands, took pictures and listened to their stories.

This was their day and Williams was happy to be a meaningful part of it.

"Oh man, there's no words like it, man. It's hard to describe. It just makes my heart feel warm," Williams said. "I feel like God gave me this amazing ability to play basketball, but he also has allowed me to use my talents to do events like this and give back.

"And, man, it's amazing. Every time I just get to hang out with kids and just see a smile on their face, it really just brings me back to when I was their age, and it's amazing, man. There's no words that can describe it."

Lakers forward Ziaire Williams dunks over Trail Blazers guard Scoot Henderson during a game earlier this month at Crypto.com Arena. (Gina Ferazzi / Los Angeles Times)

By most accounts, the 6-foot-9 Williams, 25, is having his best season as a pro.

He's averaging 9.1 points per game and shooting career bests from the field (53.8%) and three-point range (42.1%).

"Man, I would just say I just stuck with it. Just the same consistent work," Williams said of his success. "Sometimes it doesn't always pay off right away, but if you just keep sticking with it, keep being disciplined, your daily habits, it's bound to change quick. As the late [rapper] Nipsey Hussle always says, just never quit.

"Just the marathon always continues, and that's a principle and a moral I live by, just continuing to always try to be the best version of myself every day. And I'm just grateful to be in this position. I'm on a great team, a winning team, guys who care about the game and guys who want to compete at the highest level. And it's been an honor to play with the Lakers so far, and we still got a lot more work to do, but it's been a great start for sure."

Whether starting or coming off the bench, Williams has delivered by being the quintessential three-and D player the Lakers expected.

Before the Lakers signed Williams to a one-year, $3-million contract during free agency over the summer, they saw something else in him that made them yearn to have him as a member of their team.

"He's a beautiful human," Lakers coach JJ Redick said. "I didn't know him. We set up a workout for him in Vegas and he worked out. Rave reviews. I met with him the next day for about 45 minutes at our hotel and I was like, 'I got to get this guy on my team. Regardless of the player, I got to get this person on my team.' We sat there for 45 minutes and he looks you in the eye and it's 'yes sir, no sir. I got you, sir.' He's awesome. He's an incredible human."

Lakers coach JJ Redick congratulates forward Ziaire Williams along the sideline as he comes off the court for a timeout. (Gina Ferazzi / Los Angeles Times)

Both of Williams' parents were in the military and he was taught to be respectful of others.

So, what Redick saw and felt was real, because Williams was raised that way.

"Yeah, it was definitely strict, but I'm thankful for it," Williams said. "Just the discipline and just prioritizing certain things. It was never hard for me to do because I just grew up with that discipline always from Day 1. So, it was definitely hard. I got yelled at. I got my butt whipped a couple times. It was all for the greater good. My parents wanted me to just be the best young man I could possibly be and put myself in a better position than they were in."

He remembers going to LeBron James' basketball camp in San Diego and winning the MVP award. That "was the coolest thing ever" to meet James. He remembers watching NBA games on TV and thinking how they "seemed like superheroes."

Now Williams is playing against James and those players he saw on TV.

But when he does his basketball camps and his Thanksgiving events as he did last week, he doesn't want the kids to view him as anything more than a humble person.

"I don't really want them to necessarily look at me as a superhero, but more so as just a person who's always willing to give back," Williams said. "I tie my shoes just the same way they do, you know? Every morning I just wake up and I thank God and I just try to be the best version of myself.

"That's what I just hope these kids get out of it is just whatever you put your mind to is possible. You just have to really believe in it and work at your craft every day. And I work on my craft every day and now it's got me here with the Lakers."

#2825. 2026 Week 13 American Conference Previews and Predictions

The final week of the regular season here, and the American Conference championship race still has nine of 14 teams technically alive.

UTSA (9-2, 6-1 American) is the only team that controls its own destiny for the championship, and the Roadrunners can secure hosting duties with a win over Tulsa on Black Friday. Memphis (8-3, 5-2 American), North Texas (7-4. 5-2 American), and East Carolina (7-4, 5-2 American) are currently tied for second place, and since all three teams did not play each other, a three-way tiebreaker would be determined by computer rankings. Thus, UTSA is the only team that controls its own destiny for the championship.

If Memphis, North Texas, and East Carolina all lose, that opens the door for five three-loss teams — Army (5-5, 4-3 American), Tulsa (7-4, 4-3 American), Florida Atlantic (7-4, 4-3 American), Tulane (6-5, 4-3 American), and UAB (6-5, 4-3 American).

Six of the seven Week 13 matchups feature teams still mathmetically alive for the title game. Here's a preview of the final week of American play:

Tulsa (7-4, 4-3 American) enters as a slight road favorite, and that's a testament to how the Golden Hurricane have played lately. Tre Lamb's team has won three consecutive matchups, defeating Tulane by 50, Florida Atlantic by 17, and Charlotte by 28, finding an offensive rhythm down the stretch of November. Quarterback Baylor Hayes has registered the highest, second-highest, and fourth-highest passing totals of his college career during this three-game win streak, accounting for 11 total touchdowns during the span. Wide receiver Oran Singleton Jr. is also emerging as a star, and he's on the precipice of a 1,000-yard season coming off his second 100+ yard, 3-touchdown outing of November. The Golden Hurricane defense, which famously stonewalled Oklahoma State in Week 1, has also returned as Tulsa is only allowed 15.0 points per game during this win streak. Also, no American team has decisively defeated — all three conference defeats were all by one score, and the Golden Hurricane led by double-digits in two of them.

UTSA (9-2, 6-1 American) may be the underdog, but history suggests it's dangerous to doubt Jeff Traylor in the Alamodome. The head coach is 28-1 at home against conference opponents, most recently upsetting North Texas in 35-16 fashion. UTSA will look for an offensive resurgence after scoring just 19 points against UAB last week. The status of A'Marion Peterson, who averages 8.3 yards per carry and ranks fifth nationally with 16 rushing touchdowns, is unknown, but the Roadrunners still field strong running back depth with Will Henderson III and Brandon High Jr. UTSA also looks for a strong performance from Owen McCown, who will be recognized on senior day after serving three years as the starting quarterback. UTSA's defense has been quite volatile this season, surrendering 60 to Florida Atlantic but holding North Texas to as few as 16. The Roadrunners generate frequent takeaways but often struggle generating pressure, ranking 15th-to-last nationally in sacks.

Temple (2-9, 1-6 American) owns the longest losing streak in the American. The Owls dropped their sixth straight game against Rice, squandering a 10-point lead in the final two minutes of regulation. That wasn't the first time Temple lost after holding a double-digit lead after the two-minute timeout either, in a year defined by crunch time struggles. One of the few bright spots in an otherwise-lost season is the play of outside linebacker Curly Ordonez, whose 111 tackles rank fourth nationally. But the Owls will need to step up in other areas defensively against this explosive Memphis offense, especially after allowing north of 30 points in five of their last six. Offensively, Temple relies heavier on the run game. Keveun Mason is coming off his highest rushing output against an FBS opponent this season, producing 98 yards against Rice. Temple ranks 97th in scoring offense but could find a spark against a Memphis defense that has surrendered 38+ points in two consecutive contests.

Memphis (8-3, 5-2 American) likely remains in control of its own destiny to qualify for the American Championship Game, given its spot above North Texas and East Carolina in the computer rankings the conference uses to settle tiebreakers (a composite of SP+, SportSource TR116 TSR, ESPN SOR, and KPI). The Tigers are coming off a tough loss, however, surrendering a fourth down in the final seconds against Navy to fall 38-34. Still, the Tigers field one of the nation's top offenses, ranking first in yards per game and ninth in scoring. The unit is balanced and explosive, as Marcus Stokes ranks eighth in the FBS in passing, while Jaylin Carter ranks ninth nationally in rushing. Memphis ranks atop the FBS in 50, 60, and 70-yard plays, proving the ability to score from anywhere on the field. But to make its first conference title game since 2019, improvement will be need to seen defensively. The Tigers are 111th in total defense, most recently allowing 41 points to South Florida and 38 to Navy, struggling particularly with quarterback mobility.

Navy (4-6, 3-4 American) registered a very on-brand win last week. For the third consecutive year, the Midshipmen played the role of spoiler, unseating a ranked team despite entering the matchup unranked. Even though Navy won't qualify for bowl eligibility for the first time since 2023, the team remains dangerous thanks to the dominance of Jackson Gutierrez. The mobile quarterback ranks first nationally with 140.5 rushing yards per game, and he enters this Charlotte matchup coming off his third performance with at least 220 rushing yards and two touchdowns this season. Thanks to Gutierrez's mobility, Navy has scored at least 34 points in each of its last five conference matchups. But the Midshipmen aren't as sturdy on defense as they've been in the previous two seasons, surrendering at least 34 points in five consecutive matchups. Linebackers Coleman Cauley and MarcAnthony Parker will lead the charge defensively as Navy aims to extend its winning streak to three prior to the Army-Navy Game.

Charlotte (1-10, 1-6 American) can improve upon last year's record with a win on senior day. The 49ers have endured a difficult season, but they've demonstrated progress in recent weeks, defeating Temple on Oct. 17, taking Tulane to overtime on Oct. 30, and falling by one point to East Carolina on Nov. 14. Charlotte is at its best when Conner Harrell is at his best, but the team will also need to pick up its 122nd-ranked run game heading into the finale. The 49ers' defense was at its best in early November, holding ECU to 17 points and UAB to 23, but the unit took a step back last weekend. The unit, led by middle linebacker Gavin Willis, will be tested with a high-powered run game, hoping its 113th-ranked run defense can provide enough stops to upset the Midshipmen.

Florida Atlantic (7-4, 4-3 American) offers the superior offense in this matchup. The Owls rank 11th nationally with 38.0 points per game, fielding the nation's 14th-best total offense and 3rd-best passing offense. Zach Kittley's air raid offense has thrived this year, largely due to the connection between Caden Veltkamp and Easton Messer. Veltkamp, the nation's leader in touchdown passes with 33, has eclipsed 300 passing yards in six of seven conference matchups — and the other was a 60-29 win over Florida Atlantic where the run game thrived. Meanwhile, Messer is the FBS receptions leader, ranking seventh in yards and second in touchdowns. Kelby Valsin also has over 1,000 receiving yards in this offense that often substitutes the run game for quick throws. The Owls defense has been a concern for much of the year, ranking third-to-last in the country in yards allowed per game. However, the unit has improved in recent weeks, limiting UTSA to 29 and South Florida to 14. Takeaways have fueled that, and FAU has come up with seven in its last three outings.

East Carolia (7-4, 4-3 American) offers the superior defense in this matchup. The Pirates ride a four-game win streak, and they haven't surrendered more than 17 points during that timeframe, most recently stifling Army in a 10-6 decision. The Pirates are the ultimate backfield invaders, ranking first in the FBS in tackles for loss with 9.2 per game, and Kieran Davis leads the team with 12. ECU will need to rely more on the passing defense against Florida Atlantic, and that unit has been stellar too. The Pirates surrender 182 passing yards per game, and they've recorded more interceptions (11) than they have allowed passing touchdowns (8). But to compete with Florida Atlantic, ECU will need to unleash more of an offense that hasn't scored more than 20 during its four-game win streak. The main source of offense is a ground game led by TJ Engleman Jr., who is coming off his sixth 100-yard performance in his last eight games.

Prediction: Florida Atlantic 28, East Carolina 16

Army (5-5, 4-3 American) must win this week to secure bowl eligibility and reach the six-win mark for the 10th time in 11 years under Jeff Monken. The Black Knights were in excellent position for their second American championship in three years several weeks ago, but they've dropped three consecutive matchups — two by one score. Close games have been a theme for Army, which has competed in 13 one-score games across its last 13 FBS matchups. Monken's No. 2 ranked rushing offense is led by quarterback Cale Hellums, who is 30 yards away from his second straight 1,000-yard season. Additionally, running back Godspower Nwawuihe has provided a boost to the option attack lately, producing two 100-yard games in late October. However, Army has been burdened by miscues lately, committing four of its six turnovers this season in the last three weeks. The Black Knights aim to improve ball security as well as defense that ranks 97th against the run, allowing over 5.1 yards per carry.

Rice (2-9, 1-6 American) counters Army with an option attack of its own, although the scheme is different. The Owls are coming off their first FBS win of 2026, and it was a triumphant yet unorthodox one. Rice deployed three different quarterbacks during a late double-digit comeback at Temple, utilizing Gael Ochoa as the primary option, Jacurri Brown as the short-yardage specialist, and Patrick Crayton Jr. as the long-distance passing threat. The strategy worked, and Rice's offense was at its best under the atypical arrangement. Thus, anything is on the table for the Owls in their season finale. While Scott Abell's team was a strong finisher against Temple, the team is typically a strong starter, especially on defense where it hasn't allowed more than 10 first half points since Oct. 24.

Saturday, Nov. 28 at 3:30 p.m. ET (ESPN+)

Tulane (6-5, 4-3 American) clinched bowl eligibility for a fifth straight season last week, storming back from a 10-point fourth quarter deficit to upset North Texas. While mathematically alive, the Green Wave likely will not qualify for their fifth conference championship in five years, but they've saved their best for the elite teams in the conference, knocking off both Memphis and North Texas. True freshman Trace Johnson started both of those victories, and he's showing signs of development, producing the best performance of his career with 283 yards and four touchdown deliveries last week. Tulane also provides firepower in the run game with a deep running back corps of Jaylin Lucas, Maurice Turner, Johnnie Daniels, and Jamauri McClure — and three of those tailbacks have exceed 100 rushing yards this year. While the Green Wave thrive on the ground, their opponents do the same. Tulane ranks second-to-last nationally in run defense, surrendering over 223 yards per game.

South Florida (6-5, 2-5 American) was the only team in the American to sweep its non-conference slate, but the Bulls have struggled mightily against their conference peers. USF enters its final home game at Raymond James Stadium riding a three-game losing streak, suffering close defeats to East Carolina and Memphis before a multifaceted struggle at Florida Atlantic. The Bulls' defense has been respectable for most of the season, ranking 35th in fewest points allowed per game. But the team will need more offense to secure its fourth consecutive winning season. Two weeks ago, USF had its best offensive showing of the season against Memphis when quarterback Luke Kromenhoek threw for 271 yards and rushed for 146. After parting ways with offensive coordinator Tim Beck this week, the Bulls look to unearth that version of Kromenhoek one final time before leaving Raymond James Stadium.

UAB (6-5, 4-3 American) enjoyed one of the most successful rebuilding efforts in the American this year, locking up bowl eligibility in the first full season under head coach Alex Mortensen. That dramatic improvement can be traced to the defense led by coordinator Todd Grantham. Last season, UAB ranked second-to-last in scoring defense. This year, the Blazers are 47th in scoring defense, 20th in total defense, and first in passing defense. Edge rusher Marlin Dean, a candidate for the conference's defensive player of the year, has led the charge with 11.5 sacks (third in FBS) and five forced fumbles (first in FBS). The star talent on defense translates to the back end where cornerback Delvon Gulley has deflected a conference-best eight passes while picking off two — including a game-sealing pick-six against East Carolina. The defense provided enough stops to upset conference leader UTSA last week, but ultimately fell 19-17, needing more offensive contributions to win. Running back Rod Robinson II, who has 371 rushing yards and five touchdowns in November, hopes his contributions will be enough at North Texas.

North Texas (6-5, 4-3 American) had the clearest path to the American Championship two weeks ago as the last remaining team with a perfect conference record. In two weeks, the Mean Green's spectacular season was derailed by UTSA, Tulane, and quarterback injuries. Losing starter Tayven Jackson (sixth nationally in passing yards per game) due to an upper body injury was a significant blow, but things went further south for the Mean Green when backup Chris Jimerson Jr. exited last Saturday's contest with an injury, causing the team to finish with wide receiver James Tyre at quarterback. While North Texas' QB situation remains unclear for Saturday, the Mean Green know they can rely on a run game headlined by Jahiem White, who ranks fifth nationally in rushing. A shorthanded North Texas will need any offensive firepower it can get to qualify for a second consecutive championship game. After scoring 45+ points in six consecutive games, Neal Brown's team has been held to 16 and 24 in the past two weeks.

#2823. Lakers, behind Luka Doncic, must crack Wemby code, exploit these areas to beat Spurs

The stars are aligning for a special regular-season game between the Lakers and Spurs on Friday night in San Antonio.

It's two of the NBA's best teams and the Western Conference's top teams matching up for the first time this season, featuring the top early-season MVP candidates in Lakers guard Luka Dončić and Spurs big man Victor Wembanyama.

Luka Doncic of the Los Angeles Lakers shoots a free throw. NBAE via Getty Images

And it's also, essentially, a win-or-go-home NBA Group Play game for West Group C.

For the Lakers, the Spurs will be the biggest test for this still-newish group, with the reigning Western Conference champions equipped to poke the holes that most of the Lakers' previous opponents haven't been able to.

But the Lakers are also equipped to test the Spurs in ways not every team is able to.

And it starts with Dončić — one of the league's best offensive players who can force the Spurs to have to adjust their defensive strategy of keeping Wembanyama around the basket as much as possible.

Even amid a shooting slump, the Slovenian superstar's pull-up shooting and playmaking force defenses to be more aggressive with their coverages when he's the ball handler in pick and rolls.

San Antonio Spurs center Victor Wembanyama walks up the court. AP Photo/Darren Abate

Or even when he's isolating his defender, with opponents often showing proactive help to crowd driving and passing lanes.

If Austin Reaves is available against the Spurs after missing the previous five games due to a bruised left heel, the Spurs won't be able to load up their defense on Dončić in the same way.

The Spurs' defensive scheme allows for their perimeter defenders to be more aggressive with the intent of funneling actions toward Wembanyama, who is the league's best rim protector in large part due to his 7-foot-4 frame.

But the Lakers' use of Dončić starting possessions off the ball before receiving a screen to get the ball can test the Spurs' preference.

Austin Reaves (15) of the Los Angeles Lakers clapping. NBAE via Getty Images

If Wembanyama is too far in a drop and Dončić's defender doesn't stay attached, Dončić has the room he needs to get his shot off.

Wembanyama has the size and agility to play closer to the level of the screen while being in position to recover to protect the rim.

It's a cat-and-mouse game Dončić is just as equipped as any player to win against the Spurs, who once again have one of the league's best defenses.

Another area the Lakers are equipped to exploit is the Spurs' stingy transition defense.

The Spurs are one of the best teams at preventing scoring on fast breaks, but the Lakers are one of the best. They'll have to remain consistent with their throwahead passes without turning the ball over.

And defensively, Walker Kessler empowers the Lakers to prioritize protecting the paint against Wembanyama and forcing the Spurs, who are shooting 33.7% on 3-pointers (No. 25), to beat them with outside shots.

Friday will be a big test for the Lakers.

But they're equipped to come out of the matchup better than expected.

#2822. Switzerland’s biggest bank set for showdown with lawmakers as capital fight intensifies amid crisis planning

UBS's crisis planning has won qualified support from market regulators, which called its plan "executable" in principle. But Switzerland's biggest bank still faces a major fight over sweeping plans that would force it to hold more capital against its foreign subsidiaries.

FINMA, the Swiss markets regulator, said Wednesday that UBS's resolvability — or its ability to fail safely, without wreaking havoc on the economy — has improved since it integrated rival Credit Suisse, with progress made in implementing the emergency plan across group-wide resolution planning.

The preferred resolution strategy — involving plans to allow for recapitalization and restructuring through the use of loss-absorbing bail-in bonds — is "executable," FINMA said. The regulator formally approved UBS's recovery plan for the first time since its ​Credit Suisse integration.

How UBS would withstand a future crisis remains in sharp focus among Swiss authorities ever since the lender's emergency takeover of stricken rival Credit Suisse in 2023.

UBS is now the country's only global systemically important bank, and the Swiss government wants it to hold stronger capital cushions, specifically in relation to its foreign subsidiaries, which would help it withstand another banking collapse.

UBS has pushed back against the overhaul, saying the measures are disproportionate and would damage its international competitiveness, forcing it to hold an extra $16 billion in capital.

A parliamentary showdown now looms, with the National Council, Switzerland's lower house, scheduled to debate the proposal Dec. 16.

On Tuesday, the lower house's economics committee backed plans to force the bank to support its foreign subsidiaries with 90% high-quality core Common Equity Tier 1, or CET1, capital. The Council of States, the country's upper house, approved the 90% plan in September.

The Swiss government had earlier proposed a 100% threshold. UBS wants it to be no more than 50%.

UBS CEO Sergio Ermotti told CNBC in an interview Oct. 28 that 90% would not allow the company to be a "competitive player" long-term. But he would not be drawn on speculation that the measures could push the bank to relocate out of Switzerland.

In a statement, the bank said the economics committee's recommendation would herald further excessive tightening of Swiss capital requirements, "which are already among the most stringent globally."

FINMA said in its Nov. 25 update that the goal is to avoid government solvency support and emergency law.

"The aim is to enable the authorities, in the event of a crisis, to choose the option that offers the best prospects of success in safeguarding financial stability and ensuring the continuation of systemically important functions," the regulator said.

#2820. Ex-Steelers’ Mike Tomlin Gets Brutally Honest About Rodgers-McCarthy ‘Dumpster Fire’

Offering the most unique perspective possible, former Steelers head coach Mike Tomlin spoke open and honestly about what's going on within the franchise he presided over for 19 years.

And to be as candid as possible, the coach turned NBC analyst labeled the current state of the once-proud Pittsburgh Steelers as a "dumpster fire" before finishing his commentary on a 24-hour period thats saw Mike McCarthy bench Aaron Rodgers and then the future Hall of Fame quarterback take the opportunity Pat McAfee provided to unleash on the coach in a way that aired out "dirty laundry" that occurred behind closed doors, leading to his subsequent release.

"I had a range of emotions watching those course of events," Tomlin admitted at halftime of NBC's broadcast of the Kansas City Chiefs at the Buffalo Bills. "To see laundry aired out that way in a public form ran counter to NFL norms."

Tomlin hoped for a better end to a legendary career for Rodgers, the quarterback who led the Steelers to his final playoff game with the franchise last year. He also said he was surprised to see Rodgers reveal information the public wouldn't otherwise know – Rodgers accusing McCarthy of falling asleep in meetings, saying "1-2-3, go Packers!" at halftime and being disinterested in getting to know members of the defense.

"I think the prevailing one is just general sadness – sad that we might be looking at the end of a legendary career, the quarterback, Aaron Rodgers. And just on a macro level, whether it's organizationally or for the game of football at large, to see laundry aired out that way in a public forum – those are things that kinda run counterculture to professional football."

And to top matters off, Tomlin even contradicted what Steelers owner and team president Art Rooney II said about Rodgers. After Rooney II told the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette's Gerry Dulac, the longest tenured Steelers reporter on the beat, that Rodgers was a bad teammate earlier on Thanksgiving Day, Tomlin closed the night by characterizing the 42-year-old quarterback's relationship with his teammates as someone who was "beloved" and stressed he's not exaggerating that compliment.

All in all, Tomlin expressed a sadness most Steelers fans can relate to. But to be fair to McCarthy and all involved, Tomlin did admit it was far from smooth sailing drama wise during his tenure. Tomlin even said as much, placing the "dumpster fire" label on several of the scenarios he dealt with as well.
