#2819. What's ahead for AI financing after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang departs

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's departure hasn't produced a broad shock to the credit market, but it is putting the company's role as a financier of artificial intelligence infrastructure under scrutiny.

Huang, who stepped down Thursday amid an espionage and adultery scandal, built Nvidia into an AI powerhouse in the 33 years since he co-founded the company. Chief financial officer Colette Kress has been named interim CEO as the company searches for a permanent chief executive.

Nvidia not only supplies its graphics processing units to hyperscalers and tech giants, it also provides financing to other companies to help the industry expand. That could all change.

"Although we expect the company to fulfill all of its previously announced commitments, we believe that going forward, it may be more difficult for the company to negotiate new multi-party investments among ecosystem partners at the same scale it has done up to this point," Goldman Sachs analyst James Schneider said in a note Thursday.

The news of Huang's resignation comes after investors were already concerned about the massive amount of debt being taken on to fund AI infrastructure.

Tech bond yields have risen and spreads have widened on credit default swaps, most notably in lower-rated names. Credit default swaps are contracts in which investors pay for protection in case the borrower can't repay its debt. Wider spreads indicate investors view the bonds as riskier.

On Friday, the yield on Nvidia's 4.5% bond due in 2031 sat at 5.717%, nearly 5% higher week to date. Bond yields move inversely to prices.

Tech stocks slumped Friday with the Nasdaq 100 closing down 1.2% as markets continued to digest the Nvidia news. Yields on hyperscaler bonds ticked slightly higher on Friday, signaling the broader concern about AI debt lingers.

It's the smaller AI companies that could ultimately see an impact if Nvidia makes any changes to its AI financing. The company had $36 billion in off-balance-sheet AI cloud agreements, or backstops, for neoclouds, according to its last quarterly financial filing in July.

Neoclouds CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN are all in Nvidia's portfolio. Their shares were down sharply Thursday.

CoreWeave, which has become the poster child for AI debt fears, saw its bond yields retreat after its quarterly earnings on Tuesday eased investor concerns. The yield on its 9.75% bond due in 2031 was 14.79% on Friday after climbing to 16.7% last week. The spread on its five-year CDS also dropped more than 17% week to date, although it remained above 1,000 — which is generally considered a sign of distress.

It remains unclear how Nvidia's support for those companies may change, said CreditSights analyst Andy Li.

"We don't know what the ultimate strategy for Nvidia is going to be coming out the other side," he said.

"However, I think directionally, just given the fact that Jensen was so crucial in selling the Nvidia story and being a very aggressive deal maker, it's likely that a lot of this creative deal-making and circular financing and equity and credit support is going to moderate," he added.

CoreWeave CEO Michael Intrator told CNBC Wednesday, before Huang's departure, that Nvidia "is not one person."

"There are thousands of people over there that interface with thousands of people at my company every day. They integrate on the technology. They integrate on the physical infrastructure. They integrate on the networking," he said in an interview with "Squawk on the Street." "They have been a great partner for us for years. They will continue to be a great partner for us."

Bob Lang, founder and chief strategist at Explosive Options, doesn't see any big changes in terms of Nvidia's relevance or its ability to finance for now. As CFO, Kress was involved in the financing deals, and the search for a permanent CEO is going to take some time, he noted.

The real issue is just how much money the company will want to lend for AI financing, rather than, say using its hundreds of billions in free cash flow for other purposes, like share buybacks, capex, or acquisitions.

"Big companies like Nvidia and Meta, they're holding all the cards," he said. "When they decide that the game is over, that's it — it's going to be curtains for some of these smaller companies."

— CNBC'S Kif Leswing and Isabel O'Brien contributed reporting.

#2818. Bucks vs. Nets Player Grades: Turner, Burries, and rest of team come down to earth in dreadful showing

In what might have been the worst Bucks game I've watched in some time—which is saying something—the Milwaukee Bucks lost to the 3-13 Brooklyn Nets 104-97. It really felt like the Bucks got the monkey off their backs against the Raptors and came into this game without a care in the world. They didn't play as a team, nor did they play with any passion. The worst part is that there aren't going to be many games this season where the Bucks have a genuine 50-50 chance of winning, and for Milwaukee to put up that kind of performance against a Brooklyn team that really tried its hardest to lose was really disappointing. The game also brings the Bucks to 0-3 in the NBA Cup. Read our full summary of the game here and catch a six-minute audio recap on the Bucks+ podcast, Bucks In Six Minutes, below.

37 minutes, 28 points, 3 rebounds, 5 assists, 3 steals, 5 turnovers, 10/20 FG, 3/9 3P, 5/5 FT, 0

I mean, Herro was just about the team's only source of creation, so I do want to credit him for that. Overall, though, this wasn't all that impressive of a game. I didn't think Herro was as willing to get his teammates involved as he had been, settling for a fair few bad shots and dominating the ball too much; granted, he would have had a few more assists if anyone could make a shot, but alas. And then the turnovers, man; most of them felt like killer live-ball giveaways.

18 minutes, 2 points, 3 rebounds, 3 assists, 1 steal, 0 turnovers, 0/7 FG, 0/4 3P, -7

Oof. Really did not like Rollins' game. He made some nice reads to open the third, but overall, most of his shots came after he dribbled the air out of the ball for 10-14 seconds, then settled for step-back threes or wild drives at the rim. It was almost as if Rollins was trying to force his way into a groove, rather than playing instinctively and letting opportunities come to him. Moreover, we can usually rely on Rollins' defence being solid, but even that part of his game felt off; there was one possession in the third where the Bucks had finally taken the lead, were in a groove, and Rollins was guarding someone on the right wing; he was in perfect position to contain the ball, but he lunged for the steal, didn't get it, and his man went right past him, leading to the open three. Absolute coach killer.

31 minutes, 13 points, 3 rebounds, 2 assists, 1 turnover, 5/11 FG, 3/7 3P, -12

Not too many complaints about Kuzma's game. He was just about Milwaukee's only credible defender on Randle, and overall, I thought he did a solid job making the Nets veteran work. Also made some solid reads to get into the paint and then spray out to shooters.

34 minutes, 21 points, 4 rebounds, 4 assists, 2 steals, 9/15 FG, 1/5 3P, 2/4 FT, +5

Jaquez was solid in the middle game and a key part of the Bucks' best runs. He finished well around the rim and got his teammates involved. Still, can't go 1/5 from three when it feels like most of them are wide open. Just can't happen.

25 minutes, 3 points, 6 rebounds, 2 assists, 1 steal, 3 blocks, 3 turnovers, 1/2 FG, 1/2 3P, -1

Obviously, people will look at the scoring numbers, but I would say Turner's lack of production was a byproduct of the Bucks' lack of ball movement. Against the Raptors, the ball was moving, and that's how he got his opportunities; against the Nets, everything was stagnant and slow, so Turner shot just twice. The big man still impacted the game in other ways, but he also had a few backbreaking live-ball turnovers. Overall, it wasn't a good game for Turner by any means, but I thought other factors also contributed to him not playing well.

22 minutes, 13 points, 14 rebounds, 2 assists, 2 blocks, 1 turnover, 6/10 FG, 1/2 3P, -6

On balance, Ware was probably one of Milwaukee's better players. He created extra opportunities, with five of his 14 rebounds coming on the offensive glass, and he would have scored more points if just a few of those tip-ins had gone in. Also, continues to rack up blocks and be a presence around the rim (on both ends). I will say that the Nets were happy to play much higher in their pick-and-roll coverage with Ware in the game because they didn't trust his decision-making with a numbers advantage; he has to improve in that facet of the game.

21 minutes, 3 points, 3 rebounds, 3 assists, 2 turnovers, 1/6 FG, 0/2 3P, 1/2 FT, -4

Burries ended his hot streak with a stinker. He couldn't find the same creases he had been finding (which is weird against one of the league's worst defensive teams), and he also didn't impact in other areas the way he usually does. Burries also made a really odd turnover in the fourth quarter: he caught the ball with no awareness that MPJ was right there and got it ripped away; part of that was on Ware for passing him the ball there, but Burries needs to have better awareness.

21 minutes, 8 points, 3 rebounds, 1 turnover, 4 PF, 3/6 FG, 2/5 3P, 0

I mean, Ament got most of his looks off catch-and-shoot opportunities, but he also got handed a few grenades as the shot clock was winding down. The rook was the third defender (behind Kuzma and Jaquez) on Randle, and despite a major weight disadvantage, he was decent in that matchup; Ament clearly read the scout, forcing him to his right hand and into help as much as possible—good stuff. He had a few possessions where he rotated late from the weak side in help, though.

12 minutes, 4 points, 4 rebounds, 3 assists, 2/7 FG, 0/5 3P, +2

Weird minutes for Jakucionis, who played three minutes in the first half and then was thrown into the fire at the end without really getting a feel for the game. He missed all his threes, but most were the right shots to take (the one bad one being his corner three, where he had Herro wide open for the extra pass up top). Also got baited into a bad foul late as the Bucks were making a charge.

11 minutes, 2 points, 2 assists, 1/2 FG, -6

I don't know. I guess LeVert was fine in his minutes. As I'll get to below, my issue was with how much he played.

This was the first game where I truly felt Jenkins played a key role in the team losing, mainly because of rotations. He opened the second quarter with a Rollins-Green-LeVert-Kuzma-Turner lineup that had a -78.6 net rating in 3:18, with Rollins—who, news flash, has been struggling—being the only creator (and boy did he try to create!). Then, to start the fourth quarter, Jenkins threw out a Jakucionis-Burries-LeVert-Ament-Ware lineup that had a -40.0 net rating in 2:38. One downside to starting all the veterans—a unit that, to their credit, played well together in this one—is that you can eventually get to lineups like these. Granted, I get that with all of this you're robbing Peter to pay Paul to some degree: if you take one guy from one lineup to help another, that original lineup will lose something. Even so, Jenkins can strike a much better balance than he did last night.

DNP-CD: Jericho Sims, Ousmane Dieng, Bogoljub Markovic, Gary Trent Jr.

Inactive: Pete Nance, Cormac Ryan, Kam Jones,

Even the Bucks can get high on their own supply and, dare I say it, disrespect their opponent.

Jenkins: "We abandoned what was working for us in the first half. We didn't have rhythm to our offence. I guess we got bored with the stuff that was working well for us."

Kuzma: "I think we were just thinking for ourselves… How can I get myself going instead of how can I get the team going? That's the story of our season right now."

I can't stress enough how much the Nets tried to give this game to the Bucks. They shot 41.6% from the field and 26.3% from three. Michael Porter Jr. went 4/14, for goodness' sake; you have to win when that happens. It felt like the team entered this game thinking they'd get a win; they were playing a team just as bad, and another win would come easy while they all played for their own numbers.

The Bucks had 14 turnovers for the game, and nine came in the last quarter.

Assistant coach Brad Jones noted at halftime that all 47 of the Bucks' first-half points came after touching the paint in that possession—every one.

I don't get the LeVert minutes sometimes. Like, if he stands out in his first stint, sure, throw him out there for another; but if his first stint doesn't stand out in any way, why put him back in? Surely you'd rather give those minutes to Dieng or even a guard. Sometimes the rotations can feel incredibly random.

#2817. What is ‘texture-maxxing’? The food trend putting crunch on the menu

Texture-maxxing is the latest food trend taking social media by storm as consumers, driven by aesthetics and taste, look for a sensory experience.

British supermarket Waitrose's latest food and drink report highlighted "texture-maxxing" as one of the trends of the year. It describes the phenomenon as a multi-sensory indulgence that is "fuelled by texture-maxxing crunch and intense flavour hits," pushing shoppers to fill their trolleys with crunchy peanut butter, dumplings, and trifles.

"This year, the sound of food went mainstream," Waitrose's Senior Development Chef Will Torrent said in the Wednesday report. "Driven by social media's obsession with audible, multi-sensory cooking, we're creating high-contrast meals that combine shatter-crisp crunch with pillowy chew."

"The emphasis in social media content has flipped from narrative voiceovers to ASMR-inspired audio, where the evocative sounds of food are just as important as the visuals," he added.

Food trends on social media have ranged from the obvious to the absurd. Fibermaxxing and proteinmaxxing have taken off in the past few years. Meanwhile, food and beverages like Dubai chocolate, protein coffee, and ube were some of the big social media hits.

Nestlé's USA 2026 trends found that 75% of Gen Z and 80% of millennials sought out texture in snack cravings with the hashtag "crunchtok," amassing 1.5 billion views.

Waitrose noted that shoppers looking to maximize on texture bought its viral No.1 Alphonso Mango Dessert, which involves "cracking through the crisp shell" to access a "smooth mango mousse and passion fruit curd on a crunchy white chocolate base."

Waitrose's TikTok and Instagram videos of eating the dessert were watched by more than two million people, with a whopping 6,173 hours and 36 minutes of play time on TikTok. Its videos featuring crunchy toast also went viral.

The U.K. grocer's sales of jarred chili crunches, which include crispy rayu oils such as itsu Crispy Chilli Oil, saw a 13-fold jump. Meanwhile, crunchy peanut butter outsold smooth.

Dumplings also had a moment, with sales of chicken gyoza dumplings up 116% this year and searches on waitrose.com for gochujang and peanut butter udon noodles jumped 60%.

"We've seen an explosion in demand as shoppers treat dumplings not just as a quick weeknight bite, but as a total sensory experience," Waitrose's Executive Chef Stephen Parkins-Knight said.

"Driven by the rise of texture-maxxing, people want that ultimate contrast: delicate skins, juicy fillings and crispy skirts, topped with very chilli crunch. With innovation ranging from fusion fillings to rich dipping broths, dumplings have taken a delicious centre stage in 2026," he added.

Texture-maxxing also extended to desserts, as shoppers bought twice as many chocolate trifles compared to 2025, and sales of strawberry trifles increased 160%.

Tiramisu was also popular, with searches for waitrose.com's tiramisu recipe page increasing 155% year-on-year.

#2813. Former Steelers coach Mike Tomlin calls Aaron Rodgers drama a 'dumpster fire'

It may be Thanksgiving. It may be a day removed from Aaron Rodgers' stunning divorce from the Pittsburgh Steelers, who will host the Denver Broncos for the league's now-annual Black Friday game on Nov. 26.

But the four-time NFL MVP and, suddenly, NFL free agent remains at the forefront of the discourse around the league and even the country in the aftermath of his very pointed exposure of Steelers coach Mike McCarthy's alleged issues and why they drove Rodgers to the point of issuing ultimatums and later detailing just about everything that had been occurring in the Pittsburgh locker room in a remarkable break from NFL protocol − and Rodgers' long-held belief that matters that swirl about a football team's inner sanctum should remain private.

But after a little more than 24 hours of pundits, reporters, social media, Rodgers' former teammates and a handful of current ones weighing in on the situation, a man with a perspective as unique and, for the most part, as informed as any shared his thoughts regarding the shocking meltdown that's occurred in the Steel City.

Mike Tomlin, the Steelers' coach for 19 seasons from 2007 through 2025, and perhaps the primary reason Rodgers came to Pittsburgh a year ago, discussed what has happened to the Steelers at halftime of the Kansas City Chiefs-Buffalo Bills game in his current as an analyst for NBC.

Speaking remotely with NBC's NFL play-by-play man, Mike Tirico, Tomlin said he felt a "general sadness" watching the public disintegration of Rodgers' and McCarthy's relationship and the quarterback's abrupt exit from the team.

"Certainly I had a range of emotions watching those course of events yesterday," Tomlin said of Rodgers' interview on "The Pat McAfee Show."

"I think the prevailing one is just general sadness – sad that we might be looking at the end of a legendary career, the quarterback, Aaron Rodgers. And just on a macro level, whether it's organizationally or for the game of football at large, to see laundry aired out that way in a public forum – those are things that kinda run counterculture to professional football."

Tomlin said Rodgers' remarks about McCarthy "certainly did" shock him, "particularly because I know both men involved."

He also characterized Rodgers, despite the scorched earth route he took Wednesday, as a "beloved" teammate.

"I'm not overexaggerating that," Tomlin continued. "He worked at it, and people appreciated his openness to get to know and understand the Steeler culture, to be engaged with teammates."

He also touted Rodgers' patience and outreach to fellow Steelers, especially younger ones.

NATE DAVIS: For Aaron Rodgers, his 'truth' is always worth burning things down

As for McCarthy, Tirico asked Tomlin if his successor can effectively lead the Steelers in the wake of Rodgers' comments.

"It certainly created some challenges, and 'challenges' is probably an understatement if all those things are true," Tomlin said.

"But (McCarthy's) ability to overcome that or inability to overcome that, in my opinion, is based on relationships and the depth of those relationships and how those guys feel about him or how those guys buy into what he's selling.

"It makes you wonder the level of that challenge, but it will be relationship-based − his ability to overcome (this)."

Asked what it was like to see the scrutiny trained on his longtime employer, Tomlin said: "I'm upset about it. It's a dumpster fire. And I don't say that in a judgmental way − I've presided over a few dumpster fires in my 19 years (as coach). But it certainly is upsetting, and I'm sure Steeler Nation is upset."

While questioning McCarthy's dedication and efficacy at his job while speaking to McAfee, Rodgers took the opportunity to praise Tomlin anew. Both he and his former coach had long had mutual admiration before teaming up for the 2025 season. But Tomlin stepped down at the end of the campaign, which ended with a resounding defeat in the wild-card round to the Houston Texans in Pittsburgh. Per reports, Rodgers, who played quite poorly against the Texans, was in tears when Tomlin announced the decision to leave his post following the loss.

"Leader of men, he knew everybody's name, knew where they came from," Rodgers said of Tomlin on Wednesday, a description that also served to distinguish him from McCarthy.

#2812. Is a bottom in for the Nasdaq-100? Charts to watch

(See the video above for Frank's complete chart breakdown.)

Is the Nasdaq-100's recent bounce a sign that the bottom is in? We're going to look at several charts to help answer that question.

First, let's remember how we got here. In September, the NDX broke out from a bullish cup-and-handle pattern, producing a 33,200-upside target. That breakout quickly failed, however, and gave way to a bearish pattern that broke down aggressively two weeks ago.

The decline brought the index relatively close to its 26,350 downside target before the current rebound began.

Zooming out, it's telling to see where the bounce originated. Three important forms of support converged in the 25,000-26,000 area:

This confluence of support helped encourage buying after a roughly 15% decline.

For perspective, we also see what larger drawdowns of 20%, 30%, 40%, and 50% would look like … a lot worse.

The following chart tracks NDX drawdowns from 52-week highs going back to just after the financial crisis. Only a handful of declines exceeded 20%, and three produced relatively quick reversals: late 2018, the Covid lows in 2020 and April 2025.

Historically, buying into declines of approximately 15%–25% has generally paid off, even when additional downside occurred first (yellow highlights).

The chart also highlights previous declines of 10%–16% in green, putting the current pullback into perspective.

The major exception was 2022, when the NDX eventually declined nearly 36% over approximately 10 months ... a much worse outcome, which many investors are concerned could happen again now.

That raises the key question: Are we experiencing another routine correction, or the early stages of a larger bear market?

One important clue will be how far this bounce progresses.

Any rally that fails to reclaim the previous highs could establish a significant lower high. Additional lower highs would provide stronger evidence of a developing, longer downtrend.

We saw this in March 2022, when that first sharp rebound effort failed to reach the previous high before a much more severe decline followed.

The bottom line: The current bounce is encouraging, particularly given where it originated and knowing how well buying prior 10-20% drawdowns has paid off.

From here, it's all about the follow through.  We don't need to see new highs right away, but any rally from here that's met with another wave of strong selling could reignite downside momentum.

#2811. Clippers interim GM given full power to blow up roster at trade deadline

Earlier this week, Marc Stein reported the Clippers are viewed as a "certain seller" with the NBA trade deadline approaching in February.

Jack Fischer of The Stein Line said certain teams have expressed skepticism about what the Clippers might do.

Fischer described the term "skepticism" as "misplaced" and said sources told him that interim general manager Trent Redden has been given the power to make "any moves he sees fit."

Brook Lopez playing in an NBA game for the Clippers against the Mavericks. NBAE via Getty Images

Redden was the same member of the Clippers' front office who finalized the decision to move Kawhi Leonard from Los Angeles to the Raptors over the offseason.

According to Fischer, the Clippers have a few veteran pieces who could be dealt, including center Brook Lopez and wing Derrick Jones Jr.

Fischer added the club wants to assess what its roster will look like with Brandon Ingram staying healthy.

Ingram was acquired in the trade with Toronto for Leonard. He came over to Los Angeles with Gradey Dick, two first-round draft picks, including a first-round pick swap, and two second-round draft picks.

Brandon Ingram making his season debut for the Clippers on Monday night against the Rockets. Getty Images

Ingram missed the first month and a half of the season due to a partially torn Achilles tendon he suffered with the Raptors last season. He made his season debut on Monday.

Ingram was the Clippers' third-leading scorer in their 116-104 loss to Houston on Monday, but he gave the team a glimmering hope about his health. Ingram was on the court for 27 minutes and tallied 16 points, seven rebounds and four assists.

#2810. “Didn’t Play Great”: Josh Allen Doesn’t Hold Back on Criticism for Himself in Bills’ Close Win vs Chiefs

The Buffalo Bills pulled away with a 13-10 victory in a close game against the Kansas City Chiefs. Quarterback Josh Allen is now 6-1 against Chiefs QB Patrick Mahomes in the regular season, and the Bills look like a confirmed pick for the playoffs. Yet, Allen was critical of himself following the victory.

"I have to be better. I need to be better. I will be better," Allen said in the post-game press conference. "Thankful for my team, thankful for my defense, thankful for my kicker, Thankful for James Cook, and our whole linemen man. Like, this took a lot of people, and I made it a little harder on ourselves. You know, I'm gonna put my hand up there, but we found a way to get 10. Well, you can look at it that way; sure. I didn't play great tonight; I didn't play great the last week."

The Bills had a game-sealing 57-yard field goal by Tyler Bass. While the Bills' last touch on the ball defined the game, it was yet another dull performance by Allen, who finished with just 10 of 21 passes for 81 yards and no touchdowns, with the longest pass for 17 yards. He rushed for 43 yards on seven carries, too.

Allen also recorded two interceptions in the red zone while also being sacked twice. His passer rating was a disappointing 18.3.

"So I got to continue to get better and continue to elevate my game and find ways to help this team win because right now, I'm putting us behind the eight ball. You know, two turnovers in the red zone, isn't going to be winning football all the time." Allen said.

Per The Athletic, this was his worst statistical performance since his rookie season. It's not like Allen didn't know what was coming to him. The Chiefs came in allowing the second-fewest points per game at 16.3 this season, and Allen knew he was up for a task.

But he hasn't been at par since last week. Though Allen threw for 304 yards and a touchdown last week in the 26-9 win against the Miami Dolphins, he had two interceptions in that game as well, a sight rarely seen from Allen. His QB rating in that game was only a 31.7. Against the Chiefs, the number was 36.3

However, even after the tough game on Thursday, head coach Joe Brady has the QB's back.

"I'm gonna trust him," the HC said after the game. " … I know that our best version of Josh Allen is still ahead."

The Bills are now 10-1 in the league and have a great chance of securing the AFC's No. 1 seed. They will next play against the New England Patriots.

#2809. Jerry Jones still confident about Cowboys HC Brian Schottenheimer, doesn't expect coaching change after Thanksgiving loss to Eagles

Thanksgiving wound up being a very bad night for Dallas Cowboys head coach Brian Schottenheimer, but it apparently won't cost him his job.

Immediately after the Cowboys' collapse against the Philadelphia Eagles on Thursday, team owner Jerry Jones told reporters he doesn't expect to make a coaching change any time soon. Instead, Jones suggested continuity would give Dallas its best chance in the coming weeks.

Via Nick Harris of the Fort Worth Star-Telegram:

"I wouldn't anticipate that, no, at this juncture. We can give ourselves a better chance to win these coming games and be competitive, in my mind, without coaching changes."

The Cowboys face the Seattle Seahawks in Week 13, then have a bye before facing the Los Angeles Rams on Dec. 20.

Jones went on to say he was still "confident" about Schottenheimer, but made clear that confidence was based on nothing the team showed Thursday:

"Nothing we've seen out here tonight, but you've got to look at everything. That's certainly not the thought on my mind at this particular time. We've got several more games to go and we've got to have our mind on that."

Thanksgiving really was that bad for the Cowboys, who led 28-10 at halftime and held a lead as large as 21 points near the end of the third quarter.

Brian Schottenheimer had a bad Thanksgiving.

The team was then hit with a cascading series of disasters. Former Cowboys backup Joe Milton led the Eagles to touchdowns on three of their next four drives, with the Eagles also returning a blocked punt for a touchdown. The Cowboys still had the advantage in the final minute, but decided to go for it on fourth down in Eagles territory and watched Dak Prescott get sacked.

Eagles kicker Jake Elliott proceeded to make a 59-yard field goal in the final seconds. A Prescott interception ended the game.

Both the overall collapse and late-game decision-making left nearly every finger in Dallas pointing at Schottenheimer, who has been facing the hot seat for some time. He said he wasn't worried about such speculation after the game, via Jon Machota of The Athletic:

"I don't worry about that. I worry about the guys in that locker room. That doesn't affect me."

Schottenheimer's hire was controversial when it was first announced, as he was hardly a popular offensive coordinator under previous head coach Mike McCarthy (who is dealing with issues of his own right now). Jones' decision to promote Schottenheimer demanded trust in his own team's operations, and the results have been a 12-16-1 record.

In more than three decades of owning the Cowboys, Jones has fired only a single head coach during the season: Wade Phillips in 2010. Jones has said he regrets that decision and that could very well be informing his thinking here, though that will hardly protect Schottenheimer in a month and a half.

#2808. Robots could be doing household chores in just 1-2 years, Chinese EV firm says

BEIJING — The household robot could soon become a reality, Brian Gu, co-president of Xpeng, a Chinese electric car company which has entered the humanoids space, told CNBC.

"Maybe after successful deployment into commercial settings, maybe another one to two years, we can start thinking about deploying into home settings," Gu said. "Technology is moving at a much faster clip."

Xpeng revealed its latest general-purpose humanoid robot Iron on Wednesday. The company plans to start training the robot as a store assistant in its retail car locations in the first quarter next year, after starting mass production in January. Sales are set to begin in the second quarter, with deliveries expected later in the year.

Founded in 2014 as an electric car company, Xpeng beat Tesla to rolling out driver-assist in mainland China. The Chinese automaker has launched its own artificial intelligence chips. It's also expanded into personal flying vehicles and robotics. The robotics unit this summer raised $900 million at a $6.3 billion valuation in its first funding round, led by IDG Capital.

Investors, however, appear to be a tad skeptical about the developments at Xpeng, with the downturn in the Chinese auto market also weighing on the company. Xpeng's shares, listed in both New York and Hong Kong, have dropped more than 55% this year amid broad sector declines.

China's humanoid industry has faced more regulatory scrutiny on financing in recent months after Unitree's high-profile IPO and stock slump, as well as a rush of capital into the sector. That's all raised questions about commercialization and the efficacy of the core tech.

Gu said Xpeng's robotics stands out for its rare combination of the hardware, software and real-life use cases. He's expecting to add more investors after Iron's planned commercial launch next year.

"You can always make the head talk, you can always make the leg run, you can always make the hands to do certain tasks," Gu said. "But doing a task while you're walking and answering questions at the same time, that's the most challenging part. And then doing everything well, not falling down, not getting distracted. The model has to work in sync."

Most humanoid robot startups, especially in China, focus on a portion of the tech, such as hands or the artificial intelligence-powered brain. Some in the industry also see themselves as original equipment manufacturers, with another company tying the parts together for the finished robot.

Xpeng's co-founder and CEO He Xiaopeng, a software engineer, always thought that software could solve "everything,'" Gu said. "And after he got into the EV business he realized how hard it is to make hardware ... really do the things that you want to do safely and consistently."

On Wednesday, Xpeng announced its "Turing Physical AI Architecture" for using AI and real-time decision-making tech to control cars and humanoids.

Gu told CNBC that Xpeng's robotics development only needs the driver-assist chips, which the company already has, indicating limited impact from U.S. restrictions on advanced Nvidia chip sales to China.

"Right now we don't see any change to our supply chain, and also ability to have these chips."

In 2023, Xpeng's then-head of autonomous driving, Xinzhou Wu, left to lead Nvidia's automotive chip business.

As Xpeng ramps up its humanoid robotics business, Gu said the company's existing work in autonomous driving technology translates easily to a new product line — with far higher profit margins. "It's much easier to be profitable for the robotics business than the autos business."

Robotics will likely become a meaningful part of Xpeng's business in two to three years, Gu said, with profitability coming as soon as next year. That value will "dramatically" increase with robots entering households, he said.

But Gu noted that compared to commercial environments, homes require robots to act safely around elderly people, children and pets, in addition to reacting to emergency situations. That increases requirements for battery power and performance consistency, he said.

"The main thing Spurs fans are thankful for: we finally have a good team again."

Now we are in November 2026, with Thanksgiving upon us. Time to mention some things I am thankful for, and for this year, a few things which I am not thankful for.

#2805. A trading strategy to ride out the Nvidia uncertainty and generate income in the process

Jensen Huang's abrupt resignation has sent shockwaves through the tech sector, dragging Nvidia's (NVDA) stock down roughly 30% since Oct. 6. The market despises uncertainty, and losing a visionary founder, particularly one without a well-telegraphed succession plan, makes it worse.

However, for opportunistic investors, this panic has made the stock cheaper (obviously) while options have become significantly more expensive. Trading in the $160s, Nvidia's valuation has taken a big haircut, yet its underlying business fundamentals remain largely intact. While Huang was the architect of Nvidia's AI dominance, the company's moat — superior GPUs, the CUDA software ecosystem, and networking expertise — does not walk out the door with him. The company's structural advantage in the global artificial intelligence rollout persists.

Buying good companies at a discount is investing 101, but the current market dynamics may do something else for those who use options.  Huang's departure guarantees that Nvidia will be operating under a cloud of transition for the foreseeable future. Executing a permanent CEO search while navigating global regulatory scrutiny takes time. Consequently, Nvidia's implied volatility (IV)—the market's pricing of expected future price swings — has spiked to highs not seen since the tariff tantrum in the first half of 2025, and this elevated IV is highly likely to persist for several months as the leadership drama slowly unfolds.

This prolonged period of high implied volatility can be a goldmine for option sellers, specifically those executing options overlays such as covered call strategies. When you buy NVDA shares at these depressed levels and simultaneously sell out-of-the-money call options against your position, the premiums you collect are directly tied to IV. Because fear and transition-related uncertainty have dramatically inflated these option prices, the income generated from selling covered calls is now significantly higher than usual.

This lowers the risk profile of holding the stock considerably over time. Consistently collecting these inflated premiums systematically lowers your overall cost basis in the underlying shares. If the stock trades sideways or recovers slowly during the CEO search, you are generating an outsized cash yield on a stagnant asset. If the stock experiences further downside turbulence, the heavy premium income acts as a substantial downside buffer, meaningfully reducing the strategy's overall risk over time.

By deploying a persistent covered call strategy, investors can leverage the exact fear driving the stock down to generate robust, risk-reducing income while maintaining exposure to the undeniable future of AI.

#2803. Trump, NATO chief caution Russia as attacks on Ukraine’s energy infrastructure intensify

U.S. President Donald Trump and NATO chief Mark Rutte issued a joint statement on Thursday urging Russia not to take any actions, intentionally or otherwise, that would further expand the Ukraine war.

The statement comes as Ukraine's allies sound the alarm over Russia's growing threat to European security and just one week after Trump's historic trilateral meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Asia.

Trump and Rutte described their meeting at the Mar-a-Lago club in Palm Beach, Florida on Wednesday as "very impactful," with Russia's nearly five-year-long war in Ukraine and the Iran war among the key topics of conversation.

"We also discussed the importance of Russia avoiding any actions that intentionally, or unintentionally, expand the war, and the importance of obtaining a peaceful resolution to the war as rapidly as possible," Trump and Rutte said in their statement.

Moreover, the two discussed the importance of further increasing defense spending as well as investment in the defense industrial base in both the U.S. and NATO countries, according to the statement.

Trump also said in a post on Truth Social Thursday that he "briefed NATO on the tremendous progress" being made in growing defense production, noting that the focus will be on building Patriot air defense systems, THAAD systems and Tomahawk cruise missiles, as well as "many new Weapons, both Offensive and Defensive, that have not yet been viewed by the Public, or other Countries."

"There has never been a time when the United States has produced more Military Equipment or Munitions than now. Our 'cupboard' will soon be full and, when it is, our Allies and Partners throughout the World will be benefitting greatly," he said in the post.

Trump's meeting with Xi and Putin, in which he described the Russian president as his "friend," sparked alarm among European lawmakers about Washington's commitment to transatlantic security.

NATO's Rutte, a seasoned diplomat known as a consensus builder during his nearly 14 years as Dutch prime minister, has repeatedly sought to de-escalate tensions in the alliance and frequently used flattery to win over the U.S. president.

While some have questioned whether this approach has delivered any tangible benefits, Trump has previously described Rutte as a "great leader" and NATO's "biggest asset."

Russia has stepped up its attacks on Ukraine's energy infrastructure in recent weeks, with further attacks on the central Ukrainian city of Kryvyi Rih overnight disrupting power supplies and bringing municipal electric public transport to a standstill, according to Oleksandr Vilkul, head of Kryvyi ​Rih's defense council.

Ukrainian officials on Wednesday said Russian attacks on the country's power sector had damaged energy infrastructure and caused power outages in five regions as cold winter weather sets in.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Wednesday accused the Kremlin of "escalating" threats toward European security, citing actions in the Baltic region, Poland and on the Black Sea, and adding that "Russia knows exactly what it wants. And Russia wants more than Ukraine."

A spokesperson for Russia's Foreign Ministry did not immediately respond to a CNBC request for comment on Thursday morning. The Kremlin has repeatedly denied seeking military confrontation with NATO countries.

Notre Dame's defense will lock down, the game plan will be balanced and relatively conservative, and there won't be any messing around. Walk into JMA Wireless, walk out without leaving a doubt.

#2801. Knicks 121, Cavaliers 102: “The most Mike Brown victory imaginable”

It's easy to get lost in today's world. Everything is spinning so fast, so many things are out of control. Prices, taxes, wars, narratives, diabolical devices, our sense of togetherness. Life sometimes feels like an endless list of things that, no matter how much you scratch off, no matter what you decide not to worry about, gets longer by the minute. The NBA is no exception, a cutthroat world infected by influencing influences that expects daily reinvention, that wants to turn humans into brands and expand like a kraken gobbling up the last little dollars from the deepest pits of the coral reef.

As you watch another foul-baiting baller be rewarded for his deeds, followed by the 23rd commercial for guaranteed grifting, it can be tough to find the joy here from time to time, to remember why you ever thought this was fun. But then Jose Alvarado runs into the picture and steals a ball, only to rise up moments later for a three. He jumps for joy as he hits it, just like the little kid he once was on the playgrounds of the city that he now represents on the biggest stage there is in basketball. And you smile along with him.

There is something inherently right about a guy like Jose Alvarado. Sure, he is an annoying pest defensively, loudmouthed, confident on his good days, cocky on his better ones. A guy you would probably hate if he wasn't on your team. Not even in the fun way of hating an opponent, if there is one. No, you really can't stand that little bugger, like, at all. Yet even if you root for some other franchise whose name doesn't rhyme with clicks, deep down inside your basketball fan's heart, you have to appreciate a guy, a man, a kid like Jose Alvarado. Mike Brown surely does.

It didn't even take Alvarado's tide-turning performance in the Knicks' 121-102 destruction of the Cleveland Cavaliers in yesterday's NBA Cup game, which was, as PolyphonicSpreewell so beautifully put it in the Postgame Thread, "the most Mike Brown victory imaginable." It didn't take his 16 points in the fourth quarter or his 21 in total. But the light shining on Jose surely was a reminder that the big little Puerto Rican embodies what this New York basketball team is. Sure, they can beat you with Xs and Os, with the might of majestic superstars, with firepower that can put a New Year's fireworks display to shame. But there is more that makes the Knicks the Knicks. A group that has a heart and a soul beyond what is expected of them, some inner power they can turn to when things go sideways. Something that lets them play and, more importantly, enjoy the game innocently, freely. How it was supposed to be experienced.

Alvarado is not your type of guy? Pas de souci, says Pacôme Djenon Dadiet! It didn't matter that he didn't really hit shots consistently yesterday or, frankly, ever before. He still plunged into the action versus the James Hardens and Donovan Mitchells of the world like the Knicks' bench was a cliff and his name was Orlando Duque. Maybe not as gracefully, but definitely just as committed and energetic. And, most importantly, without any fear. There was no fear in Tyler Nickel, either, who at some point seemed as far away from real NBA minutes as his birthplace in the Shenandoah Valley is from Madison Square Garden. But don't worry, bench guy, Mike Brown's got a map, and he knows where to find you.

With injuries to OG Anunoby, Deuce McBride, and Jordan Clarkson, plus ineffective and almost shockingly bad nights from Jalen Brunson and Karl-Anthony Towns, the coach seemingly didn't have to search yesterday. He just hurled everyone he had on his pine into the action and watched them stick it to the Cavs. Mo Diawara hit a three. James Wiseman dominated the paint for stretches in the fourth quarter. He didn't look out of place; he didn't look like he didn't know what he was doing. Rather, he played like a man possessed, not by some evil power or the One Ring to rule them all, but by the unwavering confidence and belief of a bald, happy-go-lucky man who coaches champions.

These champions include a much-maligned Mikal Bridges, who carried the team throughout the entire second quarter. They also include Josh Hart and Landry Shamet, who did their thing and then some. They are all guys who had rough goes in the past but who never found themselves in Mr. Brown's doghouse. They deserve to be singled out for pushing the ball in transition, for point-of-attack defense, for just being themselves. But frankly, who doesn't? Everyone did a little and then a lot of what was needed from them. I'm sure Tyler Kolek was one of the biggest cheerleaders despite his rough night on the court. It all speaks to the culture that Mike Brown has bestowed upon this team, that he has created with all of his players. All of them. All these guys who know what hard work is. Who relish every opportunity they get.

And who have a way of playing basketball that is as much fun as you can imagine.

#2800. Tom Brady rips into Aaron Rodgers for breaking ‘the sanctity of an NFL locker room’

Another Hall of Fame quarterback is coming out against Aaron Rodgers' recent comments.

This time it was Tom Brady, who kept it professional but made clear that Rodgers' takedown of the Steelers after his benching needed to stay in house.

"The sanctity of an NFL locker room, it's a very sacred place," Brady said on the Fox broadcast of the Eagles' 39-38 win over the Cowboys on Thanksgiving in Dallas. "We shouldn't ever lose track of that as players. It's a privilege to be in that locker room. Fox Sports broadcast analyst Tom Brady looks on before the 49ers' win over the Cowboys on Nov. 15, 2026, in Arlington, Texas. IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect

The Steelers announced on Tuesday night that they were benching Rodgers against the Broncos in favor of Mason Rudolph, and Rodgers responded on Wednesday by going scorched earth on head coach Mike McCarthy during an appearance on "The Pat McAfee Show."

Among Rodgers' gripes was the 19-year coach falling asleep in team meetings and leading a "1, 2, 3, Packers" chant after a huddle. The Steelers cut Rodgers soon after the appearance on "McAfee," and he cleared waivers Thursday to become a free agent.

Brady, who knows a thing or two about working with longtime coaches, acknowledged that feuds can happen in the locker room, but that doesn't mean things need to boil over like they did in Pittsburgh.

"I wasn't a perfect player, [Bill Belichick] wasn't a perfect coach, but we did some things in the game that we're so proud of now," Brady said. "And even me being four years removed from the game, things that matter more than winning a Super Bowl or trophy is my relationship with my teammates, my coaches. That's going to transcend anything you do on the field.

"It's just unfortunate. I hate it, I hate to be even talking about it. It's a privilege to be in the NFL. You want to inspire the next generation of athletes, and you always want to do it the right way."

Aaron Rodgers wears a frustrated expression during the Steelers' loss to the Eagles on Nov. 22, 2026, in Philadelphia. IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect

Brady wasn't the only NFL legend who had something to say Thursday on Fox. Michael Strahan, Howie Long, and former Steelers quarterback Terry Bradshaw took time out of the pregame show to discuss Rodgers' comments.

While Rodgers now has the ability to sign with any team, his release by the Steelers may spell the end of his NFL career. ESPN insider Adam Schefter reported Thursday that it's unlikely Rodgers finds a landing spot to finish out the season.

From No. 1 overall selections to first-round picks who have gone on to become franchise cornerstones, the Central Florida powerhouse has built an impressive résumé at the professional level.

With three players selected first overall in the NBA Draft, here is a look at the 10 highest NBA Draft picks to graduate from Montverde Academy.

The third Montverde Academy product to be selected No. 1 overall, Flagg was the centerpiece of the school's undefeated 2023-24 national championship team. Achiuwa graduated from Montverde Academy in 2019 before playing one season at Memphis. He was selected 20th overall by the Miami Heat in the 2020 NBA Draft. He has since played for Miami, Toronto and the New York Knicks.

#2797. Berkshire breaks out to record high with fourth-quarter rally reaching 19%

(This is the Warren Buffett Watch newsletter, news and analysis on all things Warren Buffett and Berkshire Hathaway. You can sign up here to receive it every Friday evening in your inbox.)

Berkshire Hathaway's red-hot shares are ending a strong week with four consecutive fresh record high closes.

Since the rally began with the start of the fourth quarter on October 1, the Class A shares have closed at record highs 11 times as they soared 19.1%.

The much more widely held B shares closed at new highs just 10 times but are also up 19.1% from their near-term low.

The gains are in sharp contrast to the S&P 500's 1.2% dip as investors appear to be seeing Berkshire as a relatively safe haven amid worries about AI stocks and spending.

Both Berkshire classes were up 3.9% on the week as the S&P advanced by 2.5%, its best week since early August.

Berkshire's B shares are now 7.5 percentage points ahead of the benchmark for the year so far.

After erasing their post-Buffett CEO announcement losses three weeks ago, Berkshire shares are now up almost 10% since last year's shareholders meeting.

They've gained around 29% since last August's lows and are up around 18% year-to-date.

Berkshire Hathaway is due to disclose its quarterly equity portfolio snapshot on Monday when it files its Q3 13F with the SEC.

We won't know for sure until then, but numbers in the company's third quarter 10-Q, released last Saturday, indicate Berkshire continued to reduce its Bank of America stake.

It would be the ninth consecutive quarter of selling.

As of June 30, Berkshire reported holding 483.4 million BAC shares valued now at $24.7 billion, it's fifth largest equity position.

On June 30, 2024, before the selling began, Berkshire owned just over 1 billion shares valued at $41.1 billion.

Since then, the number of shares in the portfolio has decreased by 53.2%, not including any Q3 sales, while the stock price has increased by 28.3%.

If there had been no reductions, the position would be worth $52.7 billion.

The belief Berkshire sold more BAC shares in the third quarter is based on a $372 million reduction in the cost basis for equities categorized by the company as "banks, insurance, and finance."

The 10-Q also reports $2.2 billion of pretax gains from equity sales.

Barron's notes Bank of America and American Express are the only financial stocks in the portfolio that have a cost basis low enough to generate a gain like that. Amex is one of the four stocks new CEO Greg Abel indicated would be held for "decades" to come in his February letter to shareholders.

In any case, Berkshire's almost 23% stake in Amex would have required it to quickly disclose any sales.

Based on the numbers in the 10-Q, the warrants Berkshire received as part of a 2011 $5 billion investment in the bank that it used in 2017 to buy 700 million shares at $7.14 each, and BAC's average stock price in the quarter, Barron's estimates 30 to 40 million shares may have been sold.

That would be roughly in line with the 30.2 million shares sold in the second quarter.

The case isn't as good, but Barron's thinks Berkshire may have bought more Alphabet shares in the period. That's based on a $2.3 billion increase in the cost basis for the category that includes Google's parent.

Overall, it looks like it will be a relatively quiet quarter with $2.4 billion in equity purchases and $2.8 billion in sales.

In the first quarter, Berkshire bought $15.9 billion and sold $24.1 billion of equities. In the second quarter, it purchased $23.5 billion and sold $3.7 billion.

All those numbers exclude the company's buybacks of its own stock.

In a term sheet filed early Friday, Berkshire Hathaway says it is selling more than 182 billion yen ($1.1 billion) worth of bonds with maturities between 2029 and 2056 and annual interest rates between 2.6% and 4.6%.

Bloomberg points out the rates, compared to benchmarks, are higher than its previous sale this year.

It quotes a fund manager as saying market sentiment "has become more sensitive," forcing issuers to make their offerings more attractive.

In April, Berkshire sold 272 billion yen ($1.7 billion) of bonds.

Berkshire uses the proceeds from the yen-denominated bonds to protect its ongoing investments in Japanese stocks from currency fluctuations.

Warren Buffett recommends Benjamin Graham's book, "The Intelligent Investor," and outlines what he considers Graham's three most important ideas.

WARREN BUFFETT: On investment books, if you're asking about that, I would recommend the first two books that Phil Fisher wrote back around 1960, "Common Sense [Stocks] and Uncommon Profits" and the second one ["Paths to Wealth Through Common Stocks"]. They're very good books.

You know, I obviously recommend, first and foremost, [Benjamin Graham's] "The Intelligent Investor," with chapters eight and 20 are the ones that you really should read.

Two of the — well, all of the important ideas in investing, really, are in that book, because there's only about three ideas. And those — two of them are emphasized in those two chapters...

One is that — to think of yourself — to think of investing as owning a business and not buying something that wiggles around in price.

And the second one is your attitude, which ties in with that, the attitude toward the market, that's covered in chapter eight. And if you have the proper attitude toward market movements, it's an enormous help in securities.

And the final chapter is on the margin of safety, which means, don't try and drive a 9,800-pound truck over a bridge that says it's, you know, "Capacity: 10,000 pounds." But go down the road a little bit and find one that says, "Capacity: 15,000 pounds."

#2796. Jeffery Simmons: I didn't simulate snap count on false starts, Lions are "crying" about a them problem

Long before the Bears beat the Lions on a last-second touchdown catch by wide receiver Rome Odunze, one of the storylines of the game was a run of false start penalties by the Lions.

Center Juice Scruggs was called for back-to-back false starts and then picked up a third later in the half. Left guard Christian Mahogany was flagged for another one before the next snap and there were indications from the Lions that Bears defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons was simulating the snap count to get them to jump.

Mahogany made that accusation explicit after the game that the Bears "find out the snap count of the quarterback and they use it" while adding that Lions linemen were wearing microphones that he believes will back him up. Simmons was not penalized, but was seen speaking to the referee during a break in play. He denied Mahogany's allegation after the 39-35 win.

"We don't have to. We don't have to," Simmons said, via Dave Birkett of the Detroit Free Press "We line up and play football. They quarterback check. I said, 'Run.' I didn't say, 'Hut.' I mean, their cadence, they say, 'White 80, white 80.' I mean, when you lose football games, it's a lot of complaining and a lot of crying. I mean, there was a couple times that they false start, we didn't say a word. So that's their problem, not ours. . . . If I say, 'Run,' I'm telling my defense, run. Think I care to tell them what they about to do? I'm talking to my guys. So all the crying that they're doing, that's a them problem, not me."

Mahogany was flagged for taunting Simmons during a 70-yard Jahmyr Gibbs touchdown run in the fourth quarter and kicker Jake Bates missed the ensuing extra point to leave the score 35-24. The Lions would not score again and the Bears headed back to Chicago with an improbable victory.

#2795. Sabres Finally Get Much-Needed Production From Veteran Trio

The Sabres could be turning a corner at the American Thanksgiving checkpoint. One reason? An uptick in scoring from some struggling forwards.

With Jiri Kulich heating up in recent games, a few veteran forwards could end up joining him. In Wednesday night's 5-1 win over the New York Rangers, Josh Doan and Jason Zucker provided assists on Joshua Norris' goal at 2:37 in the second period to put the Sabres up 2-0.

While the trio linked up just once on Wednesday, it could serve as a catalyst for more production in the closing days of November. So far, the Sabres have been top-heavy, with six of their forwards averaging over a half-point per game.

As for Doan, Zucker, and Norris, the returns haven't been anywhere near as encouraging. Doan, who is in his first year of a seven-year deal that carries a cap hit of $6.95 million, has just eight points, four goals, and a 9.8 shooting percentage in 25 games.

Norris hasn't fared any better, with eight points and five goals in 25 contests. Norris, however, is posting a 20.0 shooting percentage. He just doesn't shoot the puck enough, with 25 shots on goal this season. Norris, with a $7.950 cap hit, is Buffalo's highest-paid forward.

Zucker has just two goals and three points in 16 games. Zucker enjoyed two solid seasons with the Sabres, posting 53 and 45 points in 2024-25 and 2025-26, respectively. That said, he is in his age-35 season, and isn't expected to be as effective as he once was.

Norris may be the more frustrating case this season. He appeared in 47 regular-season contests between when he was traded to Buffalo in Mar. 2025 and April 2026, posting 14 goals and 36 points.

Now that he's finally healthy and has seen 25 games, the points production has yet to follow a quarter of the way through the season. If Wednesday night marked a turning point and if he can follow up on Friday against the Pittsburgh Penguins, he will further drive home how deep this Sabres team can potentially go.

Norris has shown flashes earlier in the month. The consistency must follow.

The same applies for Doan, whose 52 points and 25 goals in 2025-26 gave fans a reason to believe Buffalo found a young forward capable of putting up at least solid numbers. But Doan has been up and down throughout his career — with nine points in 11 games in 2023-24 and 19 in 51 in 2024-25.

He has lacked year-over-year consistency. If he can find it, he too will help transform a solid top six in Buffalo into a solid top nine. That could make the Sabres dangerous between the quarter and midseason marks.

The Sabres are heading into an important part of their schedule. Following their Nov. 27 matchup with the Penguins, Buffalo will embark on a Western Conference road trip between Dec. 1 and Dec. 6.

The first matchup in that slate of games will be against the Edmonton Oilers. When Buffalo returns home on Dec. 10, they will face the Oilers again. Then, they will have showdowns with the Anaheim Ducks and Ottawa Senators.

Those are four excruciating matchups that may end up in high-octane play for both sides. If Norris and Doan can keep turning a corner, with Zucker providing supplementary help, Buffalo will match up well against their toughest upcoming opponents.

#2792. SpaceX, Musk pledge to donate a share each to active Trump Accounts

SpaceX said Wednesday it will donate one share of the company's class A stock to every active Trump Account, and CEO Elon Musk would personally match the gift.

"SpaceX is building the infrastructure of the future and working to make life multiplanetary," the company said in a statement. "We believe ownership of the company creating these systems should extend to the next generation of Americans for their long-term benefit."

The White House announced in October that nearly 70 million Trump Accounts had been created, including more than 60 million through auto-enrollment. It's unclear how many are considered active.

Musk said in a social media post on X on Thursday that the share from SpaceX would be transferred next month, without providing further details. "The share directly from me will be transferred when my lockup expires in June next year," he added.

Eligible children must have their account claimed to enable contributions from family members, friends and employers, and to receive the government's one-time $1,000 seed contribution. Auto-enrolled children can receive philanthropic contributions without a parent or guardian claiming an account, according to TrumpAccounts.gov.

Representatives for SpaceX and the U.S. Department of the Treasury did not immediately respond to a request for further details about the planned gift.

SpaceX Chief Operating Officer Gwynne Shotwell had previously agreed to make a personal gift of over 2 million SpaceX shares to Trump Accounts, with eligible account holders expected to receive them in December.

In October, Elon Musk posted on X that he would give a share of SpaceX to every kid in America next year.

Trump Accounts, also known as 530A accounts, are open to any U.S. child under 18 with a Social Security number.

Parents, guardians, grandparents and others can collectively contribute up to $5,000 per child per year in after-tax dollars up until the year before the beneficiary turns 18. The annual contribution limit is indexed for inflation after 2027.

Since the July 4 launch, families and friends have collectively contributed more than $1 billion to Trump Accounts. Total deposits now sit at more than $9 billion, CNBC first reported.

Children born from 2025 through 2028 may receive a one-time $1,000 deposit from the Treasury. Other funds may also be available, depending on certain criteria.

The Treasury rolled out temporary regulations at the end of September that allow Trump Accounts to hold stock donations, a move officials have said is meant to encourage more philanthropic gifts.

Contributing stock can benefit donors, who are able to avoid capital gains taxes triggered by selling appreciated stock. But families can face restrictions related to selling that donated stock. The policy also means some children's wealth accumulation could be tied to the performance of individual companies.

Under U.S. Department of the Treasury guidelines, families cannot refuse stock gifted to Trump Accounts and generally cannot sell it until the earlier of five years or the end of the calendar year in which the beneficiary turns 17.

SpaceX shares have been under some pricing pressure as the company negotiates a possible merger with Elon Musk's automaker Tesla. The companies have established two special committees to handle merger negotiations, and hired advisers for a potential mega-deal.

CNBC's Sam Meredith, Kevin Breuninger, Kate Dore and Jess Dickler contributed to this story

#2791. Jerry Jones backs Mike McCarthy after Aaron Rodgers' rant: 'One of the finest people around football that I've been around'

Cowboys owner Jerry Jones offered strong praise for Pittsburgh Steelers head coach Mike McCarthy after Dallas' late loss to the Philadelphia Eagles on Thanksgiving.

McCarthy, who coached the Cowboys from 2020 to 2024, has been in the headlines this week after his former quarterback, Aaron Rodgers, leveled a series of accusations against him Wednesday on "The Pat McAfee Show."

He's, frankly, one of the finest people around football that I've been around. I can't say enough about him.

I never had the type of thing that is being said about him. I never had that in consideration in any of my time with him, extending his contract, any of that it was never on the table. We never had an issue within the organization."

After the 2024 season, the two sides reportedly reached an impasse in contract talks and mutually agreed to part ways.

McCarthy ended his tenure in Dallas with a 49-35 record.

Jones is the latest to defend McCarthy this week. Ahead of each Thanksgiving Day game, hosts on pregame shows defended the head coach and criticized how Rodgers delivered his message.

Former Steelers quarterbacks Terry Bradshaw and Russell Wilson, as well as Hall of Famer Michael Strahan, were among those who spoke out against Rodgers' public delivery of criticism of McCarthy.

#2789. Nvidia has lost $2 trillion in value. Here's what options traders expect from earnings

Jensen Huang's forced exit from Nvidia shocked Wall Street and Washington, wiped $2 trillion off its market value, and raised serious questions about national security and regulation of the AI complex. Traders, for the moment, must content themselves with the comparatively mundane business of Tuesday's earnings, and options traders are expecting big moves.

With volatility in the stock near the highest since April 2025, options traders are now pricing a 7% reaction in the stock after its report, the biggest implied move going into an Nvidia report since February 2025, and well above the median move of 3.2% over the last eight quarters.

Implied volatility reached 68 Monday, compared to under 40 in early October, according to ThinkOrSwim data. Nvidia vol reached a multi-year high above 92 in the aftermath of President Trump's tariff Liberation day in April '25. In other words, the company that for much of the AI boom was the most reliable winner in the market, is now more volatile than all but 35 companies in the S&P 500.

"Longer term, I see significant downside risk unless Nvidia can attract an exceptional leader, someone like Tim Cook or AMD's Lisa Su," Nigam Arora, founder of the Arora report, said in a text ahead of the company's after-market report on Tuesday.

Since hitting all-time highs in October, Nvidia shares have fallen 35%, shedding $2 trillion in market capitalization along the way. Including Nvidia, there are only five companies in the S&P 500 worth more than $2 trillion. However, there is evidence that bulls have been holding out hope while bears snatch up profits: the ratio of open puts to call contracts has actually widened towards calls, according to Barchart data. The ratio is currently 0.87, down from a one-year high of 1.02 two weeks ago and the lowest since the first week of October.

The most popular contract by volume on Monday was the 155-strike put expiring at the bell Monday, but the most popular trade for later expiry was the 160-strike call expiring Thursday, and the second-most-common purchase was the 190-strike call expiring Friday, SpotGamma data show.

One catch is that most call contracts traded Monday looked like neutral to bearish positions opened by traders selling calls. Of the 5 million options traded on Monday, 3 million were calls, but more were likely opened by sellers than buyers. Of the $2.3 billion in options premium traded on Nvidia Monday, $1.2 billion was tied to puts, SpotGamma data show.

With bears taking profits in puts the past month, there's another potential snag on open interest. There are very few open put contracts at or below the $157 level at which the stock closed Monday. That suggests any bad surprise would find many traders with little downside protection.

By the same token, there's notable open interest in call contracts from the 175-strike and above, suggesting profit-taking on a bounce could limit Nvidia's recovery past levels it breached over the past week.

Either way, Tuesday's earnings could provide fireworks.

#2788. Spain’s Pablo Hernández de Cos set to lead European Central Bank

Pablo Hernández de Cos is set to succeed Christine Lagarde as president of the European Central Bank next year.

He received backing from euro zone leaders at the European Council Summit on Thursday. The role still requires formal appointment after consultation with the European Parliament and the ECB's Governing Council, but neither has veto power and the decision follows intense political wrangling to reach a consensus on who should serve the eight-year term.

De Cos is a 55-year-old economist and career central banker who rose through the ranks of the Bank of Spain, starting as a researcher in the 1990s and working in various departments before becoming governor from 2018 to June 2024.

He chaired the Basel Committee on Banking Supervision from 2019 to 2024, and has been General Manager of the Basel-based Bank for International Settlements since July 2025.

Both de Cos and his main rival for the ECB top job, the Netherlands' Klaas Knot, were widely seen as candidates with deep knowledge and experience in monetary policy and financial stability — attributes that took on particular importance at a time of resurgent inflation, fragmentation and political uncertainty.

Lagarde had extensive experience in financial institutions but was criticized by some early in her tenure for a lack of central banking experience.

De Cos gained sufficient political backing in closed-door discussions and negotiations since Lagarde said she would step down on Feb. 7, 2027, over seven years after she became the first woman to helm the ECB. That was despite a final push by the Netherlands at the European Council meeting this week backing Knot.

Representatives from the euro area's biggest economies — Germany, France, Italy, Spain and the Netherlands — have been horse-trading as they look to secure representation on the central bank's six-member Executive Board.

Influential roles as chief economist, expected to go to Germany's Markus Brunnermeier, and head of the Markets Portfolio, for which France's Laurence Boone has reportedly been tapped, also change hands in 2027.

Analysts say de Cos's commentary and actions over more than two decades at Spain's central bank paint him as moderately dovish — inclined to favor lower interest rates to support economic growth — but also as a pragmatist who has been willing to adapt.

That has included support for strong rate hikes during the energy price shock that followed Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, but also giving staunch backing for rates below zero and the huge stimulus package launched by then-ECB President Mario Draghi to reboot the euro zone economy in 2019.

De Cos quipped in 2024 that he was an "owl" after being asked if he was a hawk or a dove, emphasizing his focus on data and the situation at hand.

"It is true that Hernández de Cos supported the ECB's uber-dovish monetary policy during the period when inflation was persistently below target. However, his monetary policy views may well be regime-dependent," Christian Kopf, head of fixed income and foreign exchange at Union Investment, said in emailed comments.

"We are now clearly in a higher-inflation regime, with core inflation in the euro area expected to remain above the ECB's target through 2029."

Kopf added that de Cos was the candidate with the "strongest technical understanding of monetary policy and central banking," which he said was important at a time when the world is "witnessing an assault on central bank independence, not only in the United States but also in countries such as Japan."

"By appointing a career technocrat such as Hernández de Cos as ECB President, the European Council would send a strong signal that Europe will not waver in its commitment to price stability and that the euro will remain a hard currency," Kopf said.

Spain's de Cos as president, Germany's Brunnermeier as chief economist and France's Boone as head of market operations represent a "carefully crafted package deal," Kopf also noted, because it balances representation from northern and southern European countries. The result was partially due to the knock-on effects of the German government pushing hard for the chief economist position, he said.

Along with a desire among politicians for influence, a north-south balance is seen as important as the northern countries are seen as leaning more hawkish — more inclined to opt for rate hikes and restrictive policy to tame inflation — while southern are perceived as more dovish.

John Orchard, chairman of the Digital Monetary Institute at think tank OMFIF, said that as a "central banker's central banker," de Cos had "managed to earn respect from typically hawkish northern observers."

Another supportive factor of de Cos's candidacy was the stellar growth rate of many of those southern economies in recent years.

Once the "sick men" of the euro area's 2010s sovereign debt crisis, Portugal, Italy, Spain and Greece have become some of the bloc's strongest growth drivers in recent years.

Factors such as strong tourism, relative political stability, increased foreign investment and strengthening public finances have boosted southern economies. Meanwhile, the euro zone's traditional powerhouse Germany has stuttered amid soaring industrial costs and a struggling autos market.

Orchard said that some believed that Lagarde's presidency had ushered in an "esprit de corps" at the ECB, with policymakers focused on the interests of the whole European economy.

That would, in theory, reduce the importance of nationality among leadership and of traditional notions of hawkish northern nations and dovish southern ones. However, Orchard also noted the recurrent theme of national representation in the recent debate and the perception of Knot as a hawkish choice.

Diverging performance is a core challenge for any leader of the ECB, which must set monetary policy for 21 economies all growing at different speeds and with their own domestic priorities and inflationary pressures.

But it has become particularly pressing this year as the bloc's second-biggest economy, France, is teetering on the edge of its own potential debt crisis.

Moves in French markets and whether the ECB needs to take more extreme measures beyond continuing to urge fiscal discipline will remain in focus for de Cos.

The ECB Executive Board's view of what measures could be taken to prevent market disorder and under what conditions was a key topic under discussion when choosing who should fill the roles, according to insiders.

Despite political efforts to pass a budget that will reduce its budget deficit to around 5% of GDP, investors have been driving up French borrowing costs on concerns over its mounting public debt-to-GDP ratio, high budget deficit and contracting economy.

Risks are being compounded by political uncertainty ahead of France's presidential election in April, which is stymying business activity and raising wider questions about EU unity as far-right and far-left candidates pull ahead.

Rising French yields and the widening spread in France's borrowing costs over Germany's have led to speculation over whether the ECB might need to deploy tools such as liquidity injections or its never-used Transmission Protection Instrument to protect other countries from contagion and support the euro.

This would be politically controversial unless France agreed to stringent fiscal discipline measures akin to those that southern nations signed up to during the Sovereign Debt Crisis — which could be complicated if far-right presidential frontrunner Marine Le Pen, who has a combative relationship with EU institutions, wins.

Ken Egan, head of European sovereigns at ratings agency KBRA, said fragmentation was always a challenge for the ECB, which does not want to see divergent financing conditions and high sovereign spreads across the bloc.

However, he said that in the case of France he believed we were "some way from having a serious conversation about ECB intervention."

"If anything, sovereign spreads have pulled back a bit and tightened, and some measures of market liquidity have also improved in recent weeks," he said by email.

"That doesn't mean the underlying risks have disappeared, but I think it's important to distinguish between periods of market volatility and a more fundamental breakdown in monetary policy transmission."

De Cos also takes up the mantle as Europe faces yet another surge in price pressures.

Euro area inflation rose to 4% in October, its highest level in more than three years. Energy was the biggest contributor, as the Iran war drives up oil and gas prices and tightens the supply of refined fuels.

That leaves the central bank facing a difficult policy balance, preventing higher energy costs from spreading into wages and wider prices while avoiding unnecessary damage to growth.

De Cos will inherit major supranational projects, including plans for a digital euro and Europe's long-delayed capital-markets integration. In a recent speech, Lagarde warned that each year without capital markets integration meant "more of our savings are invested abroad and more of our growing firms look elsewhere for funding."

France is not the only euro area country heading for a pivotal election next year, with votes in Finland, Greece, Italy, Estonia, Slovakia and Slovenia also expected, adding to the politically uncertain climate.

It is also not the only country grappling with higher government borrowing costs, public debt and a struggle to find fiscal headroom, a growing problem among many developed countries.

The ECB's Financial Stability Review meanwhile warned this month of mounting risks from European investors' growing exposure to the U.S. economy, and equity and credit markets' vulnerability to AI.

Outgoing head Lagarde, meanwhile, told the European Banking Congress in Frankfurt this month that her biggest concern was now cyber threats, an area she said policymakers had not paid enough attention.

"The one [worry] that keeps me awake, and many of you awake ​as well ... ​is ⁠AI applied together with cyber threat," she said.
