#2787. Questions & Antlers: Early season impressions, featuring Nets Daily’s Anthony Puccio (Part 2)

Last week, we introduced you to Nets Daily's Editor-in-Chief, Anthony Puccio, with the premise that he, as a long-time Brooklyn Nets fan and writer, knows what we're going through this season following our beloved Milwaukee Bucks. In response, you came screaming off a high pick and roll, turned the corner—drawing the strongside defender—and hit him seams up in the corner with your questions. As you'll see below, he didn't let you down with the finish. Nylon.

stoneAge: Did you expect the rebuild to take so long and how far away are the Nets from being a playoff team again?

AP: I expected it to take long, but I figured they would have moved some assets to speed this thing up. I was wrong. We're looking at a Nets team currently two-three years away from playoffs—and that's being generous.

stoneAge: Which of the Nets' current players are part of their future core and what do the Nets lack the most to reach the next level?

AP: Mikel Brown Jr., Egor Dëmin, and Nolan Traore. The Nets lack a lot of things, particularly size in the front court. This isn't new. They lack athleticism. They lack three-point shooters. And they lack basic fundamentals required to build on good habits for a sustainable culture.

Mitchell Maurer: How do you navigate a landscape where so many people in the same geographic area are head-over-heels for the Knicks? A title is (as we've seen around here…) a surefire way to attract bandwagon fans, who are as vocal as they are anonymous 'round these Internet parts. The Nets are not a "nothing" franchise but they clearly don't carry the same weight (broadly speaking) as their cross-town counterparts. It's not a fair paradigm, to be considered an "afterthought" and I'm curious if there's similarities with how Bucks fans may have felt back in the heyday of the Packers and/or Brewers (who also just won a title!)

AP: Nets fans don't want to admit it, but there's absolutely an inferiority. Before the Knicks' chip, the one thing Nets fans had on Knicks fans was a better on-court product since 2000. Now we don't even have that! Put it this way: if you tell someone you're a Nets fan in NY, depending on who you tell, they might say, "Who?" Or "Why?"

Terrapin Revisited: What was it like to adjust expectations when the Nets went from title contenders to "Well, what exactly are we now?" after their big trades? Any recommendations for Bucks fans on how to adapt?

AP: There's no way of sugar-coating it—it feels like a dead end. You adapt when you simply learn to accept this is the new reality, and you never know when it might return. My recommendation: lean on the community to talk. It's difficult without picks to look forward to. Expect the worst, hope the best. Don't turn on each other though. (Editor's note: Sage advice—and one of the things I love about Brew Hoop).

Terrapin Revisited: What have you enjoyed most about the Nets during this rebuilding era? In other words, what can fans focus on as far as the bright side of such teams?

AP: Watching people in the organization make a name for themselves, hustling and shining in the shadows of the down years. Ideally it a player, but it can be any personnel. College basketball, too.

Terrapin Revisited: Do you have any insights on what to expect from veterans on the team at this time? A number of Bucks' vets are disappointing this year, I'm not sure how much that is to be expected when the stakes they are playing for are a lot lower vs. how much that provides some useful insights on the vets. What have you seen from different vets on the Nets?

AP: Right now I see two vets on the Nets who want to get their shots up and head out. It feels like they embrace the leadership role until the losses actually pile up.

#2786. Eagles' Nick Sirianni pulled away from fans after wild Thanksgiving win over Cowboys

Philadelphia Eagles head coach Nick Sirianni has been known to lose his cool on sidelines before.

A dramatic 39-38 come-from-behind Thanksgiving Day victory over the rival Dallas Cowboys, punctuated by a 60-yard field goal from Jake Elliott with 2 seconds remaining, was certainly cause for celebration.

Sirianni needed to meet Cowboys head coach Brian Schottenheimer for the customary postgame handshake between the two head coaches, but instead ran toward a smattering of fans in the first-row luxury seating at AT&T Stadium, including several Cowboys fans, to celebrate. Sirianni was pulled away by Eagles' security chief Dom DiSandro, with senior vice president for communications Bob Lange in tow.

Sirianni said after the game that he was excited to celebrate.

"There was a lot of Eagles fans back there," Sirianni said with a smile. "I was excited to celebrate with those Eagles' fans and our team and everything like that."

The Eagles trailed 31-10 late in the third quarter before erasing the deficit, with former Cowboys backup quarterback Joe Milton (eventually named the game's MVP) leading the way.

Sirianni's postgame meeting with Schottenheimer was brief. Walking in the tunnel afterward, Sirianni let out a triumphant yell.

"That's how you fight," he said. "We know how to fight."

This is not the first time Sirianni has acted oddly with regard to fans. Earlier this month, he had to deny flipping off home fans as the team dropped to 2-7. He had to apologize in 2024 for engaging with fans negatively despite a win at home.

Earlier in the game, running back Will Shipley and Sirianni got into it on the sidelines.

Other antics of Sirianni's have included staring down the camera and running toward the end zone to celebrate with his players after a touchdown. He led the Eagles to the Super Bowl 59 title and the team has made the playoffs every season he has been the head coach.

#2785. Inside India newsletter: Roaring economy, foreign investors’ return and now record auto sales

Hello, this is Priyanka Salve, writing to you from Singapore.

Welcome to the latest edition of "Inside India" — your one-stop destination for stories and developments from the world's fastest-growing large economy.

Despite 2026 being a challenging year with high global energy prices and supply chain disruptions, the Indian economy has fared surprisingly well. The auto industry, a key pillar of manufacturing and employment, has breached several records this year and is poised to report its best-ever sales.

This week, I spoke to experts to decode what this stellar performance means for one of the world's most promising consumer markets.

Any thoughts on today's newsletter? Share them with the team.

India's economy expanded at 7.8% in the June quarter, beating expectations, even as growth in several major economies cooled. Foreign portfolio investors who had been exiting Indian markets in droves for most of the year have also started returning in historic numbers.

And now, the world's third-largest auto market is set to for a record this year as better road connectivity, tax cuts, and easier financing options have fueled bumper sales over the last several months. That comes at a time when major auto markets across the world, from China to the U.S. have been seeing a slump in sales.

"10 years ago, despite having the money, people did not buy cars, but now even if they don't have the money, they take financing and buy," Amar Sheth, vice president of the Federation of Automobile Dealers Associations, told CNBC, pointing to the shift in consumer mindset.

They are becoming "more optimistic" about the future and, rather than waiting, consumers are willing to take a loan and purchase something useful to them now, he adds.

The industry body that Sheth represents said on Monday that automakers in India were poised to sell more than 30 million vehicles in the financial year ending March 2027, dubbing the sector as a "reflection of the wider India growth story."

From April to October, total vehicle retail sales in India reached 18.7 million units, up 10% from a year earlier, with car, tractor and commercial vehicle sales growing more than 15%, as per FADA data.

The optimism of the industry body is also shared by major automakers; several of whom have announced capacity expansion plans this year to meet the growing consumer demand.

Japanese automakers Maruti Suzuki and Toyota plan to raise capacity by 1.2 million units and 200,000 units, while Korea's Hyundai Motors will add capacity for 150,000 units, as per data shared by automotive industry intelligence provider Mobility Global. Leading Indian companies Tata Motors, Mahindra & Mahindra and JSW have also announced capacity addition plans, the data showed.

India is the only big auto market in the world that is growing while most others such as France, Germany, and Korea are "either declining or are flat," Puneet Gupta, director India and ASEAN at Mobility Global, told CNBC, explaining the reason behind car companies investing in the country.

Gupta said that the Chinese automotive market hit an inflection point in 2007, when the GDP per capita crossed $2,500, and now India is "at a similar point." He added that government support for the auto industry would be crucial in replicating the boom seen in the Chinese auto industry.

The catalyst for India's auto sector boom traces back to last September, when the government announced a wide range of tax cuts to spur domestic consumption.

The auto industry contributes 7.1% to the country's gross domestic product, 49% to manufacturing GDP, 15% to goods and services tax collection, and supports 30 million jobs, as per government data.

While the tailwinds from the tax cuts have faded, experts now believe that replacement demand and the growing reach of financing options to smaller cities will unlock the next phase of growth.

Consumption has been strong this year as the government has partly shielded people from rising energy costs while corporates, with their strong balance sheets, have been slow to pass on price hikes, Gaura Sengupta, chief economist at India's IDFC First Bank, said.

So far this year, wage growth has been good, the labor market has held up equity markets haven't corrected sharply, keeping the wealth effect intact, she said, underscoring the reasons driving consumption along with easy access to credit.

Despite the economy facing external shocks, producers are also "feeling confident to add capacity" as they have seen domestic demand sustain, Sengupta added.

However, experts said that the central bank's recent tightening of monetary policy and price hikes by automakers could slightly take the edge off the auto sales boom in the last few months of the financial year.

While urban demand is unlikely to get affected, rural sales growth could moderate, they added.

"Overall retail should close FY27 in high single digits," Diwakar Murugan, senior automotive analyst at Omdia, told CNBC, adding that this year's record sales are not a one-time spike but a "structural reset."

China has changed tactics but is still thwarting India's rise, a U.S. panel saysChina is "actively working to suppress India's rise," even as the relationship between the two major Asian powers has thawed in the past year, according to a U.S. panel that sees an opening for greater outreach to India.

U.K.-India trade deal faces a stiff test over Scotch whisky import taxesWithin months of taking effect, the India-U.K. trade deal is facing an early test, as New Delhi resists extending preferential tariffs to bulk Scotch whisky imports.

Investors give a thumbs down to Tata Steel-APL Apollo $1.67 billion deal, plunging sharesTata Steel, one of the world's leading steel producers, on Monday said it will buy a 26.4% stake in India's largest structural steel pipe and tube maker, APL Apollo, for 155.1 billion rupees ($1.67 billion). However, investors reacted negatively to the deal.

AMD continued to slide after hours, trading down 0.45% to $487 shortly after 4 p.m.

In the least surprising development in the NBA on Wednesday, the Knicks beat the Cavaliers.

Here are very few quotes from yesterday's affair and elsewhere. Enjoy Thanksgiving today, and make sure to save the leftovers!

On the benefits of potentially missing the NBA Cup knockout rounds:

"It is important (to win and potentially advance), but the reality of it is, when you look at the schedule, and you see that our percentage [to advance] is not that high, and so they kind of shared with me what our schedule would look like if we don't go and if we do go. And you look at it, you're like, 'Whoa, that's a lot of days off if you don't go.' And so again, you want to compete; you want to win. But if you don't, in my opinion, when you look at the schedule… you're like, there's an opportunity if you got some guys banged up to get rest and/or to work on some things in between the games that you have if you're not involved in the Cup."

On the physical and mental toll of competing in the NBA Cup:

"I didn't really break it down to an 83rd game, but when I talk about the Cup, it adds a level of stress maybe on your mind and your body because the games are intense as you go along and you're playing more games in a short amount of time.

"I remember it was like, game, game, game, and then you win the Cup, and you celebrate it that night, and you hop on a plane and go play in Indiana the next night. And so it's great. You like the competition and the setup, but it adds a lot of stress to you physically and mentally. I'm saying this because especially with the extended season we had last year and how taxing the games were for our playoff run mentally and physically, I'm trying to be smart, so if — knock on wood — we end up advancing, I'll try to be smart about it."

#2780. ‘Trying to Hold Back Some Tears': Arvid Lindblad Reveals Emotional Story Behind His Las Vegas Message

Arvid Lindblad has opened up about the heartbreak he felt after retiring from the Las Vegas Grand Prix. The Racing Bulls rookie admitted the disappointment followed him onto his flight home, leaving him close to tears.

"I was on the flight back, and I was pretty emotional, honestly," Lindblad said. "Being completely frank, there were times I was on the flight, and I was just trying to hold back some tears." He explained that he wrote his social media message in his phone's Notes app to share how he felt.

Lindblad had started fifth on the grid and looked set for a strong result. He stayed with the leading group before spinning while warming his tires behind the Safety Car. He could not recover and had to retire from the race.

In his post, Lindblad said the lost chance of a special result would stay with him. He had believed a first podium was possible, making the mistake even harder to accept. He has since turned his attention to the final two races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi, where he hopes to help Racing Bulls secure fifth place in the Teams' Championship.

Lindblad has revealed an unusual gear change before his race-ending spin at the Las Vegas GP. The Racing Bulls rookie still cannot fully explain what happened during the incident.

Arvid Lindblad had a "very bad shift" before spinning out in Las Vegas. (Source: MEGA)

"I had a very bad shift," Lindblad admitted. He also described it as "a very strange feeling" that he had never experienced in the car. He said he was gently applying the throttle when he suddenly found himself facing the wall.

Racing Bulls team principal Alan Permane said the team would investigate the gear change. He wanted to understand whether it had played a part in Lindblad's spin. The team will review the data to learn more about the incident.

Arvid Lindblad is ready to end the 2026 season on a high. (Source: MEGA)

Despite accepting responsibility, the Briton said he could not explain the strange feeling. He also stressed that he would not use it as an excuse. The rookie now hopes to put the difficult weekend behind him as he prepares for the final races in Qatar and Abu Dhabi.

Lindblad is ready to move on from his Las Vegas heartbreak as he turns his attention to Qatar. The Racing Bulls rookie hopes to help his team secure fifth place in the F1 Teams' Championship before the season ends.

"I feel a bit better. I've tried not to think about it too much," Lindblad said. Looking ahead to Qatar and Abu Dhabi, he added: "I'm looking forward to these two – it's going to be two proper tracks. I think it's going to be cool, it's going to be fast."

The 19-year-old also sees the final two rounds as a chance to learn and build confidence. Qatar's fast corners will test his pace, while Abu Dhabi offers another chance to show his progress. He wants to carry that experience into his second season in Formula 1.

Racing Bulls now face two important races as they fight to hold fifth place. The team leads Alpine by 114 points to 87, giving it a 27-point advantage. Lindblad wants to help protect that lead and end his rookie season on a stronger note.

#2779. Even the price of toys is on the rise. How Americans are scaling back holiday plans

As Amanda Brecht planned how her family would spend Thanksgiving this year, she had to make some difficult decisions.

Because of high gas prices, the 30-year-old decided she wouldn't drive across her home state of Michigan to celebrate with extended family. Instead, Brecht and her husband will spend the holiday with just their three kids. And with food prices rising, they'll be skipping appetizers and serving turkey breast instead of a whole bird.

"Thanksgiving is definitely going to look different this year," Brecht said. "Money doesn't grow on trees. You can only do so much."

With inflation accelerating, Americans like Brecht will see higher prices almost everywhere they look this holiday season. At a time of year synonymous with food, gifts and big spending, many consumers are instead pinching pennies, paring back their plans and making tough choices about how they'll celebrate.

Some are raiding their savings accounts and running up debt on credit cards. They're reporting downbeat outlooks about the economy in surveys. And they've become more selective with spending as inflationary pressures mount.

"Families are facing some tough choices this year," said Alexander Smith, an associate professor who researches behavioral economics at the Worcester Polytechnic Institute. "They might have to cut back on holiday spending in whatever way that they can."

A classic Thanksgiving feast will be harder to pull off as grocery prices rise.

The price of a 10-person Thanksgiving dinner increased 6% to $58.63 in 2026, according to an annual survey from the American Farm Bureau Federation. Faith Parum, the organization's deputy chief economist, said the price increase was a result of higher costs for labor and transportation.

Grocers including Walmart and Aldi have gained traction on social media by offering Thanksgiving meal bundles as a value-focused workaround to higher prices. Walmart's offering promises to feed 10 for $35, and includes a turkey and ingredients to make mashed potatoes, green bean casserole, cranberries, marshmallow-topped sweet potatoes and a pumpkin pie.

Still, some consumers will feel disappointed by having less choice in their menus due to higher prices, according to Joe Bruseulas, chief economist at tax firm RSM.

"We're missing the point here if all we're doing is focusing on the fact that Walmart will sell you a homogeneous dinner meal" at a discount, Bruseulas said. "People feel horrible that they have to go to that because the price of everything has just risen so significantly over the past five years."

Inflation is affecting more than Thanksgiving staples like turkey or stuffing. Food prices on average have jumped around 24% over the last five years, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Some items have seen even sharper increases: Coffee and ground beef, for example, have each climbed by more than 40% in the same period despite pulling back from recent highs.

At the same time, millions of Americans lost SNAP benefits under policy changes included in President Donald Trump's "big beautiful bill." Food banks across the U.S. have seen foot traffic skyrocket this year as the reduction in federal nutrition aid coincides with rising prices in grocery aisles.

The Salvation Army said some of its food pantries in October provided double or triple the amount of groceries than they did in the same month a year ago. Demand is now so high that some food banks in Feeding America's national network are worried about running out of supplies.

"We want to make sure that our food banks are as full as they possibly can be going into the holiday season," said Linda Nageotte, Feeding America's president and operations chief. "Far too many of them have empty shelves."

High energy prices as a result of the war with Iran are also affecting Americans' holiday plans.

Slightly fewer Americans will travel at least 50 miles around the Thanksgiving holiday in 2026, marking the first year-over-year decline since the country was in lockdown from the pandemic in 2020, according to AAA. Stacey Barber, a vice president at the auto association, attributed this year's pullback in part to higher fuel costs.

AAA said that about nine out of every 10 Thanksgiving travelers will do so by car. While gas prices have come down from a May peak, they are still up about 18% year over year and could set a new record for the month of November, according to the organization's data.

Travelers are paying about 31% and 23% more for roundtrip domestic airfare around Thanksgiving and Christmas, respectively, than they did a year ago, according to booking platform Hopper. Airlines have blamed the ticket price hikes on rising jet fuel costs in the wake of the war.

"There will be a significant shell shock when they see the price of traveling," said Hayley Berg, lead economist at Hopper.

Berg said price increases would feel more noticeable on routes previously serviced by Spirit, the budget airline that shut down in May. Travelers are booking holiday flights earlier than they did in past years, a sign that prices are top of mind, she said.

Staying home for the holidays isn't a silver-bullet solution, either, as heating costs jump.

The average American household is expected to spend 7% more on home heating this winter than they did last year, according to the National Energy Assistance Directors Association. For the typical family, that equates to an increase of about $66 and a total bill for the season above $1,000.

To be sure, some families will feel it more than others. Heating oil, which is used mainly in homes in the Northeast, has jumped around 70% year over year. However, natural gas, which is one of the most common heating types in the U.S., costs about the same as last year.

Some U.S. states, like Massachusetts and New York, beefed up their home energy support programs to account for higher prices. But Mark Wolfe, NEADA's executive director, said federal aid offerings haven't been meaningfully expanded this year.

"Some of these increases are caused directly by the decision to go to war," Wolfe said. "Why isn't the federal government helping families pay these higher bills?"

The spirit of giving will take on a different meaning for consumers this year.

Retail sales during the all-important holiday season are expected to grow almost 5% this year and surpass $1 trillion for the first time, according to Bain & Company. But the consulting firm said most of that growth would come from inflation, rather than from consumers buying more products.

And Citi on Wednesday said that increased holiday spending would be mainly driven by higher earners this year. The bank said that's a result of the "K"-shaped economy, a term used to describe a scenario where better-off Americans splash out while others struggle.

Toy prices have climbed more than 9% over the past year and now sit at their highest levels since 2019, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics. Manufacturers have raised prices in response to higher costs for transportation and plastic, according to Chris Byrne, an independent toy industry analyst. The artificial intelligence boom has driven up prices for the chips that power gaming devices and other electronics.

Byrne said that's causing shoppers to focus more on the quality of gifts rather than quantity.

"The toy industry always reflects the culture at large," Byrne said. "It's almost true economically as well. As inflation is rising, people are being a little bit more cautious about what they're buying."

Just 16% of respondents to a Morning Consult survey said they planned to spend more in the 2026 holiday season than they did a year ago. Respondents who were older or had lower earnings were more likely to say their budgets were shrinking, the survey found.

Some are doing away with gifts altogether. A poll from consulting firm TSG and the Electronic Transactions Association found 5% of Americans did not plan to buy any presents in 2026, up three percentage points from last year.

One shopper, Wendy Cooper, set a limit of one gift for each of her three adult children this year. For her teenage daughter, the 56-year-old Atlanta resident has scoured Five Below, the trendy value retailer, for budget-friendly presents.

"It's super stressful," Cooper said. "You have to weigh: Do you guys want lights on and a place to live? Or do you want gifts?"

Across the board, the Bureau of Labor Statistics' consumer price index reaccelerated after the U.S. first struck Iran in late February. Annual inflation rates have begun rising faster than wages in the same period, leaving consumers with less purchasing power.

Even if Americans keep spending for the holidays, economists caution that high prices during this busy shopping period can further drag on their economic outlooks. In the CNBC Voter Poll early this month, about three-fourths of participants rated the economy as poor or not good. Consumer confidence gauges had dropped significantly this year, but have regained ground in the runup to the holiday shopping season.

From her home in Northern Michigan, Brecht is doing everything she can to make Christmas feel special without breaking the bank.

The graduate student has been delivering DoorDash orders in her spare time and listing clothes on resale platforms to save up money for her kids' holiday gifts. Brecht is watching closely for discounts and will look for potential presents at thrift stores in the coming weeks.

If necessary, Brecht said she would turn to credit cards for some holiday purchases. She isn't alone: TSG and ETA's survey found that about one-third of Americans said they expected to go into debt during the holiday season, a roughly 74% increase from 2025.

"I don't really know how we're going to do it," Brecht said. "I'm just praying for good Black Friday deals."

#2778. The stealing, running Mavs are the perfect cast for a high-IQ duo that could change basketball

The Mavericks just beat a very good Denver Nuggets team through aggressive defense, forcing steals, and running on offense. It is indeed a new day in Dallas.

Kyrie Irving, a player that has pretty much seen it all by now, didn't even have an efficient night (5/19 on field goal attempts, 1/8 from three). He did, however, lead the team to a victory that shows the whole league that the Dallas Mavericks now are the exact opposite of who they used to be.

In a gesture as moving as it was telling, Kyrie showed the world that he and Cooper Flagg have the rarest of connections. This is a high-IQ duo who could change the trajectory of what basketball looks like. And they may be on the way to doing that as we speak.

It is not only the gesture that's important here, it's the ultimate look away pass and the back door cut by Flagg that shows a connection between the two, usually built through years of ups and downs. It was almost like they could read each other's minds. This is what real chemistry looks like.

Kirk Henderson said it best: "There are lookaway passes, then there's something like this where I feel as if Kyrie's head never even moved the direction where Coop cut to."

Jamal Crawford interpreted the gesture as "me and you", and either way this is a gesture of connection, we – as in us – we got this. And even though Kyrie meant Cooper, we all feel it a little bit.

You may be watching from across the globe, you may not even be a Mavs fan, but anybody watching, knowing what this team and city have gone through recently, felt it.

Because no one has worked harder to get the Dallas Mavericks back together than Kyrie Irving. After it was torn apart, he did everything he could to hold it together. He mentored, he was everyone's vet, he led, he coached when injured – he showed the way and the light in the dark times.

And Dallas is reaping the benefits right now. That is also why it felt so touching, seeing the vet who worked so hard to hold it all together, make this gesture to the young superstar with the highest ceiling imaginable.

They took away his running mate, his brother and a genuine friendship and on-court chemistry, resulting in the most negative period in Dallas, in which he forced himself to play too much and carry more than he should have. His resulting ACL injury took him away from his craft for more than a year, and now – finally – his hard work is really paying off. Kyrie Irving deserves this.

And despite the spiritual experience it can be to watch Irving play, especially when he has chemistry with his teammates, he didn't carry the team to this extraordinary win. Neither did his co-star Flagg really.

It was a cast of teammates who decided to outwork, outhustle and believe in their connection, along with a well-prepared coach, who had clearly done a lot of work to get this team ready. It was no easy feat. But the Mavs made it look easy.

They had 13 steals. The league leader averages 10.6 (Los Angeles Lakers). The Mavs average 9.44 this season, but led by the surprising hero of the last games, Caleb Martin, with five, they kept the pressure on the passing lanes all game, stressing the Nuggets in a way we don't see every day. Not only that, they had 16 steals last game versus Utah, and a whopping 50 steals the last four games (which all happen to be wins).

Martin started this game on fire on both ends, secured the first six points by knocking down two threes in a row and continued to force five steals in the first half, constantly the first to run in transition.

This is exactly the leadership a team needs from a role player next to superstars, and with Zaccharie Risacher next to him, the two have the potential to cause havoc defensively on every team in the league, followed by easy transition points, if they keep this up.

Caleb Martin explained the game plan in the half:

"High sense of urgency. A high level of respect for a great team," he said during the broadcast.

He went on to explain that steals were an emphasis, as well as just being active. "The more active we are," Martin said, "sense of urgency, the better a team we are, positive things happen".

And not even interview questions were about to distract Caleb Martin, who is on a mission in Dallas right now.

When asked in the half whether the loud colors of the court, which are usually a little on the bright side during Cup games, was giving him a headache, too, he answered deadpan:

"I don't know, I'm trying to win a game right now."

#2777. Anthropic was supposed to save the AI trade. What went wrong?

Anthropic's historic IPO — the largest in U.S. history — delivered a big win for the company and its investors. But it failed at another task: reviving animal spirits in the AI trade.

The Nasdaq Composite closed down 2.25% amid a broader market pullback with the S&P 500 declining 2% to 7,175.

Investors had been looking forward to the Anthropic IPO as a "clearing event" — reviving the tech sector after months of choppy trading, the Nvidia espionage scandal, and growing concerns that AI chip sales to Asia are likely to slump as Washington cracks down on potential violations of export controls.

Some of those worries resurfaced Thursday as a short seller, Hunterbrook Media, alleged in a report that firmware sold by chipmaker AMD had turned up in U.S.-blacklisted companies. AMD stock closed down more than 7%. The chipmaker told CNBC it complies with U.S. law.

Adding to the worries, the House Foreign Affairs Committee released documents showing that a subagency of the Commerce Department approved the sale of more than 879,000 AI chips to Chinese companies. That also raised the prospect of an Asia sales slowdown under stricter export controls.

Many investors and analysts continue to express confidence in the AI trade, noting that Anthropic's successful market debut — the stock closed up 17% from its IPO price and raised more than $81 billion — bodes well for capital spending across tech.

But investors acknowledged that this is a high-tension moment and said it's time to be more strategic about the trade.

Dan Niles, founder of Niles Investment Management, described himself as a "circumspect bull," making the comparison to market conditions in 2022 when the big indices tanked in the back half of the year.

"You could have still made money that year. You just needed to have the right combination of longs and shorts," he said.

Part of the challenge, Niles said, has been a price war between the two cutting-edge frontier labs, Anthropic and OpenAI. That has posed a threat to the overall revenue and profit potential of AI and the capex going into it. Fierce competition on price is producing collective losses between the two top companies, he notes.

"The combined revenue growth for OpenAI plus Anthropic went from growing 75% sequentially in Q2 to 48% in Q3," he told CNBC. "The combined losses went from $7.9 billion to about $8.4 billion from Q2 to Q3."

While uncertainty is high now, some resolution may be on the horizon if a greater degree of commercial and regulatory clarity emerges over the next few months.

Trading experts also told CNBC that the tech sector's troubles Thursday were a more serious matter than Anthropic simply siphoning capital from other parts of the market.

"There's a reset of AI in general," said JJ Kinahan, senior vice president at Cboe Global Markets.

Investors for years have profited in tech by buying the dip, he said, but "there's been an attitude change that [you] can't buy things blindly and they'll all go up." Nvidia's ongoing declines have shaken confidence in the buy-the-dip strategy, he said.

Anthropic's next few trading days will be a key gauge of the market's strength. Friday will be a "wild card," Kinahan said. It could be a "final flush out" for the market, or a bounce that leaves the market in "no man's land" while volatility remains elevated.

A better gauge may be Monday, when options on Anthropic start trading, providing insight into whether retail investors will back the company in force — providing more of a vote of confidence in the AI trade.

"If people think we're going up [on Anthropic] they'll buy stock, but retail particularly will just buy calls," he said. "There's a bigger test coming Monday."

For now, investors continue to sell AI-related stocks.

Neoclouds, the generally highly indebted AI-dedicated computing providers at the outer edges of the AI trade, were down substantially Thursday, with CoreWeave closing down more than 6%.

Hyperscalers such as Alphabet and Amazon.com, viewed as relatively defensive AI bets, also finished lower.

One bright spot: Cybersecurity stocks continued to rally, with Palo Alto Networks and CrowdStrike both closing up. AI is finding security holes across software infrastructure, creating a scramble to patch the vulnerabilities before hackers can exploit them.

— CNBC's Daren Fonda contributed reporting.

#2774. How Moe Wagner and Danny Wolf have become offensive bright spots for the Nets

It's pretty doom and gloom in NetsWorld right now, and that's justified. Sitting at 3-13 after Monday night's blowout against the Minnesota Timberwolves, the team has now suffered nine double-digit losses this season.

When a young, rebuilding team isn't winning, it's one thing, but getting completely outmatched consistently is another. That's pretty much what's been the case for Brooklyn, as nine of their 13 losses have come by 10+ points.

Interestingly, one of the biggest questions entering the season surrounded Brooklyn's frontcourt. It wasn't clear how the rotation would take shape.

Day'Ron Sharpe entered the season as the team's starting center following Nic Claxton's departure, while Moe Wagner arrived in free agency. Wagner's health was in question after he played just 66 games over the previous two seasons, including time missed due to a torn ACL. Danny Wolf was another question mark after an up-and-down rookie campaign.

So far, the frontcourt has produced more offense than expected. Brooklyn's rim protection remains a work in progress, and its defense has struggled at every level. But offensively, two of the team's biggest surprises have been Wagner and Wolf.

Offensively, two of Brooklyn's biggest surprises have been Wagner and Wolf.

Wagner has been known for his offensive game since entering the league—most notably his success from beyond the arc and his consistency.

Although injuries have hindered him significantly over the past two years, Wagner is starting to pick up where he left off before the ACL injury forced him out of action for 98 games.

Through 16 games, Wagner owns a 70.7% effective field-goal percentage, ranking in the 98th percentile among bigs, per Cleaning the Glass. A large part of that production comes from his remarkable 62.5% shooting from three-point range. That percentage almost certainly won't hold over an 82-game season, but it's an encouraging start to his Brooklyn tenure.

What's even more encouraging, though, is the success beyond just the 3-point line. For a big like Wagner, who isn't necessarily touted for rim protection or stout defense, being a multi-faceted offensive contributor is crucial.

Worth noting, though, he only played four minutes in Wednesday's win over the Milwaukee Bucks after exiting with left knee soreness.

Overall, he's returning to the offense that worked at the peak of his career in Orlando. Last season with the Magic, just 44% of his overall attempts came at the rim, while 25% came from the midrange. This year, those numbers have shifted to 60% and 19%, respectively. That's much more in line with what we saw from Wagner during his two most efficient seasons (2023-24, 2024-25), with his effective FG percentage finishing north of 60% in both of those campaigns.

Wagner has also improved drastically at creating his own shot. Last season, 88% of his made baskets at the rim were assisted. Meanwhile, that has dropped to 61%, despite a 15-percentage-point increase in his shot usage around the basket.

Obviously, there's only so much that Wagner could be expected to do. Signed to a two-year, $18.4 million contract this offseason, he was widely viewed as the Nets' backup big behind Sharpe. So far, that has held. Sharpe has started all 17 of Brooklyn's games, while averaging 24 minutes per game. Meanwhile, off the bench, Wagner has averaged 17.1 minutes a game.

Entering the season, one of the biggest concerns with the Nets' roster was where points would come from off the bench. So far, their bench scoring hasn't been too shabby, ranking 13th in bench points per game (38.7). More impressively, though, their bench ranks 11th in 3-point percentage (35.7%). Wagner is clearly a big reason behind that.

Having a big who can stretch the floor while also generating offense around the basket is a luxury.

The bigger question mark entering the year is what the Nets really had in Wolf. Just like the four Flatbush 5 members behind Egor Dëmin, whose start to the year had been disappointing, the Michigan product had a lot to prove heading into the season.

So far, though, that development has been encouraging. Just like Wagner, the 27th overall pick in last June's draft has emerged as a threat from beyond the arc. After shooting just 32% from deep as a rookie, he is converting at 46.7% this season, ranking in the 95th percentile among bigs.

There has also been an uptick in volume: 54% of his overall shot attempts have come from the 3-point range, up from 44% a season ago. His mark this year ranks in the 88th percentile among bigs. Beyond that, 35% of his overall attempts have come from non-corner 3s, which ranks in the 91st percentile.

Wolf's output has also had a large impact on Brooklyn as a whole. Last season, the Nets scored 5.1 fewer points per 100 possessions with him on the floor than with him on the bench. This season, they're scoring 5.4 more points per 100 possessions with him out there, ranking in the 83rd percentile among all players.

Additionally, the Nets' effective field-goal percentage improves by 3.2 percentage points with him on the floor, while the offensive rebounding percentage also rises by 8.3 percentage points. The latter ranks in the 96th percentile among players who have logged a minute this season. For context, he has only played 244 minutes this season, but those numbers are still fascinating.

Even more interesting is how he's been used. After opening the season outside of Jordi Fernández's rotation, Wolf has worked his way into the lineup, but in an odd spot: as the Nets' starting shooting guard. How many people had that on their bingo card entering the season?

In fact, six of his seven starts this season have come at the 2.

Against the Magic on Friday night, Fernández inserted Wolf into the starting five for Dëmin, and Wolf responded with a 20-point outing. In his second straight start, against the Minnesota Timberwolves on Monday, he finished with 11 points, four assists, and five rebounds on 4-of-7 shooting, including 3-of-5 from deep.

As our own Anthony Puccio noted earlier this month, Wolf played every second of his initial breakout performance against the Charlotte Hornets alongside either Sharpe or Wagner. That trend has held mostly true since then, letting him work away from the basket and avoid many traditional big responsibilities.

Is he truly a 5 in the NBA? There need to be more reps to make the case for or against it, but he doesn't ideally fit as a shooting guard. At 6'11", it's just not a natural fit, and it is easy for him to get exposed guarding shifty playmaking guards at the top of the key. Even though he was a ball handler at Michigan, being a guard in college versus the NBA are two completely different responsibilities. Nonetheless, the versatility is highly encouraging.

Regardless of where Wolf ultimately settles in the long term, he and Wagner have given the Nets more offensively than anyone could have asked for before the season.

#2773. Cathie Wood’s Ark Invest was a big buyer of Anthropic as she tells CNBC she’s ‘quite optimistic’

Cathie Wood was a major buyer of Anthropic following its debut Thursday on the Nasdaq, adding shares in all her major funds.

Wood's firm, which already owned private shares of the artificial intelligence company in its Ark Venture Fund leading up to the initial public offering, bought $90.8 million worth of Anthropic in six funds, according to a trade notification from the firm.

"We've owned Anthropic since early '23," Wood told CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Friday. "It's our best performing equity by far in ARKVX, our venture fund. ... Our confidence has grown with time as it really took over the enterprise" AI business.

Anthropic shares jumped 17% in their first day, but closed well off the highs of the session and were headed for sizable losses Friday. The Nasdaq, which was expected to get a boost from a major IPO reviving enthusiasm about the technology trade, fell by 2% on Thursday.

"We're climbing a wall of worry," said Wood. "Everybody is worried about AI hype and the political situation after the election, but I think we'll look back and say, OK this is more like the '80s and '90s, climbing a wall of worry you know with bricks much like what we have today: inflation, interest rates, wars, new technologies and so forth so quite optimistic here."

The Anthropic stakes are relatively small across the funds, but Wood typically will buy shares in companies she likes steadily during long stretches. Wood said she is "averaging down" with her purchases of Anthropic.

In her $6.1 billion Ark Innovation ETF, Anthropic is a 0.3% stake. The biggest holdings in that fund are Tesla and SpaceX, representing more than 21% of the fund together.

Ark Innovation, which retail investors piled into during the pandemic as it gained about 150% in 2020, tumbled the subsequent next two years, losing 67% in 2022 alone. Wood's following was dented after the big losses.

The fund had a comeback stretch as the bull market revved back up from 2023 to 2025, but has fallen on hard times again this year, down more than 10% in 2026. The S&P 500 is up 4.8% this year.

Wood dismissed comparisons of today's environment to the dot-com bubble.

"Back then if an Anthropic had gone public, it probably would have gone up threefold the first day," she said. "That's how crazy things were."

#2772. Mike Tomlin on current Steelers situation: "It's a dumpster fire"

Many folks in and around football have had opinions about the recent brouhaha between former Steelers quarterback Aaron Rodgers and Steelers coach Mike McCarthy. Few have the insight and perspective that former Steelers coach Mike Tomlin brings to the table.

Appearing on NBC's Chiefs-Bills halftime show on Thanksgiving night, Tomlin shared his thoughts on the situation in a conversation with Mike Tirico. (A portion of it was on the live broadcast; the full interview is here.)

"I had a range of emotions watching those course of events yesterday," Tomlin told Tirico. "I think the prevailing one is just general sadness. Sad on a micro level, sad on a macro level. And by that, I mean, you know, just from an individual perspective, sad that we might be looking at the end of a legendary career of the quarterback, Aaron Rodgers, and just on the macro level, whether it's organizationally or for the game of football at large, to see laundry aired out that way in a public forum.

"Those are things that kind of run counterculture to professional football. So, just a lot of emotions, but probably more than anything, man, general sadness on a lot of levels."

Tirico asked Tomlin if he was shocked by Rodgers's decision to air dirty laundry in a public forum.

"It certainly did," Tomlin said, "but, you know, and particularly because I know both men involved, certainly had a lot of intimate work and development of relationship with Aaron over the last couple of years, and have known and competed against Mike, you know, respected and appreciated him as a coach for a long time. But I don't — what I acknowledge is I don't know them as a collective, the nature of their relationships, and so certainly I was surprised by that."

Regardless of Rodgers's conduct on the way out the door, Tomlin explained that Rodgers was viewed favorably by his teammates in 2025.

"He was beloved, and I'm not, you know, over-exaggerating that," Tomlin said. "He worked at it, and people appreciated his openness to getting to know and understand the Steeler culture, to be engaged with teammates, and particularly from my perspective, I worked with a lot of veteran players over the years and at times they lose a little patience for the process, or they lose patience for relationships with younger guys, et cetera. Man, he seemed to embrace all of that and really embrace it in a real, natural way. He was a tireless worker regarding the process.

"I called early-morning quarterback meetings on Wednesday and Thursday. He was always early and engaged. Did a heck of a job in terms of engaging and developing, assisting in the development of young players. Specifically, Will Howard was always in that meeting, and, shoot, man, [Rodgers] and I were shoulder-to-shoulder in terms of the development of Will and challenging Will to develop professional habits. And so, you know, it was early and extremely consistent during my time with him, in terms of his willingness to work in those areas, and I think that's why he's so beloved in that locker room, as been reported by multiple sources in light of this incident. That is real. The guys in that locker room love and appreciate Aaron Rodgers."

Had Tomlin gotten any sense that things were so close to breaking down?

"Absolutely none, but it's a really specific reason why, to be honest with you, man," Tomlin said. "One of my cultural mantras, when I worked there for the 19 years, is don't talk to people about your problems unless they can be a component of the solution. Because if you do, it's counterproductive, and people know where I stand there. And by that I mean if you have a problem with your playing time, don't talk to your teammate about it. Talk to somebody that can do something about it. That's problem solving.

"And so everybody understands my posture on some of that stuff, and so although I have really good, fluid communication with many of those guys, particularly, the more veteran guys, they know me and know me well enough to know that I didn't want to hear about any potential issues, because I'm not a component of the solution. And so although, particularly, like, Cam Heyward, he and I spent a little time together doing his bye week. Man, we had no mention of anything bubbling under the surface, if you will."

Can McCarthy effectively lead the team, given what Rodgers said?

"You know, it certainly created some challenges and challenges is probably an understatement if all of those things are true," Tomlin told Tirico. "And certainly the '1-2-3 Packers' is, because he acknowledged that. But his ability to overcome that or inability to overcome that in my opinion is based on relationships and the depth of those relationships and how those guys feel about him, or how those guys buy into what he's selling. And so, certainly, he's been there a short period of time. And so it makes you wonder, the level of that challenge. But it'll be relationship-based, his ability to overcome the things that you mentioned."

How does Tomlin think the Steelers will fare against the Broncos on Friday?

"Based on my knowledge of the men, particularly the leaders, the longstanding guys, they'll do a great job of getting hyper-focused on what really matters, and that's that football game," Tomlin said. "They'll use it as a mantra to bring them together. I expect those guys to fight. Now, fight and quality play are two different things. I'm certainly not gonna expect those guys not to fight. I think they're gonna fight and fight extremely hard. What I'm interested in is quality of play, quality of execution. And those are things that could be impacted by the level of distraction that they had on a short week in particular."

Tirico then asked Tomlin how he feels, overall, about what has transpired this week.

"I'm upset about it, you know, it's a dumpster fire," Tomlin said. "And I don't say that in a judgmental way. I presided over a few dumpster fires in my 19 years. But it certainly is upsetting, and I'm sure Steeler Nation is upset."

If owner Art Rooney II calls Tomlin for advice, what would Tomlin say?

"Hey, Mike, that's a hypothetical, because I know he wouldn't and, and because I know how he's trained," Tomlin said. "You know, Art is a guy that's not a hedge fund guy that bought a football team. He's not a, you know, artificial intelligence guy that bought a football team. This is a family business. It's generational. Any advice or thought process in that way, I imagine he just says, 'What would my dad do?' Or, 'What would my grandfather do?' Their mode of operation is time tested, it's generational. And so, I doubt, very, very seriously, that he called anyone for outside advice."

Finally, Tirico asked whether Tomlin believes Rodgers will get another NFL opportunity this season, if he wants one.

"There's certainly a possibility for that," Tomlin said. "And I just say that based on the 19 years that I held the position that I held. It's a 32-team league. All it takes is one. Over time, I've laughed and watched that people talk about, you know, 'No, that could never happen.' In a 32-team league, when everybody is highly competitive and there's some real challenges, particularly as you get to this portion of the journey from a player availability standpoint, there's certainly a possibility if he desires that he could play again, because all it takes is one suitor."

Having cleared waivers, Rodgers is available to that one suitor, if/when that one suitor calls. Still, that one suitor will need to be willing to accept the risk that, if Rodgers doesn't have things go the way he wants, he'll choose to do again the same thing he did this week.

#2771. Liesman: Why Greenspan could bet on productivity — and Warsh needs to hike

In a discussion on CNBC's Halftime Report Wednesday, the question came up: Why can't Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh hold the line on interest rates the way his icon Alan Greenspan did at the beginning of the dot-com era?

Greenspan famously leaned against inflation hawks on his committee in 1995 and 1996, holding the line on interest rates amid strong growth, because he believed in the productivity promise of the internet revolution.

It would be nice if Warsh could follow the same playbook amid the artificial intelligence build-out and keep rates steady until the productivity arrives. Unfortunately, a quick look at the numbers shows just how different the situation is for Warsh when it comes to inflation, the magnitude of the capital-investment boom and the monetary and fiscal stimulus boosting the economy.

Bottom line: the Fed looks like it has to hike — and maybe substantially — to be anywhere close to the position where the Fed was in Greenspan's time at the dawn of a major technological revolution.

It may be that the massive capex spending on AI will mean more productivity and less inflation down the road. But the front-end build-out is proving to be more inflationary, and more challenging, to a Fed already dealing with high inflation. In many ways, that's the opposite of what Greenspan had to handle.

#2768. Buyer beware? Nvidia's volatile swings expose risks of single-stock ETFs

Nvidia's latest bout of volatility is highlighting risks tied to single-stock exchange-traded funds.

Among the hardest hit: the GraniteShares 2x Short NVDA Daily ETF (NVD). The fund sank 63% on Monday after Jensen Huang got reinstated as the chip giant's CEO. Meanwhile, the firm's 2x Long NVDA ETF (NVDL) soared nearly 62% on the same day.

ETF Action founding partner Mike Akins joined "ETF Edge" as Nvidia shares soared 31% during Monday's session, wiping a large portion of the losses from the days following Huang's resignation. Shares cooled on Tuesday and Wednesday, however.

"Historically speaking, we do not see these types of large drawdowns followed by huge drives up in a healthy market," Akins said on Monday. "It usually tends to be when you're in a recession or in a bear market territory, which we're not technically in for the broader market, but we are in for this AI trade."

But it may not be time to go cold turkey on single-stock funds.

"[Leveraged ETFs are] definitely a retail trading vehicle…  I think it's OK to have a little fun trying to trade that," Akins added. "I'm certain there are people that are better at trading these than others. But on the whole, timing the market is very, very hard."

GraniteShares founder and CEO Will Rhind also joined "ETF Edge" on Monday as Nvidia single-stock short ETFs overshadowed his firm's new Anthropic launches: The 2x Short Anthropic Daily ETF (ANS) and the 2x Long Anthropic Daily ETF (AIL).

"We thought this was going to be the biggest news event of the day with Anthropic the first leveraged ETFs going live," he said. "I can tell you this is like a sideshow compared to what we're seeing with Nvidia."

Rhind suggests Nvidia's wild swings aren't dampening enthusiasm for single-stock ETFs.

"As long as there's enthusiasm in the underlying name… people will want to trade it and most likely want to trade it with leverage either on the long on the short side," added Rhind.

"Fast Money" tackled the risks tied to ETFs that are tied to single stocks, too.

"If this is somehow part of a portfolio, [then] that is a dangerous game to be playing," trader Guy Adami said on Monday.

Karen Finerman also addressed the strategy's downsides.

"Leverage is always the thing that kills. It's always leverage," said Finerman, co-founder and CEO of Metropolitan Capital Advisors, in the same interview. "You can survive anything but leverage."

As of Wednesday's close, the GraniteShares 2x Short NVDA Daily ETF plunged 55% so far this week while the GraniteShares 2x Long NVDA Daily ETF is up 31%.

#2766. ‘Beyond Ridiculous,’ ‘Such a Bad Call’ — NFL Legend Terrell Owens Joins Former Players’ Outrage Over Refereeing Controversy In Chiefs vs. Bills

Thanksgiving night in Orchard Park came down to the final kick, but a controversial catch that was ruled incomplete stole the spotlight and sparked debate among former players.

Tyler Bass drilled a 57-yard field goal as time expired to give the Buffalo Bills a 13-10 win over the Kansas City Chiefs, after a fourth-quarter catch by Chiefs wide receiver Rashee Rice was ruled complete on the field and then overturned on review.

NFL legend Terrell Owens joined Robert Griffin III, Chad Johnson, Gehrig Dieter and Kurt Benkert in criticizing the officiating on Thursday night in what was a truly thrilling matchup with serious implications in the AFC's playoff race.

Bass tied it at 10-10 with a 54-yard field goal early in the fourth quarter, and Harrison Butker missed a field goal attempt at the end of Kansas City's 11-play answer. With the score still tied, Buffalo's next drive stalled after six plays, and its punt pinned the Chiefs at their own 9 with two minutes left.

Patrick Mahomes then found Rice for what was ruled a catch and a first down on the field. But replay review flipped it to an incompletion and ended the drive. That said, replays did show the tip of the ball touching the ground.

"If that wasn't a catch, NOTHING is," Owens wrote, adding that "these calls by refs are beyond ridiculous." Owens did so even though he was "actually barracking for my Buffalo Bills."

By the time Owens weighed in, Rate The Refs had already broken down the replay.

Former Chiefs wide receiver Dieter also zeroed in on how little the ball moved after its tip reached the turf. "The ball literally does not move! That's such a bad call," he wrote.

Although the tip of the football touched the turf, that alone does not constitute an incompletion under NFL rules. According to the postgame pool report, replay officials determined that Rice lost control of the football as he made contact with the ground.

PREDICT THE NFL SEASON: PFN's Free NFL Playoff Predictor

Former NFL QB and Heisman winner Robert Griffin III also saw it the same way. "Chiefs fans HAVE EVERY REASON TO BE UPSET. THAT WAS A CATCH BY RASHEE RICE," he wrote.

While Griffin and Dieter focused on whether Rice made the catch, former Green Bay Packers quarterback Kurt Benkert did not mention Rice or the play. Instead, he took aim at the officiating as a whole.

"There's more money than ever floating around on NFL games, and the ref issue is getting worse by the week," he wrote. "I don't like this version of football that's going on at all, and I want the commissioner to save our sport."

Former Bengals receiver and "Nightcap" co-host Chad Johnson also weighed in on the controversy. "Every week it's some….Never mind," he tweeted, before biting his tongue.

The reversal forced Kansas City to punt from its own 9, and Buffalo took over at the Kansas City 47 with 1:40 left, already on Kansas City's side of the field. The Bills could not cash in right away, losing 6 yards on a three-and-out and punting it back.

Kansas City went three-and-out from its own 11 on the next series, and its punt gave Buffalo the ball at the Kansas City 39 with four seconds to play. Notably, Bass' winner came on that possession, the Bills' second after the review.

Buffalo is 10-1 and first in the AFC East, and Kansas City is 8-3 and second in the AFC West.

#2765. How Trump’s latest tariff moves hand India an edge over rival Asian exporters

The latest U.S. tariff rates announced Wednesday have signaled that Washington is willing to offer India an edge over its competitors if New Delhi agrees to finalize a long-pending trade deal.

The Office of the United States Trade Representative has proposed a tariff of 17% on Indian exports if New Delhi "were to reach an Agreement on Reciprocal Trade" with Washington. It added that without a trade deal, India could face tariffs of up to 25% under Section 301 investigations encompassing excess production capacity that harms U.S. interests.

Meanwhile, the USTR has proposed tariffs of 18% on Bangladesh, Cambodia, Thailand, and 20% on China and Vietnam, subject to their respective trade deals, handing India a competitive advantage over rival exporters.

The U.S. expects the announcement of a lower tariff rate will encourage New Delhi to sign off on a trade deal before the G20, Atman Trivedi, partner at Washington-based DGA Albright Stonebridge Group, told CNBC.

India has got a "better bargain with Washington than its main competitors," and it may be enough for the Indian government "to declare victory and secure domestic backing for the deal," Trivedi said.

In February, U.S. President Donald Trump had announced a deal with India, claiming that New Delhi had accepted to "Buy American" at a much higher level after the U.S. agreed to slash tariffs to 18% from 50% earlier.

The India-U.S. trade deal has been pending with both sides indicating there was little room to grant concessions, while the Supreme Court annulling Trump tariffs allowed New Delhi to demand preferential tariffs that give it an edge over competitors.

"Today's announcement increases the urgency of reaching an agreement," Ronak D. Desai, visiting fellow at Hoover Institution, Stanford University, told CNBC. He added that while the prospect of a 17% tariff may strengthen the economic case for the deal, the threat of a 25% tariff could stir the sensitivity of the Indian government.

"The Modi government will be particularly sensitive to any perception that India is conceding under American Pressure," Desai said.

India's commerce ministry on Wednesday said it "does not have structural excess capacity in any sector," denying the findings of the USTR investigation, but added that it remains committed to "working closely with the United States towards the early conclusion of the India-U.S. Bilateral Trade Agreement."

Despite India facing steep tariffs, which were raised to 50%, New Delhi's trade surplus with the U.S. rose to $57.3 billion in 2025 from $45.2 billion in 2024.

Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Trump are likely to meet in December for the G20 leaders' meeting in Florida, and several experts believe the two leaders could seal the trade deal on the sidelines of the summit.

#2764. Eagles vs. Cowboys Thanksgiving: The good, the bad, and the ugly

Nick Sirianni had to be redirected away from the stands more than a few times by the Eagles' media relations team at AT&T Stadium. He tried to high five everyone wearing midnight green Thursday afternoon. The Eagles were dead two times, three times, 10 times, it seemed, and they managed to stage the largest Thanksgiving Day comeback in NFL history, overcoming a 21-point deficit (31–10) to beat the Dallas Cowboys, 39-38, in one of the most improbable victories games in Eagles' memory.

It sets the Eagles up to now become NFC East contenders, considered where the Eagles were two weeks ago.

The Eagles never gave up. They were banged up, without Cooper DeJean, Dallas Goedert, relying on Ty Robinson's blocked punt, and pivotal nine-yard sack that turned the ball over and set up Jake Elliott's game-winning 59-yard field goal with 2 seconds left.

The pickup from the Cowboys' practice squad hauled the Eagles from a 31-10 deficit to complete 21 of 31 passes for 331 yards and three touchdowns being named MVP of the game.

DeVonta Smith was amazing in a career-high game, catching a career-high 11 passes for a career-high 200 yards on 14 targets.

It is a signature victory in Sirianni's six years.

The Eagles are now 4-7 with the lowly Arizona Cardinals and Indianapolis Colts next, two teams with a combined 6-16 record, which could bring the Eagles to 6-7 record with Seattle coming to Lincoln Financial Field on Dec. 19.

The Eagles are still at the bottom of the NFC East, but in a position to push the 6-3-1 New York Giants, and the 4-5-1 Washington Commanders.

The Eagles' 20 fourth-quarter points exceeded the 17-points per game the Eagles were averaging this season.

The Eagles continued playing hard for Sirianni.

He still made dubious choices, like the decision to go for a two-point conversion after Milton's 15-yard TD run with 9:09 left to play, and the Eagles trailing 38-30.

The Eagles were down at one point 31-10 with 3:35 left in the third quarter, then proceeded to score on four of the next five drives.

There was a lot of good, some bad and some ugly in the Eagles' 39-38 win over the Dallas Cowboys.

Joe Milton exploding on national TV in completing 21 of 31 passes for 331 yards and three touchdowns. He just had a habit of coming up in clutch situations to make big plays. He probably made himself a pile of money from some NFL team, too, whether the Eagles are in his future or somewhere else. Wherever he goes, no Eagles' fan will forget what he did on Thanksgiving Day 2026 against the Dallas Cowboys, bringing a dead team back to life.

Ty Robinson's blocked punt and Kenny Moore's 3-yard scoop and score suddenly made what looked like a blowout into a game. Robinson came slicing through the line and dove at Dallas punter Bryan Anger to catch the punt with his right hand, and Moore ran after the loose ball and gathered it in for a three-yard score. Robinson later came up with a huge nine-yard sack at the Eagles' 48 with 55 seconds left, setting up the Elliott game-winner.

Jake Elliott coming through big again. He was 2-for-2 on a 48- and 59-yard game-winning field goal. This came after Elliott went 4-for-4 the previous week against Pittsburgh with field goals of 41, 29, 53 and 55 yards. Elliott is 13 of 14 on field goal attempts, and 21 of 21 on extra points—including 5-for-5 on field goals attempts of 50 yards or more. Sirianni is going to have to think more of Elliott kicking field goals instead of trying to go for it on fourth down. What sometimes gets lost is Elliott is a two-time Super Bowl champion who has made huge field goals in huge games.

DeVonta Smith seemed to be the only weapon the Eagles had, and despite added attention, he caught a game-high 11 passes for a game-high 200 yards on 14 targets, including 50- and 45-yard touchdown catches. It was Smith's 45-yard TD catch with 15 seconds left in the third quarter that continued to make the game intriguing pulling the Eagles within 31-17.

Milton's 50-yard rainbow to DeVonta Smith for the Eagles' only touchdown in the first half. Milton was about the only thing the Eagles had going in the first half. Otherwise, it was bad.

Two of Milton's first three passes converted third downs. They were the first two good signs the Eagles might be able to move the ball against the NFL's 31st defense. Milton's first completion was a nine-yard completion to Dallas Goedert on a second-and-eight to the Eagles' 17. Three plays later. Milton connected with Smith for a 16-yard reception to the Eagles' 35. Of course, the Eagles blew it by going for it on fourth-and-one at the Dallas 37.

Money on third down. Milton completed eight of his first 11 passes, three of which came on third down. On the Eagles' first drive, he hit Smith for 16 yards on a third-and-8, and on third drive, he hit Makai Lemon for 20-yard pass on a third-and-12 to the Dallas 34. It led to Elliott's 48-yard field goal.

Byron Young with nine tackles from the defensive tackle position. He had five solo tackles, assisting on four.

Jeremiah Trotter Jr. continues to lead the defense. Every time the linebacker out of St, Joe's Prep and Clemson has started this season, he has led the Eagles in tackles. Thanksgiving against Dallas was no different, with a game-high 12 tackles, seven solo, with a sack and two tackles for loss. Trotter is now second on the Eagles in tackles with 64 tackles, although has a team-high 41 solo tackles.

Cobie Durant's interception with 7:05 to play seemed to seal the victory for the Cowboys after the Eagles' fourth stop of the game. Brandon Aubrey missed a gimme 40-yard field goal attempt bailed out the Eagles.

The Eagles losing Cooper DeJean, Saquon Barkley and Dallas Goedert to injury in the first quarter. Not that it mattered.

Cornerback Quinyon Mitchell flagged with pass interference on the very first play of the game. The 17-yard call took the ball from the Dallas 23 to the Cowboys' 40 and jumpstarted one of the NFL's most potent offenses. Mitchell was called for two pass interferences penalties for a total of 46 yards. It was not a good game for Mitchell, who was later burned for a 39-yard completion on a second-and-16 right after the Eagles' blocked punt score. The quick euphoria the Eagles had after the blocked punt was quickly zapped on a Dak Prescott 14-yard touchdown scramble with 10:11 to play.

The Eagles first half. Everyone may have given up by then and began eating their Thanksgiving Day dinner. The Cowboys scored on four of their first five drives. They had outgained the Eagles, 245 to 169, had 17 first downs to the Eagles' eight, and the Eagles committed penalties for 71 yards, including Quinyon Mitchell's second interference call for 29 yards, and Riq Woolen's 10-yard interference call leading to the Cowboys' last touchdown in the first half. The Cowboys converted 6 of 7 third downs to the Eagles' 2 of 5.

With 5:09 left in the first half, the Cowboys scored on three of their four possessions, had amassed 208 total yards of offense, averaging 8.3 yards a play, 12.9 yards a pass and 5.3 yards a rush. Zak Prescott was 6 of 10 for 129 yards and a touchdown.

Dak Prescott's 31-yard touchdown pass to Kavontae Turpin for a Cowboys' 14-0 lead with 36 seconds left in the first quarter. It looked like the route was on.

The Cowboys' second drive. This time,the Cowboys needed just five plays to score. But they came up with a big third-down play again, this time, on a third-and-16, when Prescott hit George Pickens for a 36-yard completion to the Eagles' 33. Riq Woolen made the tackle, and earned a benching again, but the Eagles were so depleted, they had to keep the problem on the field.

Sirianni opting to go for it on fourth-and-one at the Cowboys' 36, passing on a 53-yard field attempt by Elliott.

Will Shipley caught jawing on the sideline with Nick Sirianni in the first quarter, no doubt about playing time.

The Cowboys' first drive of the game. It was an 11-play, 77-yard drive that chewed up 6 minutes and 11 seconds off the clock. Of the Cowboys' 11 plays, they only faced three third downs—converting all of them. The true backbreaker was Prescott's 28-yard completion to CeeDee Lamb right down the middle of the field to the Eagles' 7. Three plays later, Javonte Williams scored from a yard out for a 7-0 Dallas lead with 8:50 to play in the first quarter. Of the Cowboys' first 11 plays, they threw it only three times, while Williams gashed them for 35 yards. It was the ghost of the previous Dallas game, when Williams sliced his way through the Eagles for 155 yards rushing, averaging 6.2 yards a carry. In the first game, the Cowboys ran 65 plays against the Eagles' defense for zero tackles for a loss. Dallas pounded the Eagles for 416 total yards, averaging 6.4 yards a game, with 204 yards on the ground, averaging 5.4 yards a carry. The Cowboys' first drive seemed to give loud warnings for another long day for the Eagles' defense.

There is a reason why Jihaad Campbell has struggled, it's because he gets lost in coverage. The linebacker once again managed to lose CeeDee Lamb on a third-and-18 on the Cowboys' first drive to the Eagles' 7. Campbell thought he was reading Prescott's eyes while Lamb ran right past him. It led to the first score of the game.

#2763. As Anthropic shares tank, investors scramble to hedge. It could be very expensive

As Anthropic shares tumble toward their IPO price of $83, investors are looking for ways to hedge. Unfortunately, they may have to wait until Monday, when options on the AI giant are expected to list.

If Anthropic breaks its IPO price, it will represent a 27% decline from Thursday's intraday high of $113. The wild price swings offer clues on how expensive it might be to buy protection on the new tech giant once options begin trading.A 20% intraday move points to an implied volatility somewhere between 100 and 150 for Anthropic options, according to estimates from single-stock market-makers on the Cboe trading floor in Chicago.

Options traders are also looking at how SpaceX traded in the days following its offering for clues on how options might price.

Implied volatility in SpaceX started at 116, but that didn't deter options traders big and small from piling into the contracts tracking the stock, with about 1.7 million contracts traded on the first day for a total options premium of about $2.5 billion. Far out-of-the-money call contracts were some of the most popular trades as the stock soared 40% in its first three sessions.One key difference between now and then? Anthropic is trading against the backdrop of S&P 500 volatility close to 30, compared to 17.3 when SpaceX debuted. "I expect ANT options to be super active," said Tom Sosnoff, co-founder of the trading platforms ThinkOrSwim and TastyTrade. "I expect heavy options volume."One thing Anthropic and SpaceX have in common is heavy retail involvement in both IPOs, with retail brokerages receiving a 20% allocation from SpaceX and reports pointing to between a 15-20% allocation from Anthropic on Thursday. "Round one of the Anthropic IPO easily goes to the individual investor," Sosnoff added. "Retail participants bailed early at the best prices of the day while institutional investors paid up to top off their underwhelming allocations. I believe retail was aggressively reloading in the mid-90s."Further signs of retail demand will become evident when options likely begin trading on Monday. One thing to watch: the spread between out-of-the-money call and put contracts, which was heavily skewed toward calls in the case of SpaceX. "I would be careful comparing Anthropic to SpaceX," said Dennis Davitt, CIO and Co-Founder of Millbank Dartmoor Portsmouth. "From a market-structure perspective, the two are dramatically different. The availability and cost of borrowing will be different, the companies are at very different stages of maturity, and SpaceX has allowed employees to monetize portions of their holdings over time. All of those factors matter when pricing options."

#2762. Planes, trains and automobiles: The best ways to beat travel fatigue—so you can come home feeling rested and fulfilled

Five-hour flights. Eleven-hour road trips. Fifteen-hour train rides. All potentially exhausting options for the annual tradition of convening around the dinner table with loved ones on Thanksgiving.

An estimated 81.5 million Americans are projected to travel, or have already traveled, at least 50 miles from their homes between Nov. 24 and Nov. 30, according to the American Automobile Association. And their mode of transportation is shifting: Fewer people are flying or driving this year compared to 2025, and more are traveling by buses, trains and cruises, AAA data shows.

High gas prices and soaring plane ticket costs may factor into the shift. As of Wednesday evening, fuel prices are roughly 17% higher than they were on the same date in 2025, according to AAA data. Meanwhile, "months of elevated jet fuel costs due to the conflict in Iran have contributed to Thanksgiving and Christmas airfares reaching 10-year highs," according to fare-tracking platform Hopper.

The alternate modes of transit may open travelers up to new experiences — and new forms of travel fatigue to keep you from returning home feeling rested and fulfilled. You're probably already familiar with the exhaustion you might get from a day of plane travel, for example. In airplanes, "there can be lower humidity, maybe lower oxygen levels at cabin pressure. Sometimes people report feeling more dehydrated or drained. You're adjusting to that change in altitude," says Alaina Tiani, a Cleveland Clinic behavioral sleep medicine psychologist.

But even waiting in places like train stations or cruise ports can feel draining due to sheer sensory overload, Tiani says. And then, depending on your mode of travel, you may still need to deal with cramped seating and limited ability to get up and walk around or drink some water and eat a snack.

Once you arrive at your destination, managing responsibilities like remembering where you put your hotel key and deciding what to eat and how to structure your day can also take a mental toll, says travel writer Shannon O'Donnell, who's written about managing travel fatigue. "All of that actually requires a lot more thinking and planning for your brain," she says, adding: "People just don't understand how those add up and why a relaxing vacation suddenly has them feeling wrecked."

The consequences can sneak up on you, O'Donnell notes. Travel fatigue can "present as maybe a lack of interest in something that you might usually find fascinating," she says. Instead of looking out the window on a plane ride or playing car games with your kids on a road trip, you might disengage and appear apathetic to the people around you.

You might stand a better chance of a fulfilling, restful holiday if you prepare for your travel fatigue. Here, Tiani and O'Donnell share their advice for how to do it:
