#2761. Fast cars, big money: Why sportswear races into Formula 1 as sponsorship spending soars 75%

The race for dominance in Formula 1 is no longer confined to the racetrack, with some of the world's biggest sportswear brands, including Nike, Adidas and Puma, vying for a piece of the action.

Sportswear sponsorship spending in F1 has surged 75% over two years and topped $200 million in 2026, according to Adam Lewis, a senior analyst at research firm Ampere Analysis.

Brands are competing for access to the sport's increasingly young and affluent fan base, while looking to capitalize on its growing influence in fashion and popular culture.

Nike gave fans a sneak preview of its F1 partnership in Las Vegas this month with a limited-edition collection sold during the Grand Prix. From 2027, Nike will supply F1 staff uniforms, a role Puma has held since 2024, and sell footwear and apparel under the championship's brand.

Other sportswear majors have taken a different approach. Adidas signed with Mercedes in 2025 and added Audi for its debut season this year, while Puma still has its longstanding deal with Ferrari, covering racewear and licensing for Ferrari-branded products.

Unlike football leagues such as the English Premier League, where sportswear brands spread their budgets across numerous clubs, F1 has just 11 teams, limiting the number of apparel partnerships up for grabs.

"F1, by contrast, is a closed market with only a handful of teams," Lewis said, adding that the scarcity of deals makes brands more willing to pay higher prices as contracts come up for renewal.

What makes F1 particularly attractive, however, is its growing influence.

"For major sportswear and lifestyle brands, F1 has grown beyond motorsport, into a powerful, year-round pop-culture and storytelling platform," Joey Khong, global consumer trends manager at market research firm Mintel, told CNBC.

F1 brings together fashion, music, luxury and celebrity culture with athletic performance and technological innovation, offering brands multiple avenues to engage with consumers, Khong said.

Team apparel has also crossed over into everyday streetwear, with social media amplifying the visibility of what drivers and team members wear off the track.

Some 34% of people who engage with F1 do so through social media, while 22% engage through online content, according to Lewis.

That constant stream of content has turned team apparel into what Lewis described as a "living billboard" for sportswear brands.

Nearly a third of F1 fans are now under the age of 35, with that share rising 18% since 2023, according to Lewis. Meanwhile, 45% of F1 fans fall into the two highest-earning socioeconomic groups, compared with 36% of the general population.

For sportswear brands, F1 offers a way to build loyalty among younger, affluent consumers.

Asia-Pacific has been a key driver of F1's fan growth, helping deliver a larger audience for its commercial partners, analysts said.

Markets across the region have gained more than 25 million F1 fans since 2023, up 36%, according to Ampere Analysis. That outpaced growth in other markets by 11 percentage points and accounted for 84% of overall fan growth.

That offers sportswear brands a growing audience to engage with in a region where F1 already races in Melbourne, Suzuka, Shanghai and Singapore.

Research also points to why that engagement could resonate. In a 2026 Mintel survey, 29% of respondents in China said sporting events would prompt them to pay attention to or try related brands, rising to 37% in households earning at least 24,000 yuan ($3,600) a month.

Fans are spending more on F1 merchandise than ever before.

F1 merchandise sales have grown by almost 200% since 2017, according to Fanatics, the sport's e-commerce partner, cited in a License Global report.

Retail sales of F1-licensed consumer products also rose 44% in 2024, one of the fastest growth rates among the sports properties tracked.

The appeal may stretch beyond race-branded gear. F1 fans were 29% more likely than the average consumer to say they planned to buy sports apparel in the next year and 27% more likely to say the same about non-sports apparel, according to Ampere's consumer research.

Mintel's Khong said F1 merchandise alone is unlikely to move the needle quickly for sports apparel giants the size of Nike or Adidas.

Instead, the bigger potential payoff could come from the partnership boosting demand across the brand's everyday product lines outside F1-specific collaborations or the sport's licensed merchandise.

"There is a route to revenue growth, but being associated with the sport is only the starting point," Khong said.

#2760. Kenny Smith Pays Backhanded Compliment To LeBron James When Explaining His Longevity

Philadelphia 76ers superstar LeBron James' longevity is quite remarkable, and he made history yet again on Wednesday. James broke his own record for the oldest player to record a triple-double in the 76ers' 111-104 win over the Miami Heat at Xfinity Mobile Arena.

It shouldn't be possible for a 41-year-old to play this well, and Kenny Smith thinks the rules are helping James. Smith explained the 22-time All-Star's longevity on Inside the NBA on Wednesday.

"We can't forget, without Luka [Doncic] in the playoffs, he dominated the first round of the series," Smith said. "And he still has that ability because the way the game is played today, obviously, with the lack of hand-checking, it is a parallel game. And so what happens is if you're like a track star, and he can just stay in track shape, and he's pushing the ball like a track star and not getting touched, not getting slowed down.

"And he's still 6'9″, 240 lbs, and can still move on a track pace," Smith added. "And the NBA is still in danger with him on the floor."

The NBA banned hand-checking in 2004, and Smith believes James wouldn't be as effective at his age were it still allowed. The 61-year-old thinks his athleticism and size are enough to succeed in today's league, which is quite the backhanded compliment.

Yes, James being a very good athlete helps, but he is still very skilled, and his mind remains sharp. It's the combination of all three that still enables him to dominate games.

James shone for the Los Angeles Lakers in Luka Doncic's absence in the first round of the 2026 NBA playoffs against the Houston Rockets. The Lakers had been written off going into the series, but he led them to victory in six games.

We saw that version of James again against the Heat, as he had 25 points (9-15 FG), 10 rebounds, 12 assists, and one steal. He scored 14 points in a row for the 76ers at one point in the second quarter, and we're so blessed to still see him in action. James doesn't always have to take over with all the talent around him, but made it clear he can dust off the cape when need be.

The 76ers improved to 15-4 with this win over the Heat and remain atop the standings in the Eastern Conference. They are definitely a serious title contender, and James has his eyes set on winning his fifth championship. While some believe this would help his GOAT case, others don't. Smith likely falls in the second category. He has made it clear that Michael Jordan is his GOAT.

Smith has also said James is touching the Magic Johnson-Larry Bird "fiber," not the Jordan "fiber." He believes defense is what separates his former UNC teammate from LeBron.

James isn't going to get any better defensively at his age, of course. He'll continue to be a big threat on offense, though, and he'll be in action next when the 76ers take on the Indiana Pacers at Gainbridge Fieldhouse on Friday at 7:30 p.m. ET.

#2759. China’s factories are growing profits again, but the AI boom is picking the winners

China's industrial profits in October grew at their fastest pace since May, supported by an AI-driven electronics boom and higher energy prices, while consumer-facing industries squeezed by weak demand continued to be a drag.

Profits at sizeable industrial firms surged 20.1% in October from a year earlier, according to data released Friday by the National Bureau of Statistics. For the first 10 months this year, the earnings grew 16% year on year, having risen 15.5% through September.

That extends a notable rebound in 2026 after three years of declines followed by a tepid 0.6% growth last year, with profits on track to log their strongest annual expansion since 2021.

Despite the sharp headline figure, "the recovery has yet to broaden into a more durable improvement in corporate profitability," said Tianchen Xu, senior economist at Economist Intelligence Unit, as the rebound was largely led by upstream sectors amid higher energy prices.

China's economy has been running at two speeds, with AI-related manufacturing and exports powering growth while household consumption has been lagging. Retail sales grew a smaller-than-expected 0.4% in October, and fixed-asset investment steepened declines to 8.1% in the first 10 months.

Profit gains were concentrated in a set of sectors tied to the global AI buildout and higher commodity prices, while consumer-facing manufacturers struggled to pass on higher input costs, squeezing margins.

Earnings in the electronics sector doubled in the first 10 months from the same period last year, as demand for AI computing power lifted memory chips and related manufacturing, said Yu Weining, chief statistician of the NBS.

Profits in high-tech manufacturing jumped 50.9%, outpacing the industry as a whole, Yu added. Makers of spacecraft and launch vehicles reported a 63.2% rise.

Commodity producers also saw sharp growth in profits as demand tied to renewable energy and AI pushed up copper and aluminum prices, Yu said. Petroleum processors swung to a combined profit from a loss a year earlier.

Showcasing an increasingly bifurcated economy, industries tied to consumers and construction recorded steepening losses. Automakers saw profits drop 26% in the first 10 months, wider than the previous month, as costs outpaced a modest revenue increase.

Producers of construction materials such as cement and glass, and furniture makers continued to suffer the fallout from a prolonged real estate slump, with profits falling 46.7% and 52.4%, respectively.

Accounts receivable, or money owed to businesses by their customers, and finished-goods inventories also grew faster than revenue, official data showed, underscoring the strain on companies across sectors.

Overall activity in October picked up "substantially" compared to the past couple of months, expanding 2.4% from a year earlier, according to Capital Economics' China Activity Proxy, a gauge that excludes official data in favor of low-profile indicators, such as freight and port traffic, that are "less politically-sensitive and so less likely to be manipulated."

The growth in October was led by strong external demand and exports, even as manufacturing activity for domestic goods languished, said Leah Fahy, senior China economist at Capital Economics.

Local governments stepped up fiscal spending for the first time since February last month, Fahy said, but that "had little impact" on arresting the property slump and reviving domestic demand.

"Local governments [are] clearly struggling to make full use of their allocated funds, [and] there is a limit to how much fiscal policy will be able to support the economy," Fahy added.

The AI-driven growth in external demand has reduced the need for Chinese policymakers to ramp up stimulus to support domestic demand and the overall economy. China's GDP growth of 4.6% in the first three quarters has put Beijing's annual growth target of 4.5-5% within reach.

As global AI-related investment starts to slow, exports would also become a "waning prop to growth," Fahy said, with overall economic expansion to decline to just 2.8% next year in her estimates, from 3.9% in 2025.

Adding to fresh headwinds on trade, the U.S. proposed new tariffs that include a 20% headline rate on Chinese goods and punitive rates on several Asian economies that analysts say have been targeted for transshipments to China. The levies would rise to 40% if the U.S.-China truce does not get extended beyond January.

"Chinese firms now export intermediate goods to the rest of Asia and reach the U.S. indirectly," said Alicia Garcia Herrero, chief economist for APAC at Natixis, adding that economies with more Chinese inputs may face higher tariff risks.

#2758. Nvidia chip buyers told to rule out Chinese renters to purchase GPUs, sources say

Neoclouds are being told they won't be able to purchase Nvidia chips if any of the computing capacity will be rented by Chinese companies, sources told CNBC.

It comes after a new rule restricting remote access to artificial-intelligence semiconductors was announced by the Trump administration on Nov. 16.

Chip sellers communicated the messaging to neoclouds after the announcement, which seeks to close an export controls loophole allowing Chinese companies to rent access to Nvidia's most advanced chips when hosted in data centers overseas, two people familiar with the situation told CNBC. The people asked not to be named when discussing private information.

The interim final rule was announced by the Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security, or BIS, and came into effect on Nov. 19. Previously imposed export controls have effectively banned the sale of the most advanced Nvidia chips to Chinese companies and their import into China.

Prior to the new rule's announcement, Nvidia had said it would not sell its chips to customers renting more than 50% of the graphics processing units, or GPUs, to Chinese companies, CNBC reported.

The new rule impacts the full supply chain, from the companies selling Nvidia chips to the neoclouds who rent access to computing power. Neocloud stocks have come under renewed pressure lately as investors questioned the sustainability of the AI boom.

Nvidia and the U.S. Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The change has prompted Nvidia chip sellers to look for new buyers of the semiconductor giant's GPUs, CNBC reported on Wednesday, citing three people familiar with the matter. Two of those people said it appeared chip sellers were seeking to offload GPUs because they were originally for use in data centers through which Chinese companies would rent access.

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told CNBC's "Squawk Box" on Wednesday that the new BIS rule was intended to close "loopholes."

"Some rules were issued by the Commerce Department last week to close off indirect access, either smuggling through places like Southeast Asia or remote access from data centers in third countries," he said.

U.S. lawmakers have been looking to clamp down on China's access to advanced compute.

Separately, Nvidia warned its customers that the proposed Remote Access Security Act — which has passed the House of Representatives but is yet to pass the Senate — would give the U.S. government broader authority to control access to cloud services, potentially exposing both parties to "legal action," sources previously told CNBC.

#2755. Prediction markets outlook for stocks in 2026 dims amid AI sell-off

As stocks continue their tech-driven sell-off, prediction markets traders are seeing a bleaker outlook for the remainder of the year.

On platform Kalshi, speculators place just 6% odds that the S&P 500 will cross 8,000 in 2026. On Oct. 13, those odds were as high as 72%.

Contracts ask traders if the S&P 500 will go above various levels in 2026, and they're resolved using data from S&P Dow Jones Indices.

On Friday, the Nasdaq Composite turned negative for the year as investors continued to dump tech stocks, primarily those with exposure to the artificial intelligence build-out. The Dow Jones Industrial Average and the S&P 500 fell into correction territory, too.

The S&P 500 has slashed its year-to-date gain to just over 2%.

The Stock Trader's Almanac in a Thursday note broadly agreed that the hopes for a December rally are fading, with the caveat that a "Santa rally" could still appear at the end of the year.

"The market is under pressure and more downside can't be ruled out," the note said.

The Stock Trader's Almanac sees 2026 following the year-end pattern of 2018, when the Federal Reserve was in a tightening cycle in a midterm year. The Fed is widely expected to hike rates at its December meeting.

In that scenario, the Stock Trader's Almanac thinks more churn is to come. "The low is more likely in mid- to late December than this week."

#2754. U.S. tariff-hike threats pile pressure on partners to sign trade deals

The Trump administration has unveiled a fresh tariff salvo on more than a dozen trading partners, with China, Vietnam, and India facing some of the steepest potential rates and mounting pressure to conclude trade deals with Washington.

The proposed tariffs, framed as curbing excess industrial capacity, start at 15% for the European Union, South Korea, Switzerland and Taiwan and rise to as much as 35% for Vietnam.

The U.S. Trade Representative's Office said it intends to cap the new duties at lower levels for countries that have completed trade deals or are still negotiating with Washington.

The overall impact on the region is likely to be limited, said Mark Williams, chief Asia economist at Capital Economics. The proposal "puts most of the targeted countries back where they were earlier in the year," he said, after the Supreme Court struck down Trump's emergency tariffs in February.

Still, the proposal could give some countries an incentive to speed up trade talks in order to lock in lower tariff rates, analysts said.

On Wednesday, U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said that the new policy likely will not take effect for months, with a senior U.S. official saying the duties could take effect as early as January.

China faces a capped rate of 20%, on top of an existing 25% tariff imposed during President Donald Trump's first term. The rate could rise to 40% if the trade truce reached in South Korea last October is not extended beyond January, the USTR said.

Beijing has rejected Washington's claim of excess capacity while vowing to take measures necessary to protect its rights.

On Thursday, Chinese Commerce Ministry spokesperson He Yadong called on Washington to "rectify its wrongdoing and return to the right track of resolving issues through dialogue."

He was responding to Washington's plan to raise tariffs following its Section 301 investigations, while the ministry also urged the U.S. to implement $30 billion of reciprocal tariff cuts agreed by the two sides in late September.

The renewed tensions come despite several conciliatory meetings between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping this year, as well as what Williams described as Trump's "apparent lack of concern" about allegations that Chinese technology firms have circumvented U.S. chip export controls.

The two leaders are expected to meet for a fourth time this year at the Group of 20 leaders summit in Miami in December.

"While not happy, Beijing seems prepared to live with the new rates provided that they don't exceed 20%," said Wendy Cutler, senior vice president at the Asia Society Policy Institute.

By retaining the option to raise levies if bilateral talks deteriorate, Washington is using the tariffs as leverage to "secure expected shipments of critical minerals and rare earths, and further purchases of U.S. agricultural goods," Cutler said.

Washington has warned that tariffs on Chinese goods could double to 40% if the USTR finds that Beijing is not engaging. "If the trade war did start up again, today's measures provide the U.S. with some ammunition," Williams said.

Even the sweeping actions against the other 13 trading partners appear aimed squarely at China, said Williams, who tallied that the word "China" appears 253 times in the USTR's report on Vietnam, and 315 times in the document on the European Union.

"Foremost among the 'unreasonable acts, policies, and practices' that these countries are criticised for is being slow to restrict imports and FDI from China," Williams said.

While the proposed tariffs generally lift average rates only modestly, India and Vietnam stand out because of the wider gaps between the rates they would face with and without a deal, analysts said.

India and Vietnam face proposed tariffs of 25% and 35%, respectively, but those rates could fall sharply to 17% and 20% if ongoing talks with the U.S. produce reciprocal trade agreements.

The two countries have "a strong incentive" to conclude deals with Washington to secure the lower rates, Cutler said.

Vietnam's trade ministry said Thursday that it was working with the U.S. to complete a trade deal as soon as possible, according to Reuters. India could also gain an edge over some Asian rivals through comparatively lower levies if New Delhi concludes its long-pending trade deal with Washington.

Singapore faces a similar challenge. The proposal sets a maximum potential rate of 20% on its exports, net of existing Section 301 tariffs, which could fall to 10% if it reaches an agreement on reciprocal trade with the U.S. or concludes other negotiations addressing the USTR's findings, according to Singapore's Ministry of Energy, Trade and Industry.

The ministry said it disagreed with the findings and was "very disappointed" with the proposed action, arguing that it failed to account for the structure of Singapore's economy.

Speaking to reporters, Deputy Prime Minister Gan Kim Yong said that about 33%, or 9.4 billion Singapore dollars ($7.2 billion) of direct exports will be affected, and the effective tariff rate on affected Singapore exports will rise to 10.3% from the current 7.8%, should Washington impose the highest levy of 20%. "I'm also very surprised that this has happened because this is not something that you would expect from an important major trading partner," Gan added, saying "We have been working together for many years, and we have an FTA with the U.S.," Gan said, referring to the U.S.-Singapore Free Trade Agreement that was in force since 2004.

Under the FTA, Singapore imposes zero tariffs on U.S. goods, while the U.S. has run a trade surplus with the city-state for more than 20 years, the ministry said. That surplus grew to $33 billion in 2025 from $27 billion in 2024.

Singapore said it would submit further comments during the public consultation period and urge the USTR to reconsider.

Exemptions for semiconductors and other electronics should cushion the impact on South Korea and Taiwan, whose economies are heavily concentrated in those sectors, analysts said.

The USTR singled out South Korea for its concentration in memory-chip production and what it described as outsized government support. Yet it excluded the country's chips from the proposed excess-capacity tariffs.

Taiwan, which faces an excess-capacity tariff cap of 15%, also benefits from exemptions for other electronics, including mobile phones and networking equipment. Its effective tariff rate would rise to about 9% from 6%, Williams estimated.

Switzerland was hit with a shock 39% tariff rate back in 2025, targeting significant exports, from chemicals and pharmaceuticals to gold, watches and chocolates. In November 2025, it negotiated a deal that slashed U.S. duties to 15% in return for a commitment to invest billions and increase manufacturing Stateside.

In March 2026, the U.S. launched further Section 301 investigations into Switzerland over "unfair or discriminatory trade practices," landing on a recommendation to impose an additional 15% tariff.

Switzerland's Economy Ministry told CNBC that the country rejected the allegations raised during the investigations and said it had already presented its arguments during bilateral consultations with the U.S. Treasury.

The ministry added that it assumed the latest recommendation was consistent with the deal struck in November 2025 and said it was in close contact with U.S. authorities as it reviews next steps.

Officials for both Switzerland and the European Union said during trade discussions last year that while they had a trade surplus with Washington in goods, the relationship was balanced when accounting for both trade and services, where the U.S. dominates in areas such as technology and finance.

Brussels said it was assessing the U.S. report but rejected its finding that Europe was a source of industrial overcapacity.

"To the contrary, Europe is among those most exposed to overcapacity," European Commission Spokesperson Olof Gill said in a statement.

"The EU and the U.S. share a real concern about global overcapacity, much of it state-driven and concentrated in third countries. We regret the lack of joint action," Gill said.

The EU expects any measure taken from the investigation to respect the existing joint agreement of a 15% all-inclusive ceiling on EU goods, Gill added.

EU trade ministers are due to speak with U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer on Monday.

Citi analysts noted they expected a hit on European retailers if the measures stay as announced, with the likes of Adidas, H&M, Puma and Primark potentially seeing downgrades on full-year 2027 earnings.

Inga Fechner, senior economist for global trade at ING, said in a Wednesday note that the U.S. "tariff wall keeps changing, but it isn't coming down," adding that "U.S. protectionism is becoming increasingly difficult to unwind."

While the newly Democrat-controlled Congress could try to restrict presidential tariff authority, remove individual duties or apply greater scrutiny via hearings and investigations, actually reversing the measures will be difficult while Trump retains veto power, she said.

"We don't think the blue wave will mark a return to free trade. The Biden years already showed that tariffs in strategically important sectors enjoy support across political camps."

Protectionist moves become more targeted, she added, adding to a complex system of country- and sector-specific duties based on different legal authorities.

— CNBC's Evelyn Cheng contributed to this report.

#2753. Tech German software major SAP is reportedly weighing cutting at least 10,000 jobs in AI push

SAP is preparing a plan to eliminate at least 10,000 positions as the German firm reshapes its software business for the artificial intelligence era, Bloomberg reported on Thursday, citing people familiar with the matter.

The report came as the company flagged a cybersecurity attack, but said it had found "no evidence of unauthorized access to customer business data."

"SAP has identified suspicious activity and promptly implemented the necessary measures to protect its customers and preserve the security of its services," a company spokesperson said.

"Our customers trust us to protect their data, and that remains our highest priority. In a highly dynamic threat environment, we will continue to strengthen our security to provide the secure and resilient environment our customers depend on."

The company did not respond to a request for comment on the reported job cuts. The number could change after labor negotiations.

Other software companies have also tied workforce reductions to AI initiatives, though for different reasons. WiseTech Global said in February it planned to cut about 2,000 jobs over two years as it integrated AI into its products and operations.

Atlassian said in March it would cut about 1,600 jobs partly to fund further AI investment, while Cloudflare said in May it would eliminate more than 1,100 roles as it moved toward an AI-first operating model.

In the U.S., employers cited AI in 121,401 job-cut announcements through October 2026, accounting for about 20% of the total, according to a Nov. 5 report from outplacement and executive coaching firm Challenger, Gray & Christmas.

SAP employs more than 110,000 people worldwide. Bloomberg reported that all departments had been asked to identify potential cuts, with product, engineering and sales in particular focus.

The company also underwent a reorganization in 2024, when it eliminated around 10,000 positions through a program that relied mainly on voluntary departures and retraining.

Its headcount later remained relatively flat as it hired for new roles, Bloomberg reported.

In 2023, SAP CEO Christian Klein told CNBC he did not necessarily expect a reduction in the workforce, saying he expected the company to grow and "accelerate" its total revenue.

The reported cuts come as Klein pushes SAP toward an AI-first strategy. This year, SAP completed four acquisitions — Reltio, Dremio, Prior Labs and TechWolf — and made strategic investments in AI-focused companies including Parloa, n8n and Conduct.

The acquisitions are intended to help SAP organize company data, develop AI models for business information and analyze workforce skills.

#2752. Trump demands probe into ‘record setting error’ after third-quarter GDP data gets massive revision higher

President Donald Trump on Thursday falsely deemed the latest gross domestic product revision a mistake, claiming that it should be "immediately investigated."

Data released Wednesday from the Commerce Department revealed that the U.S. economy exhibited much stronger growth for the third quarter than initially estimated, showing that real GDP grew at a 4.3% annualized rate. That was revised upward from the department's advance estimate of 3.4%.

That revision was a "RECORD SETTING ERROR," Trump said in a Truth Social post, suggesting that the initial release could have influenced the outcome of the 2026 U.S. midterm elections, where Democrats flipped both chambers of Congress and even multiple governorships.

"I would like to wish a Happy Thanksgiving to even those who issued fake Economic Numbers, just prior to the Election, and corrected them yesterday, three weeks late, showing that the GDP was actually 4.3%, versus 3.4%, A RECORD SETTING ERROR, and one so grave that it should be immediately investigated," Trump wrote.

However, the difference between the advance estimate and the figure in the second release is far from being an all-time record. It was the largest revision since the 1.2 percentage point revision seen in the second quarter of 2020.

On an absolute basis, the latest revision was tied for 16th among all revisions from the advance estimate to the second release since 1990. It also tied four other quarters with a similar 0.9 percentage point difference — and was approximately double the average revision of 0.43 percentage points for all 147 quarters.

The upward revision shows Trump's policies are "delivering results" that defy expectations, White House spokesman Matthew Middleton told CNBC.

Revisions to U.S. economic numbers are not out of the ordinary. Initial reports count on partial survey data and early estimates. Those data are later updated with more survey responses — which sometimes leads to changes from the initial reports.

GDP data is revised repeatedly over a five year period. By the time the final revision is done, the average absolute error from the second release to the final is 1.14 percentage points.

The advance estimate for Q3 U.S. GDP, which came just days before Election Day in early November, was still better than the figure economists had expected at the time. It also showed a significant step-up in growth from the second quarter.

Because that was a strong showing for the economy, some on Wall Street consider this week's revision to be a confirmation of the economy's recent growth trend.

Jim Baird of Plante Moran Financial Advisors said immediately following the release that it "reinforces an increasingly familiar tension" that the economy is "performing quite well, but its resilience also gives the Fed an even stronger case for further rate hikes."

"The economy isn't merely hanging in there. It continues to demonstrate considerable resilience, with consumers spending, businesses investing and few signs that restrictive monetary policy is creating significant cracks in the broader expansion," the firm's chief investment officer said.

Traders are currently pricing in a nearly 100% chance of a hike at the Federal Open Market Committee's December meeting, per the CME FedWatch tool. They're also anticipating an additional hike in January.

— CNBC's Jeff Cox and Fred Imbert contributed reporting

#2751. How Fury and Joshua changed British boxing forever

They have conquered the world, filled stadiums and transformed British boxing.

Now, after more than a decade of lingering tension and endless debate, Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua are finally preparing to share a ring.

They are from different worlds, with contrasting personalities and wildly different journeys to the summit of heavyweight boxing.

Fury is the unpredictable showman who dethroned a seemingly unbeatable champion. Joshua is the Olympic golden boy who became a global superstar.

Who is better? Who has achieved more? The arguments have raged in pubs, boxing gyms and across social media.

We may soon get our answer, but whatever happens when the first bell sounds in Cardiff in the early hours of 12 December, their greatest achievement may already be secure.

Together, Joshua and Fury have taken British heavyweight boxing to new heights, attracting wider audiences and inspiring the next generation.

Britain had produced heavyweight champions before, but for years many of the division's biggest fights took place overseas.

Lennox Lewis fought some of his defining bouts in Las Vegas and Memphis. Challengers travelled to Germany when the Klitschko brothers reigned.

In November 2015, Fury outpointed Wladimir Klitschko in Dusseldorf. Less than five months later, Joshua knocked out Charles Martin at London's O2 Arena to win his first world title in his 16th professional fight.

"Bosh, that's it. The revolution starts in that six-month period," said BBC Radio 5 Live boxing pundit Steve Bunce, who was interviewed for the BBC documentary Rivals: Fury v Joshua.

Joshua's former trainer Rob McCracken saw an early sign of his appeal in Birmingham, where a show sold out with Joshua on the undercard.

"I'm from Birmingham, and it's hard to get a big crowd that sort of size," McCracken says. Promoters soon realised Joshua was bringing in a different audience and could sell tickets almost instantly.

By 2017, Joshua was fighting in front of 90,000 fans at Wembley Stadium, where he stopped Klitschko, while Fury's trilogy with Deontay Wilder made him a box-office draw in the USA.

"The two of them have been in eight massive stadium fights over an eight-year period," Bunce says. "That's reshaping British boxing history."

Yet for all the domestic ground they broke, both men eventually helped export the division's biggest nights back overseas - trading British stadiums for Saudi Arabian paydays, with even this Cardiff homecoming bankrolled by Turki Alalshikh's 'Riyadh Season' and timed for an American streaming audience.

Fury and Joshua's reach extended beyond boxing. Joshua became a familiar face on chat shows, while Fury stepped into a WWE ring and welcomed Netflix cameras into his home.

Derek Chisora, who lost three times to Fury, could see that wider appeal in the crowd on fight night.

"You've got a guy who's running a hedge fund for £2.5bn having a drink with a guy who works for the local council," Chisora says.

Crossover contests - both faced former UFC champion Francis Ngannou, while Joshua fought YouTuber Jake Paul - reflected a sport increasingly blending competition with entertainment. But a lot of boxing fans viewed those fights as lucrative, low-risk detours that stalled the division.

Even so, that mainstream visibility turned Fury and Joshua into household names - and sustains Britain as a major centre of the division for another generation.

Today, a new wave of British heavyweights - Daniel Dubois, Fabio Wardley and Moses Itauma - are stepping into a landscape Joshua and Fury helped create.

Seven years after Joshua stopped Klitschko at Wembley, Dubois beat Joshua on the same ground. "Two legends of the sport," Dubois says. "What they've done for the sport in the last few years has been great."

Highly rated British prospect Leo Atang was 10 when he watched Joshua beat Klitschko on television at home in York and decided to give boxing a go. Seven years later, he won gold at the World Under-19 Championships.

Wardley remembers Fury's win in Dusseldorf as the night that "re-sparked a lot of people's love for boxing".

Yet for all Fury and Joshua have achieved, the one question has followed them both throughout their careers is: what would happen if they met in the ring?

After failed negotiations, lost titles and shifting circumstances, some believe their bout is arriving too late. Chisora describes it as "getting the last drink in the barrel".

For years, promotional politics, rival broadcast deals, and mutual risk aversion kept both camps protecting their commercial brands rather than risking undefeated records.

In the time it took to make the fight, both men lost twice to Oleksandr Usyk and Joshua was beaten by Andy Ruiz Jr and Dubois.

Fury's father John Fury did not even want the fight to take place.

"Both men are bigger than boxing, both men [are] bigger than the event. Leave them, they're both multi-millionaires. They don't need to fight," he says.

But former world champion Natasha Jonas believes legacy ultimately comes down to what fighters feel they have achieved.

"Legacies are a huge thing. Once you walk away, you want to be happy and satisfied with what you've done and what you've left behind," she says.

The reality is that - barring a late withdrawal - Fury and Joshua will put their reputations on the line in front of 80,000 fans in Cardiff.

But, whether their rivalry is settled in 12 rounds or a single punch, Fury and Joshua's wider legacy has been built over more than a decade of filling stadiums, drawing new audiences and making British heavyweight boxing a global attraction.

Two Italians have been killed after an alleged Iranian attack on Kuwait, Kuwaiti forces said Thursday.

Separately, Israel said Thursday that it was prepared to carry out strikes against Iran "at any moment," even without U.S. forces joining the effort, according to Israeli military spokesman Effie Defrin on Israeli broadcaster Kan.

The comments came after U.S. envoy Jared Kushner told a podcast Wednesday that Israel "needs to get out of the constant wartime mindset."

Israel has been pushing the Trump administration to back another offensive against Tehran, with Reuters reporting on Nov. 18 that Israeli spy chief Roman Gofman pushed for joint strikes when he met U.S. officials earlier in the month.

Late Thursday, President Donald Trump said on PBS that the U.S. had "victory at hand" in the Iran conflict and reiterated that victory would come "whenever I want it to be, to be honest."

Speaking during a Thanksgiving call with U.S. military personnel, Trump said Washington was still trying to give Iran "every chance to make a deal and save a lot of lives."

But he added that he was not sure whether Tehran would agree.

"Some people question why. Are they crazy? Maybe they are," Trump said.

#2749. What we learned from the Spurs’ loss to the Trail Blazers

One of the few things I hope for as a spectator is that teams playing the late-night game bring it. It's too hard to stay awake as it is after a long day, so fans need excitement to keep them from falling asleep. Fortunately, it was not a problem for these teams, yet the only issue the San Antonio Spurs had late was their basketball IQ.

I had this game circled on the calendar because the physicality was off the charts the last time they played on Nov. 7. It appears it was not a distant memory for the Portland Trail Blazers, as the ESPN broadcast highlighted how they felt embarrassed by that game and wanted their lick back. Nonetheless, it was grown-up hoops and it wouldn't be a surprise if these squads didn't like each other.

Wednesday night being an Emirates Cup game added to the fun because the winner would keep their hopes alive of getting to the quarterfinal, still needing to get by Friday's game. Keep in mind that getting to the next round guarantees the players $60,499 and half of that for the two-way guys.

I wish that coach Mitch Johnson hadn't stuck to his usual substitution patterns in the third quarter, because when Wembanyama sat the Spurs were instantly outscored by eight. They got back on track when Victor checked in to clean up the mess, and the team likely could have separated itself had he had a longer shift. Games like this with absences to key guys magnify every decision. While the most part Mitch was good, I shook my head as he tried to buy time for the starters with Carter Bryant and Ja'Kobi Gillespie at the start of the fourth.

Johnson was probably thinking about preserving his main guys for later games, but this wasn't this a big one? Every now and then, 40 minutes against good teams is not so bad, and he probably would have broken 50 points for the third time this year.

Aside from their cup chances, the three late turnovers and failure to stop Portland's two 3-pointers ruined Wemby's 44-point masterpiece. Of course, the Trail Blazers deserve credit, but the Spurs also beat themselves down the stretch. Stephon Castle's eight-second violation was a killer.

Props to coach Micah Nori. He has a serious team, while he's basically on a prove-it deal, and they've been without Ja Morant. A lot of it has to do with them having one of the most balanced teams in the league, and it helps that Damian Lillard is still one sport'a clutch shooters. He has come back from his Achilles tear with his first step intact, and his outburst in the second half was vintage.

Without De'Aaron Fox and Dylan Harper, the Spurs were without two of the league's best penetrators (sorely needed against a high-level defense) which is a big reason why Wemby was the only one to score more than six points in the lane. The Spurs only had two quarters in which the offense was running smoothly (posting a 112.1 offensive rating) and that is one of their four-worst showings of the season. Portland was able to slow them down by making them pass less often.

Wembanyama stepped up. He poured in jumpers as Portland got physical with him. He kept the pressure on Donovan Clingan and fouled him out with four minutes left. In the past, Wembanyama wouldn't always assert himself in those situations and now it's like radar is beeping when his man gets five personals.

The Spurs mostly get the shot they are looking for when running the horns set, which has a screen to the left and right for the ball handler. The team has the best results on these when the screener is the scorer and the ball handler is the decoy.

Bryant should model his game after Keldon Johnson's. The latter barely scored but has mastered the art of hustle and had 12 rebounds, including five offensive, on Wednesday.

Portland is arguably the best paint-attacking team in the league, averaging 61.7 drives per game, and Deni Avdija has a lot to do with that.

Wembanyama had 12 points in the third quarter when he was subbed out and had only logged 21 total minutes to that point. As his rampage was paused, I was reminded of the old joke about how the only person who could stop Michael Jordan was Dean Smith.

#2747. Cowboys vs. Eagles: Brian Schottenheimer tops our losers list

The Dallas Cowboys looked like they were going to run the Philadelphia Eagles out of AT&T Stadium on Thanksgiving.Then everything changed.

Dallas built a commanding 31-10 advantage before allowing the Eagles to storm back, turning what should have been a comfortable victory into a frantic finish. There were some outstanding individual performances, but also several familiar problems that ruined the afternoon and saw the Eagles secure a comeback victory.

It's hard not to lay a lot of the blame for this loss on the shoulders of head coach Brian Schottenheimer. His repeated inability to finish out games has crushed the Cowboys hopes this season.

Late in this game, Schottenheimer had a chance to be aggressive and go for the killing touchdown with Dallas up 38-36. Instead, once he got in field goal position he got conservative and played for the three points. Brandon Aubrey missed the kick.

Later in the fourth quarter, he had a 4th-and-1 decision to make. He chose about the worst avenue. Instead of punting, or kicking a long field goal, he went for it even though not converting would give the Eagles the ball close to field goal range. To make matters worse, while going for it, he didn't use Javonte Williams, or got Prescott out on the edge with a run/pass option. Instead, he called a drop back pass which resulted in a sack.

It was gross mismanagement of the end of the game.

Dallas stopped Philadelphia from running the football. Then Joe Milton and DeVonta Smith ripped the secondary apart. Milton threw for 331 yards and three touchdowns, averaging over 12 yards per attempt.

Smith was even more damaging, producing 11 catches for 200 yards and two touchdowns, including scores of 50 and 45 yards, those numbers are insanely brutal.

Dallas repeatedly allowed receivers behind the secondary and surrendered exactly the kind of explosive plays that have plagued this defense throughout the season. The Cowboys had Philadelphia buried at 31-10. The pass defense gave them a route straight back into the game.

This might have been the single worst play of the afternoon. Dallas led 31-17 early in the fourth quarter and simply needed to get the punt away. Instead, Philadelphia blocked Bryan Anger's punt and recovered it for a touchdown. Suddenly, a comfortable two-touchdown advantage became a seven-point game.

A blocked punt returned for a touchdown while trying to protect a fourth-quarter lead is about as bad as it gets. Then, of course, there's the missed Brandon Aubrey field goal that would have kept the game out of reach at the end of the fourth quarter. That field goal was crucial and he failed to connect the kick for three points. It's a brutal miss but it was just another addition to the miscues on special teams this week.

Dallas led 31-10, Philadelphia then scored 29 points while Dallas managed only seven. The Cowboys allowed a backup quarterback to turn what looked like a Thanksgiving demolition into a game that came down to the final minute.

The blocked punt played a major part, but this wasn't one isolated mistake. Explosive passes, penalties and defensive breakdowns all contributed. Dallas has shown repeatedly that it can build leads, but they haven't learned how to finish opponents. We've failed to see this repeatedly so don't expect it to change.

Dak Prescott gave Dallas everything it needed offensively. Prescott completed 19 of 28 passes for 291 yards and two touchdowns, while also adding a 14-yard rushing touchdown in the fourth quarter. He consistently attacked Philadelphia downfield, protected the football and kept answering whenever the Eagles threatened to take control of the game.

CeeDee Lamb continued his outstanding run of form. Lamb finished with seven receptions for 134 yards, averaging more than 19 yards per catch despite not finding the end zone.

His ability to create explosive plays consistently stretched Philadelphia's defense and opened opportunities elsewhere for George Pickens and KaVontae Turpin. Lamb has reached the stage where 100-yard performances almost feel routine.

Javonte Williams carried a massive workload and rewarded Dallas for sticking with him. Williams rushed 29 times for 101 yards and two touchdowns, while also catching a 12-yard touchdown pass from Prescott.

His one-yard touchdown opened the scoring, his 12-yard run extended Dallas' first-half advantage, and he later added the receiving score just before halftime. Three touchdowns on Thanksgiving is a pretty convincing way to land in the winner column.

#2746. ‘Done & Dumb!’ Cowboys Lose In Historic Fashion To Eagles On Thanksgiving

The semi-tanking Philadelphia Eagles – playing backyard football with little real motivation – somehow erased a 21-point deficit on Thursday to mount the largest Thanksgiving Day comeback in NFL history, beating the heavily favored Cowboys 39-38.

Dallas' loss dropped the Cowboys to 5-7, bringing on the reality of their slim-to-none playoff hopes. They have mastered the art of failing to win back-to-back games, and there has been another season-long constant under pack-your-bags head coach Brian Schottenheimer:

This is the dumbest football team I've ever seen.

Once again, reasons for me to testify to that same thing I've said in the last couple of weeks (which has caused an army of Cowboys-lovin' fans to come hard at me) are everywhere.

Want just one crunch-time mini-bundle? Multiple times in the final seconds, Eagles QB Joe Milton – the Cowboys' third-string practice-squad reject, if you will, who made Dallas look foolish for letting him go to Philly this season – was simply trying to throw the ball out of bounds to eat clock … and not even move closer for the eventual game-winning field goal.

Let me repeat: Philly, down by 2, had no designs on bothering to risk moving closer for the kick.

And yet multiple times, Cowboys defenders interfered with the intended receivers … even though the intended receivers weren't even intending to receive!

Dak Prescott put up fat numbers. CeeDee Lamb put up fat numbers. Javonte Williams put up fat numbers. Quinnen Williams put up fat numbers.

Said Prescott: "Pretty stunning. … (Numb) is a good description of how I'm feeling right now."

A team that has vehemently objected to the word "embarrassing" will now have that very word etched on its NFL gravestone. A coach who pretended to believe he is "elite" is now obviously over his head and inept. ("I would not anticipate coaching changes in the near future.") And a promising season – promising because the NFC East has never and will never be easier to win – is done.

The Cowboys are done … because the Cowboys are dumb.

A 40 VIX, which it touched Friday, might provide those opportunities. Amazon's cloud business is growing at its fastest pace in nearly five years. AWS revenue rose 39.3% YoY in the third quarter, and management reported a $578 billion backlog. Its shares are only off 14% from its recent highs, comparatively better than the Nasdaq Composite's near 19% decline.

AWS demand supports the lower end of the range. The backlog gives Amazon a basis for adding capacity even as investors scrutinize the cash cost. Cash spending could temper an upside rerating.

The next leg higher may require evidence that new capacity can earn attractive returns at this scale, and that evidence may be in short supply over the next couple of months.

Breakevens at expiration — $229.10 and $290.90.

#2744. Sovereign wealth funds are acting more like private equity giants — and inheriting their risks

For decades, sovereign wealth funds were among private equity's most deep-pocketed backers, entrusting billions of dollars to buyout firms to invest on their behalf. Increasingly, they are doing the dealmaking themselves.

From originating transactions and taking controlling stakes in companies to building their own investment platforms, some of the world's largest state investors are adopting the playbook of traditional private equity giants, according to industry veterans.

"The imminent change is that the lines between LPs and GPs are becoming increasingly blurry. This could bring more fundamental changes in the long term," Diego Lopez of Global SWF told CNBC.

Limited partners, or LPs, typically commit capital to private equity funds, while general partners, or GPs, are responsible for sourcing deals and managing investments.

Sovereign funds and state investment companies are increasingly taking on the GP role, Lopez said, pointing to the establishment of their own private equity management platforms, such as Mubadala Capital and Singapore's Seviora.

The shift is also reflected in the way some of the world's largest sovereign investors are approaching dealmaking.

"They originate transactions rather than waiting for them. They build platforms rather than buying single assets. They take control positions and operate what they own," PwC said in their latest report on sovereign wealth funds.

"Whether you're a company, a general partner, or a government, you'll find that these institutions are no longer the limited partner you're raising money from; they're the principal sitting across the table."

Last year, Abu Dhabi's MGX, an investment vehicle established by state fund Mubadala in 2024, anchored the roughly $40 billion acquisition of Aligned Data Centers alongside BlackRock, Nvidia and Microsoft. A year earlier, a consortium led by Mubadala Capital acquired a 68% equity stake in alternative asset manager Fortress, which at the time managed more than $48 billion.

Some sovereign funds are striking deals at a speed typically associated with large private equity firms, according to PwC.

Singapore's GIC recorded 553 transactions between July 2023 and July 2026, Abu Dhabi's Mubadala 397 and the Abu Dhabi Investment Authority 367, according to PwC's analysis of PitchBook data, which includes transactions by subsidiaries.

The shift comes as sovereign wealth funds command unprecedented financial firepower. Their assets have surged about 59% over the past five years to $16.5 trillion, up from $10.4 trillion in 2022 and more than nine times the $1.8 trillion they managed in 2005, according to data provided to CNBC by research firm Global SWF which focuses on state-owned investors.

PwC projects that sovereign wealth fund assets to reach $22.4 trillion by 2030.

While sovereign funds' push into direct investing has been underway for years, a more challenging fundraising environment for PE firms and a resurgence in megadeals have recently accelerated the trend.

The fundraising slowdown has tilted bargaining power toward large institutional investors, allowing them to negotiate more opportunities to invest directly alongside private equity managers, said Kyle Walters of PitchBook.

A key attraction is the potential to save on fees. Co-investments typically carry little or no management fees and no carried interest, which is the share of investment profits that managers receive. Additionally, direct deals can eliminate external manager fees altogether.

"For a large SWF writing big checks, the fee savings in dollar terms can be substantial," Walters said.

Sovereign funds also enjoy structural advantages over traditional buyout firms. Unlike conventional private equity funds, which operate within predetermined lifespans, sovereign investors can hold assets for decades, the experts highlighted.

They can also deploy substantial sums from their own balance sheets without having to raise fresh capital, an advantage particularly valuable in capital-intensive sectors such as AI infrastructure and energy.

But deep pockets and patient capital alone do not guarantee success.

As sovereign wealth funds take controlling stakes in companies, they assume operational responsibilities traditionally borne by private equity managers, while potentially stretching their own capacity to source deals, conduct due diligence and manage complex assets, PwC cautioned.

"Building the required capability, the talent, the systems, and the governance is a slower process than committing the capital," PwC said. The firm also flagged concentration risks as sovereign investors increasingly pile into similar investment themes, particularly AI, data centers and power infrastructure, leaving even geographically diversified portfolios vulnerable to the same underlying risks.

Despite their growing ambitions, industry experts are skeptical that sovereign wealth funds will supplant established private equity managers.

"This new path these large LPs are paving is more of a partnership than a competition between GPs and LPs," Walters said, noting that much of the increased activity is taking the form of co-investments.

He pointed to the $55 billion take-private deal for video-game maker Electronic Arts announced last year, in which Saudi Arabia's PIF contributed significant capital, as an example of how both sides ae joining hands.

Traditional buyout firms also retain an edge in sourcing deals and managing portfolio companies.

"However, capital alone does not replace the specialist sourcing, operational expertise, and active ownership capabilities required to consistently create value, which experienced managers have built over time," said Vincent Ng, managing director and co-head of Asia at Partners Group.

Direct investing also raises concentration risks, while illiquidity could become a problem during crises when governments need access to capital, experts said.

Rather than displacing traditional buyout firms, sovereign investors' growing ambitions could change the economics of private equity, forcing managers to become more flexible in how they work with their biggest clients.

"This is likely to reshape the relationship between asset owners and managers, with more customized mandates, co-investments, and long-term partnerships," Ng said.

#2743. The Lakers will need help to advance in the NBA Cup

In news that should shock no one, the Kings sit at the bottom of Group C in the NBA Cup this year, winless in four games.

Above them sit four teams, including the Lakers, at 2-1. Each has a path to advance as we head into Friday, the final day of NBA Cup play, setting up an exciting finish.

The Spurs and Lakers will have their anticipated showdown on Friday evening. At the same time, the Warriors and Blazers square off in Portland. All four teams need a win and results going their way in the other game to advance, setting up some good ol' scoreboard watching during the game.

So, let's look at how the Lakers can win the group and their much slimmer path to a wild card spot.

The Lakers' desire to beat the Spurs on Friday likely centers on making a statement against arguably the top team in the Western Conference. The added bonus, perhaps, is that they can advance in the NBA Cup as well.

Any path out of the group requires a win on Friday. A loss drops them to 2-2 in the group and with two teams guaranteed to finish with just one loss, the Lakers can't advance as a wild card with a loss.

But winning isn't enough. The Lakers' loss to the Warriors in Golden State — a game they led by 25 points — leaves them needing help to move on. If LA and Portland both win, the Lakers hold the head-to-head tiebreaker and win the group. However, if Golden State upsets the Blazers in Portland, then that Halloween Eve loss stings a bit more as the Warriors will top the group.

Those two-leg scenarios exist for each side. Portland must win and have the Spurs win to win the group while San Antonio needs a victory and a Warriors upset to do the same.

However, winning the group isn't the only way to advance to the knockout rounds.

Along with the three group winners, one wild card advances to the knockout rounds. For the Lakers, this only comes into play if they win and the Warriors win, leaving them with just one loss in the group.

Point differential is how the wild card spot is determined and the Lakers aren't in an ideal spot. LA's close win one week ago over the Kings didn't offset the big loss to the Warriors. As a result, they enter the final game with a -9 point differential.

The simplest way for all this to play out is for the Wolves, who may be without LaMelo Ball, to beat the Grizzlies, leaving no one-loss teams in Group B. Then the tiebreaker will be between the Lakers and the Nuggets.

Denver has a -3 point differential, but get to play the Jazz, who are winless in the NBA Cup. If both the Nuggets and Lakers win, LA would have to beat Denver's margin of victory by at least seven points, assuming Denver wins.

The potential wrench in these plans is the Grizzlies-Wolves contest. Coming into Friday, Minnesota has a +39 point differential and Memphis is at +18. If the Grizzlies win a close game, then the Wolves likely have the inside track at the wild card spot. It would take a really big Memphis win to bring the Wolves into the point differential range of the Lakers and Nuggets.

These wild card races always have so many moving parts, so here's perhaps the simplest rooting guide for Friday:

Grizzlies huge blowout win or loss at Wolves

#2742. What happens now for Bayern Munich and Musiala?

Bayern Munich - and representatives of one of their most prominent players -have collided over recent weeks.

During the summer, the public became aware that their star 23-year-old midfielder Jamal Musiala suffered from absence seizures.

This neurological condition causes a brief, sudden lapse in awareness and responsiveness. Musiala had two of these lapses during pre-season games, but episodes already happened during the previous year.

At first, the shock among fans and observers was huge. Bayern kept Musiala's condition a secret for some time, and only a few insiders knew about it. In the days after Musiala's lapse during a friendly against Heidenheim, speculations arose over whether the player's medical issue had been known before he signed a highly lucrative contract extension in February 2025.

But it has been confirmed by sources close to the team - and Bayern themselves - that the condition had not been detected before April 2025. One source described Musiala, at the time of signing his new contract, as being "in great health".

In April 2025, days after suffering a muscle tear, Musiala caused a high-speed car crash which cost him his driver's licence. Munich's public prosecutor's office responded to a recent enquiry saying there is no evidence that the accident was caused by a lapse, nor that it was the cause of Musiala's condition.

Nevertheless, checks a couple of days after the crash revealed he was suffering from absence seizures. Musiala's camp consulted numerous experts and hired doctors to treat the player, with the knowledge of Jochen Hahne, Bayern's team doctor. How close the consultations between the external doctors and Bayern's medical staff are remains a point of discussion, among many other things in this complex matter.

Soon after, Musiala's football-related injuries became an issue. He broke his fibula and injured his ankle during the Fifa Club World Cup after colliding with then PSG goalkeeper Gianluigi Donnarumma. He needed months to recover and suffered a subsequent ankle injury, likely related to the leg injury.

After the 2026 World Cup he had a metal plate removed from his left foot, which affected his pre-season preparation. Musiala just recently recovered from a weeks-long absence due to a hamstring tear.

On top of that, new incidents related to his neurological condition have come to light. Days before his recent return to training Musiala had another lapse, just like he did on the morning of a Champions League game against Real Madrid in April.

All of this is the tragic story of a highly talented footballer who might never return to his previous level and must deal with a medical condition for the rest of his life.

Absence seizures require daily medication. There are other high-level athletes, such as England rugby union player Tommy Freeman, who have had to deal with the same condition.

A controversy erupted last Friday, as Bayern faced Cologne in what was supposed to be an ordinary league game. Karl-Heinz Rummenigge, once chairman of the board and now a member of Bayern's supervisory board, asked a TV crew to come to his section in the stands.

The unscheduled post-game interview unfolded in a way that no-one at Bayern, not even other members of the club's hierarchy, expected.

"He has a health issue, which is known, and it is known that he has a contract which includes hefty sums of money," Rummenigge said. "You need to talk to the family, to the player and most importantly to the agency, because these sums are - with all due respect - not justifiable any longer."

A day later, chairman of the board Jan-Christian Dreesen and club president Herbert Hainer tried to defuse the situation at the yearly membership assembly, but were also attacked by club member Jonathan Hoffmann.

Hoffmann, a neurologist, said it wouldn't help to go after Musiala publicly, for which he received applause from many of the present members.

One might wonder why an experienced deal-maker like Rummenigge would willingly put down one of his players who could still be valuable to the club, even if it's just for a sale.

He might have been agitated by the way the home game against Cologne went. Harry Kane suffered a ligament tear in his ankle early in the game and star winger Michael Olise had to leave the stadium on crutches.

But, even more importantly, it has become clear that Rummenigge was unhappy with how contract negotiations with Musiala's camp - between October 2024 and February 2025 - unfolded.

Bayern and particularly Max Eberl, the club's director of sport, were running out of time, as Musiala's contract would have ended with the conclusion of the 2025-26 season. If they hadn't reached an agreement before April or May 2025, Bayern would have felt obliged to sell Musiala during the summer transfer window.

Musiala played an impressive Euro 2024 for Germany and was one of Bayern's best players during the period of negotiations. Among others, Real Madrid were interested, but only for a free transfer in 2026.

Keep in mind, Musiala has quite a unique profile as a No 10 that can also come from the wing and break down low-block defences with his dribbles and passing.

Under pressure and confronted by a shrewd negotiator in Christian Schmid, Musiala's agent and a trained lawyer, Bayern agreed to a salary package that could earn Musiala, in a best-case scenario, £21m a year, with £15m as a base salary. Bayern also agreed to grant a signing fee of close to £25m, paid over the stretch of the contract. Musiala even got his wish granted of receiving his own box at Allianz Arena.

Some reports indicated that the fact Musiala's deal includes sick pay for six months, in the case of injury or illness, could be interpreted as circumstantial evidence that the player's representatives may have known about his condition beforehand. A standard Bundesliga contract only offers sick pay for six weeks before insurance would shoulder the payments.

But even six months is a short period in comparison. Premier League players receive their full basic wage for the first 18 months. And, when Bayern negotiate with top players, they ultimately compete against Europe's elite.

Rummenigge, and to a lesser extent his long-time boardroom compatriot Uli Hoeness, made Eberl responsible for the unfavourable terms - arguing that Schmid essentially played Eberl.

Eberl has been the target of criticism from the two former powerbrokers for quite some time. At a recent supervisory board meeting, Hoeness is said to have attacked Eberl for his inactivity over the Musiala issue in the past six months.

That being said, Bayern bought into the Musiala hype for a couple of years, hoping that they would have a superstar of their own who could be marketed across the globe.

The relationship between the club and agent Schmid has been strained to say the least, with Rummenigge particularly disliking him. Some sources believe this was one of the root causes for Rummenigge's recent attack on live TV.

When a 16-year-old Kennet Eichhorn came on the market during the summer, as he wanted to leave second-division side Hertha Berlin, Bayern were interested but ultimately dropped out of the race for the highly touted midfielder. Eichhorn is represented by Schmid and ended up joining Bayer Leverkusen.

Bayern boss Vincent Kompany (left) has himself recently been diagnosed with meningeal irritation - an inflammation of the protective membrane surrounding the brain and spinal cord [Getty Images]

Hoeness met with Schmid during the summer to discuss how to proceed with Musiala, but the player's agent did not indicate that they would agree to a wage reduction. Hoeness called the matter a "dilemma" for Bayern during a TV show earlier this month, but did not go as far as Rummenigge.

As long as Musiala is not medically forced to retire, he will receive the wage that was agreed upon in February 2025. Even if Bayern would intend to part ways with the player, they would need to do everything in their power to get the player as close to his previous form as possible.

The release clause of £125m, which could be triggered next year, seems unrealistic. Any comments by Bayern bosses against Musiala, or further leaks to the media, may indeed lower his market value down to zero - unless the player can simply shake things off and perform again.

Eberl and head coach Vincent Kompany have come out to back Musiala. Joshua Kimmich, one of Bayern's veteran players, also criticised the treatment of Musiala after a 2-1 loss to Lille in the Champions League on Wednesday. "Of course, the club is above all and bigger than the player, but not bigger than the human. This is an absolute no-go and also not Bayern-like," Kimmich said.

Even football players' union Fifpro condemned Rummenigge's comments. On Wednesday, Bayern put out a statement saying that a meeting between the club and Musiala's representatives took place on Tuesday, in which it was agreed that the player's health should be paramount.

Whether the damage can be repaired is up in the air. As Bayern have a number of attacking players sidelined, they need a healthy and mentally prepared Musiala in the coming weeks and months.

Fifpro criticises Bayern Munich for Musiala comments

#2741. Mike Tomlin on Aaron Rodgers-Mike McCarthy situation in Pittsburgh: 'It's a dumpster fire'

Former Steelers head coach Mike Tomlin discussed with NBC's Mike Tirico his reaction to everything Aaron Rodgers said in a scathing critique during Wednesday's episode of "The Pat McAfee Show."

The highlight of the interview was Tomlin's response when asked about his emotions watching what is happening with the Steelers after coaching the team for two decades.

"I'm upset about it. It's a dumpster fire and I don't say that in a judgmental way. I've presided over a few dumpster fires in my 19 years, but it certainly is upsetting and I'm sure Steeler Nation is upset."

Tomlin started the interview by being asked for his general reaction to what was said.

"I had a range of emotions watching those course of events yesterday. The prevailing one is general sadness.

"Sad that we might be looking at the end of a legendary career in the quarterback, Aaron Rogers, and just on the macro level, whether it's organizationally or for the game of football at large, to see laundry aired out that way in a public forum, those are things that kind of run counterculture to professional football."

The former Steelers head coach said he was "shocked" at how the team's dirty laundry was aired.

" … I know both men involved, certainly had a lot of intimate work and development of relationship with Aaron over the last couple of years and have known and competed against Mike [McCarthy] and respected and appreciated him as a coach for a long time."

Tomlin was asked his opinion on whether or not this will negatively impact McCarthy's ability to lead the Steelers.

"It certainly created some challenges and challenges is an understatement if those things are true. But his ability or inability to overcome that is based on relationships and the depth of those relationships and how those guys buy into what he's selling. Certainly he's been there a short period of time so certainly you wonder the level of that challenge. Certainly it is relationship-based."

On Tuesday night after 11 ET, it was announced that Rodgers would be inactive for the Steelers' Friday game against the Denver Broncos, and that Mason Rudolph would start.

The next day, Rodgers went on "The Pat McAfee Show" and went scorched-earth on McCarthy, accusing him of sleeping during meetings, not watching film, and using the wrong team name during a breakdown of a team huddle.

The rant sent the football world into a frenzy as local reporters confirmed anonymous sources saying it was all true, and former players and coaches, current analysts, NFL insiders and a team owner came out in support of McCarthy.

Tomlin was the head coach of the Steelers from 2007 to 2025. He famously never had a losing season, but also hadn't made the Super Bowl since the 2008 season.

At the end of the 2025 season, Rodgers' first year with the franchise, Tomlin resigned, triggering a coaching search that ended with McCarthy's hiring.

#2739. Top Wall Street analysts favor these 3 dividend stocks for strong returns

Investors often favor dividend stocks for their regular income and the promise of potential share price appreciation. But selecting the right dividend stocks from a huge pool of companies can be difficult.

Top Wall Street analysts can help shortlist attractive dividend-paying stocks, as their recommendations are backed by thorough analysis of a company's financials.

Here are three dividend-paying stocks that are highlighted by Wall Street's top pros, as tracked by TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Devon Energy (DVN), an independent oil and natural gas exploration and production company, reported better-than-expected third-quarter results. The company announced a quarterly dividend of 32 cents per share for the fourth quarter, payable December 30. Based on the fixed dividends paid over the trailing 12 months, DVN yields 2.85%.

After hosting a virtual investor meeting with management, Goldman Sachs analyst Neil Mehta reiterated a buy rating on Devon, with a price target of $59. Mehta said that he is now more confident in management's outlook for delivering strong near-term capital returns as well as efforts to drive operational efficiencies and productivity gains.

Devon sees an opportunity to increase share repurchases, driven by solid free cash flow (FCF), contributions from the Eagle Ford divestiture and continued improvement in the balance sheet, Mehta said. Devon expects share buybacks worth more than $1 billion in Q4 2026, up from $414 million in the third quarter, backed by a strong pricing backdrop and improved capital efficiency.

Mehta, a 5-star analyst, said Devon expects about $6.3 billion of excess FCF in 2027, including about $3.5 billion of net proceeds from the Eagle Ford sale. That would enable the company to accelerate buybacks while progressing toward its goal of reducing gross debt to about $9 billion by early 2027. Mehta noted that under DVN's framework to return up to 70% of annual FCF, management favors share buybacks as it believes the stock is discounted compared to large-cap peers.

"Management expects continued capital efficiency gains from merger synergies, extended laterals, surfactant adoption and development of the newly acquired federal acreage," Mehta said.

Mehta ranks No. 876 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 57% of the time, delivering an average return of 8.1%. See Devon Energy Stock Buybacks on TipRanks.

Energy Transfer (ET), is a limited partnership that operates about 140,000 miles of pipeline and associated energy infrastructure. The company recently announced third-quarter results showing net income per common unit growing about 18% year-over-year, to 33 cents. ET's cash distribution for Q3 2026 was 34.25 cents per common unit, up more than 3% year-over-year. At an annualized distribution of $1.37 per share, Energy Transfer yields more than 7%.

The company delivered better-than-expected Q3 results and announced the 1.2 billion cubic feet per day (bcf/d) South Mississippi Pipeline, a 215-mile, 36-inch natural gas line linking the Perryville Hub to the Florida Gas Transmission (FGT) network, Gabelman said.
