#2702. Semiconductor chips are the new oil. Here's why

The artificial intelligence boom has pushed semiconductors past oil and gas in global export value for the first time, according to a Deutsche Bank analysis of International Trade Centre data.

Yet the milestone arrives at an awkward moment, just as investors reassess the outlook for artificial intelligence spending and drive down the price of semiconductor stocks. Last week, before Monday's breathtaking reversal, semiconductor stocks suffered their worst weekly loss in a quarter century, with the PHLX Semiconductor Index (SOX) plunging nearly 11% last Friday alone, capping a more than 17% weekly decline.

Nvidia soared more than 31% Monday after the leading maker of artificial intelligence chips had fallen for a seventh straight week, plunging 46% during that stretch. Then it fell again, dropping almost 10% on Tuesday and Wednesday. Advanced Micro Devices tumbled 20% in two days last Thursday and Friday. Micron Technology sank 27% over the seven days ended last Friday.

"For decades we've talked about the petrodollar. Perhaps increasingly we need to think about the chip dollar," Jim Reid, global head of macro and thematic research at Deutsche Bank wrote in a report this month.

Semiconductor exports overtook oil and gas for the first time during the January-March quarter of 2026, reaching about $1.61 trillion, compared with $1.53 trillion for oil and gas, the report said, using four-quarter rolling totals.

The gap widened in the second quarter, when semiconductor exports totaled about $1.60 trillion and oil and gas exports reached about $1.47 trillion. Disruptions to oil supplies through the Strait of Hormuz after the Iran war helped widen the gap. Daily oil flows through the Strait collapsed nearly 77%, to 4.9 million barrels in the second quarter of 2026 from 21.6 million barrels in the fourth quarter of 2025, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration.

Yet the demand for semiconductors has proven insatiable in the face of soaring data center construction, boosting global trade in the increasingly scarce AI component. Hundreds of billions of dollars of orders for graphics processing units and data centers aim at providing AI computing power, Rothschild & Co. Redburn wrote in a report last Thursday.

"Compute will be the new commodity fueling this transformation on a global scale," Rothschild analyst Cara Thomson said.

The shift toward chips has macroeconomic implications just as the explosion in oil trade did in the 1970s.

Oil-exporting countries historically recycled much of their surpluses into the purchase of U.S. Treasuries and other bonds, helping finance U.S. deficits and underpin demand for other government debt.

Reid at Deutsche Bank said that since semiconductor-surplus countries in Asia are more closely tied to U.S. tech companies, some chip-export earnings could flow back into U.S. technology stocks, startups and data centers, further helping to finance the AI investment cycle.

The changing dynamics in global trade could also tilt the mix of global financial flows, Reid said. "So welcome to the chip-dollar era: potentially more growth, more excitement, more volatility, and structurally higher yields" in corporate and government debt.

#2701. Bears stun Lions on late Rome Odunze TD

The Bears suffered an agonizing defeat in Detroit on Thanksgiving a couple of years ago, but they found themselves on the other side of things this time around.

Caleb Williams hit wide receiver Rome Odunze in the back corner of the end zone for a six-yard touchdown with three seconds left on the clock. The extra point gave the Bears a 39-35 lead and the game came to an end after the Lions’ attempt to lateral down the field failed to produce a miracle.

It was the first time the Bears led all day, but that’s all it took for them to end the day in sole possession of first place in the NFC North. Odunze’s score capped a wild second half that saw the two teams put up 55 combined points in one of the most entertaining games of the season.

The game-winning touchdown drive came after Lions head coach Dan Campbell passed on a 51-yard field goal with 2:22 to play in the game and went for it on fourth-and-4. A pass to running back Jahmyr Gibbs was complete, but he was yanked down by linebacker T.J. Edwards and stopped short of a first down.

Campbell’s decisions on the previous possession will also merit a second look. The Lions chose to have Jared Goff roll left to throw on a third-and-1 while in field goal territory and Goff’s pass behind Jameson Williams wound up being intercepted by Bears safety Dillon Thieneman. The Lions chose to run with Sione Vaki rather than Gibbs on the previous play, which was a curious choice on a day when Gibbs ran 21 times for 205 yards and three touchdowns.

That aggressiveness has been a hallmark of the Campbell era, but the calls backfired on a day when the Lions led by as many as 11 points. The defense coming up with big plays to thwart Campbell’s gambles deserves credit for the ultimate result and so does Williams, who finished the day 30-of-44 for 345 yards and two scores despite losing tight end Colston Loveland to a knee injury early in the first quarter.

Williams proved his mettle in big spots several times last season and Thursday’s win is the latest reminder why the Bears are building their future around him. They’ll return home next week for a date with another division leader in the Jaguars and these two teams will do it again in Chicago in Week 17.

The Lions will try to rebound in Atlanta next Sunday and they can’t afford too many more stumbles in a jam-packed NFC playoff race.

#2700. From bible study groups to Ballers in God: The rise and rise of Christianity in modern football

A growing number of high-profile footballers are both joining the religion and making overt demonstrations of their faith on the pitch and online, but is there something more sinister behind the movement?

"I want to thank my Lord and Saviour, Jesus Christ."

That phrase, or some variation of it, has often become the first thing to come out of a player's mouth in a post-match interview of late. We had become accustomed to Christian footballers subtly showing their faith by crossing themselves or pointing towards the heavens in celebration in the modern era, but now we are increasingly seeing much more overt demonstrations of Christianity, in the Premier League and beyond.

While the movement might seem harmless on the face of it, as a community forms among previously disconnected Christian players on and off the pitch, we have also seen this wave of evangelism cause friction and land certain individuals in hot water amid ambiguity over the views that they hold. But what is behind the seemingly unstoppable rise of the religion in football?

We are seeing many more players make overt displays of their Christianity on the pitch and online than ever before

"First of all, I want to thank Jesus Christ, my Lord and Saviour," Manchester City's Rico Lewis said in his post-match interview with TNT Sports after the Champions League victory over AEK Athens in October. "Can't even fathom doing anything without him, so all the glory and honour goes to him." That was just one example of the kind of evangelical Christianity that has become prevalent in the English game in recent years.

Lewis is among a growing cohort of English and Premier League-based players who are increasingly vocal about their faith. Alongside Jeremy Doku and a clutch of other City players, he participates in weekly bible study online, according to The Athletic. Marc Guehi is another team-mate who has been open about his beliefs, the son of a former church minister.

Meanwhile, at Arsenal, a group of Christian evangelical players that includes England internationals Bukayo Saka, Eberechi Eze, Noni Madueke and many others has been dubbed the 'Bible Brothers', also gathering on a regular basis to discuss passages of scripture. That was something that was replicated among members of the Three Lions camp at Euro 2024.

There was an unprecedented moment at the end of England's World Cup third-place playoff clash against France in the summer that reflected the relentless growth of this movement among players, as stars from both sides including Saka, Eze and Guehi gathered together in an impromptu prayer circle on the pitch after the full-time whistle.

Away from post-match interviews, social media has increasingly become a platform for these footballers to convey their message. Doku regularly captions his posts using relevant bible verses, Saka often uses the hashtag #GodsPlan and has the moniker 'God's Child', Jurrien Timber will cryptically reference bible passages and Madueke's Instagram bio reads "Follower of Jesus Christ!".

Dr Graham Daniels, a former Cambridge United player and general director of the charity Christians in Sport, believes this is the new normal. "The era that any of our young professionals live in now is an era where you have Instagram," he tells GOAL. "Your life story is told on Instagram. That's how it is. These just happen to be very famous young men who have millions of followers.

"Initially, I'd want to say that this simply is the cultural context of our world now. Your life is lived in the public arena via social media. The fundamental thing isn't whether it's a good thing or a bad thing to share your beliefs, whatever they may be, on social media. It just is. It's normative. That's what these people do. That's what these young men do."

Christianity has declined sharply in wider British society, but in the world of football it is alive and well

What's fascinating is that this swelling wave of Christianity within the football sphere doesn't reflect wider British society, where the religion has declined sharply. In the most recent census in 2021, for the first time ever, less than half the population of England and Wales described themselves as 'Christian' (46%, 27.5 million people) - a 13% decrease from the previous survey in 2011 (59%, 33m people).

In the world of football, at least, Christianity is thriving. According to research commissioned by the charity Christians in Sport that was published in the summer, there are Christian players in the first-team squads of 75% of clubs in England and Wales, while half of Premier League clubs reported regular Christian gatherings which are often led by players.

"Professional football is often portrayed as a world shaped by money, fame and performance. What this research reveals is a different story," Daniels said at the time. "Across the professional game, Christian players are gathering to pray, study the Bible and support one another.

"Perhaps the most striking finding is that, in an environment where identity is constantly tested by success, failure and public scrutiny, many players are looking beyond football itself for meaning, purpose and security. Christianity is not disappearing from the professional game; it is far more present than most people realise."

Daniels believes a number of factors have paved the way for this new wave of the faith in football, including the dawn of the Premier League, respected figures in the game becoming Christians, such as Cyrille Regis, and the overall progression to a more empathetic culture. "When the Premier League came in 1992, that was a sea change in terms of international footballers. There was a whole new dynamic of people who had Christian faith, and Muslims and Christians particularly, who didn't find it culturally difficult at all to express their faith," he tells GOAL.

"There were a handful of really good professionals, not necessarily superstar pros, but very good professionals who said they were Christians. That was a pretty unorthodox thing to do, but their team-mates saw that they remained good professionals, good at their job and good blokes. They had their weaknesses and strengths, but they were good pros and good men in the changing room.

"Finally, there's just been a change in culture. We're in a postmodern world and it's a therapeutic world, and everyone's free to say how they feel. You really can't bully very easily anymore, and rightly so. It's a much more comfortable environment to express your inner emotions in a way that would never have happened 15 years ago."

Dr Graham Daniels was one of very few Christian sportspeople when he found the religion early in his playing career at Cambridge United

Daniels was something of a trailblazer in English football, laying a foundation for the many Christian footballers who enjoy such visibility at the highest level today. The 64-year-old came to the religion during his time at Cambridge United in the 1980s - a time when there were very few openly-religious players anywhere in the game.

"I came to faith, really, because I'd been to Cardiff City as a kid and studied there while I was at university, while at the club," he says. "I moved to Cambridge to play, so I was away from home for the first time in my adult life, really away. Of course, I was in the sharp end of football.

"I'd done philosophy as an undergraduate, so I read quite a lot about a range of things and stumbled upon reading defences of the Christian faith, evidence and historical evidence. Somewhere in that window of a year or two, I started going to church. I've kept going ever since."

Life as a Christian footballer then was a stark contrast to what it is now. "I really did think I was the only one," Daniels continues. "It sounds a bit absurd and a bit full of hubris to say it, but I could say it then because every Saturday you'd play against people you'd met over the years through games, reserve games and youth games.

"I'd ask, 'Any Christians here?' I never got a positive response from anyone. Then a chap showed up at Cambridge who had founded Christians in Sport. He came to my club. He asked whether I knew there were Christians in the Football League. I said, 'No, there really aren't'. He said, 'No, there are'. I was thrilled. There were 92 clubs, so I thought this bloke had an organisation and must know. I asked how many there were, and he said, 'Well, four'. I asked who they were. He named three. I said, 'Well, who's the fourth?' He said, 'You!'.

"It was hard. It was a different cultural era. Aggressive, bullying, really hard. If you were slightly different, wore a pair of glasses or something, let alone having some kind of faith or worldview that would set you apart, there was plenty of what we today call micro and macro aggressions that went on. But, of course, you're in a tough world, in a tough game. I was able to navigate that most of the time."

Players like Arsenal's Noni Madueke have expressed concerns over whether this new wave of evangelical Christianity could become performative

Interestingly, the BBC reports that there has been growth in denominations of the religion like Pentecostalism in wider society - the form of evangelical Christianity that many footballers practise - and most evidently in Greater London, where a number of current Premier League stars hail from, which has been "partly driven by immigration". Several of the English players who have become more candid about their faith come from immigrant backgrounds, with the diversification of the Premier League over the years inherently making all religions more visible.

It has been reported by members of the clergy that people are "expressing their faith with more zeal and vigour" than before. "The discourse, the tenor of the conversation, is different in the last two years. We're seeing a greater confidence among active Christians, particularly those who are younger," Dr Rhiannon McAleer, director of research and impact at the Bible Society, told the BBC.

Sceptics will question whether this more vocal form of preaching is performative, in an age where engagement is undeniably a driver of what players will post on social media, while others will argue that this new loud and proud strain of Christianity among footballers has the characteristics of a trend that might eventually pass.

Speaking on the Four8TV YouTube channel in October, Madueke admitted: "With Christianity and the football, it can become a bit performative. I've definitely been there as well, these times where you're gonna be thinking like 'Cool, let me do a caption for God so that maybe next week I'll score again'. I'm being real bro.

"So I feel like it's important to really make sure your heart posture is honouring, 'Yo, I'm just trying to show you guys what he's done for me so that maybe he can do it for you too', not because I'm trying to ram it down your throat or say I'm better than you or say I'm now a pastor. Nah bro, I'm a footballer. I'm a footballer bro. But it has to come from a place of actual genuine love. I genuinely want to see other people experience this type of love. Power in their life. It's difficult to get the balance, for sure."

Meanwhile, City team-mates Lewis and Doku have both revealed that they only recently discovered their faith; the former told The Athletic that he suddenly made the decision to buy a bible in the past year or so, while Doku said in an interview after an impressive display against Liverpool last November: "What changed for me this season, I have God in my life."

In defence of Madueke and his fellow worshippers, evangelism is quite literally defined by sharing the message and teachings of Jesus Christ, and from that perspective it would be remiss not to use a platform where they can collectively reach millions of people almost instantly to spread the Christian gospel. The aim is also to invite others to the faith, and that is seemingly what has happened with both Lewis and Doku.

London City Lionesses and England star Nikita Parris believes she would not have been able to overcome adversity in her early life without God

Background aside, it's not difficult to see why some footballers might turn to God. Considering just how difficult it is to become an elite-level professional footballer in the first place (it has been estimated that just five percent of academy players will go on to play the game at the highest level), you can understand why some might believe there had to have been some divine intervention.

As Dr Daniels said, many are also "looking beyond football itself for meaning, purpose and security", while others are convinced that they would not have been able to overcome setbacks in their lives and playing careers on their own. Speaking on Four8TV, Nottingham Forest defender Ola Aina says: "There's just some things that's happened in life, in our careers, that you couldn't say, 'Yeah, I manufactured that one'. There's just so many things that I could say that I know that's a higher power, that's God man, that wasn't me. I'm just grateful for it because, who knows? If I tried to manufacture that, I could have collapsed my whole journey."

That was echoed by London City Lionesses and England attacker Nikita Parris, who said: "I think I lean on God's understanding more in the bad years of football and the setbacks. I think you never truly understand or comprehend how he has his hand on you until maybe a couple of years down the line you're like, 'Wow, how have I come so far? Inner-city kid, low-income background, single-parent household, four kids, and I'm the one that made it?!'. For me it's crazy. Now I sit back and think, 'Thank God he's on my side'."

Former Tottenham and Crystal Palace midfielder John Bostock founded Ballers in God in 2015

One of the driving forces behind the rise of evangelical Christianity in football, especially online, seems to be the initiative Ballers in God, which was founded by former Tottenham and Crystal Palace midfielder John Bostock, a devout Christian, in 2015. It describes itself as "a global, player-led community dedicated to supporting professional footballers and their partners to know Jesus deeply and grow in their Christian journey", with a mission to "use the global platform of football to make Jesus known".

Their 600 members meet online on a weekly basis to discuss football and their faith and also occasionally gather in person, while there is also a WhatsApp group that is hundreds strong. Several high-profile players seem to be associated with the group including Eze and Semenyo, who both feature in a social media video about 'who Jesus is' to them.

Professional players are invited to apply to join the community on Ballers in God's website, with a form requiring them to enter a list of their former teams, the highest level they've played at and their Instagram handle. A separate page is dedicated exclusively to merch; there you can buy crucifix shinpads and gloves, base layers with 'I belong to Jesus' emblazoned across them and branded grip socks.

"Ballers in God is a pro-to-pro football ministry," Bostock said in an interview with Premier Christianity last year. "We're a disciple-making, soul-winning movement in the beautiful game. It was birthed in 2015 out of a longing in my heart, really. I moved from Spurs and went to Belgium to play for Antwerp. I felt quite isolated in my faith. I prayed: 'God, what do I do?'

"I sensed that if I was struggling, other players must be going through the same thing. So, I called a few players and asked them: 'How do you fancy coming online once a month just to pray, read the word, encourage each other?' When people see Ballers in God, they might see the online brand, but the heartbeat is a community that serves professional players. We've baptised players, won many to the Lord, sowed even more seeds."

He added: "Football breaks down barriers. There's been Christians in the game for years, but now there's a centralised place where their voices can be heard. And because of that, players see other players being bold, and it encourages them to step out. In the UK, there's talk of young people turning back to the Lord, and I think players are recognising that football is an instrument God wants to use."

The rise of evangelical Christianity and questions over the intent of some of its messaging have already caused friction at the highest levels of the game

In the UK and other European countries where Christianity is on the wane, the emergence of this new strain of very public, outspoken Christian evangelism within football has occasionally caused friction. That has usually stemmed from certain players being accused of holding fundamentalist views that emphasise biblical literalism, which can include being against same-sex relationships and abortion.

In English football, the most infamous recent incident came in December 2024 during the Premier League's LGBTQ+ inclusion initiative Rainbow Laces, when then-Crystal Palace player Guehi scrawled 'Jesus loves you' and 'I love Jesus' on his rainbow armband in two separate games, defying the league's rules on displaying religious messages. The defender ultimately avoided punishment.

Speaking during the controversy Guehi's father John, a church minister, suggested that his son was indeed opposed to the campaign. He told the Daily Mail: "Marc said 'Yes' and did the right thing by ­wearing it but people are having a go at him for what he wrote, he accepted to wear the armband, he was just trying to balance the message. He was saying: 'You gave me the armband, as a Christian I don't believe in your cause, but I will put it on.'"

Last summer during Pride Month, Ballers in God posted on social media questioning whether Christian players should have to wear the rainbow armband, writing: "In football, Pride Month often brings pressure to wear rainbow symbols to show solidarity. But what if that celebration clashes with your convictions and the Word of God?...We don't take this stand because we hate. We stand because we honour God over culture. Because the Bible calls all sexual immorality, straight or gay, out of bounds.

"Sometimes, obedience means kindly saying, 'I can't wear that'. This isn't arrogance. It's worship...We don't see the LGBTQ+ community, or anyone, as enemies. We see people deeply loved by God, just like us, all in need of truth and grace. So while many wear the rainbow this month, we choose to wear the cross." The group later welcomed the decision to discontinue the Rainbow Laces campaign, posting: "We prayed. We fasted. And God heard us...True inclusion makes space for different beliefs, without pressure or judgement."

The outspoken nature of this very online movement also clearly has the capacity to rub people up the wrong way, especially in light of the ambiguity surrounding the overarching message. Earlier this month, a social media post by FC Twente's former Manchester United striker Wout Weghorst, that included an image with the message 'I AIN'T FORCING JESUS ON NOBODY. BUT DON'T EXPECT ME TO HIDE MY LOVE FOR HIM' and was reshared by Ballers in God, drew the ire of ex-Germany and Aston Villa midfielder Thomas Hitzlsperger, who responded by writing: "Well said. How do we feel about 'I AIN'T FORCING HOMOSEXUALITY ON NOBODY. BUT DON'T EXPECT ME TO HIDE MY LOVE FOR MEN'?" The tweet would go viral.

In Germany, there was a significant backlash from sections of Borussia Dortmund's support when midfielder Felix Nmecha - who is among those closely connected to Ballers in God - was signed from Wolfsburg in the summer of 2023, with some even protesting outside the stadium. Earlier that year he had shared homophobic and transphobic posts on social media, including one that equated the concept of 'Pride' in the LGBTQ+ movement to the devil.

Felix Nmecha has sparked controversy in Germany by performing a celebration that is linked to a Ballers in God campaign that seems to promote homophobic and transphobic ideas

Three years on, Nmecha has found himself at the centre of another storm that has also thrust Ballers in God and the perceived ambiguity surrounding its intended message into the spotlight. The Dortmund and Germany midfielder landed himself in hot water for performing the 'Crowns Down' celebration, which involves kneeling, symbolically removing an imaginary crown from your head and placing it on the floor.

The gesture is believed to be a nod to Ballers in God's 'The King's Return' campaign that launched ahead of the World Cup. A video on the official website, which appears to be AI-generated, explains: "We all want the crown, a symbol of status, success, recognition and control...But the crown was never ours to keep...And now we have a choice: to hold on to a broken fading crown or place our trust in the king who reigns forever."

While that might seem innocent on the face of it, an investigation by German media outlet ARD found that the campaign's homepage linked out to a live chat carrying The King's Return's crown logo, which provides counselling from US-based digital evangelism ministry Groundwire. It's claimed that counsellors on that platform told ARD's reporters, who used fake names, that homosexuality is a sin and abortion is "Satan's plan".

The chat is still active at the time of writing and can be accessed through a link in the bio of The King's Return's official Instagram page. When GOAL asked a so-called 'coach' about homosexuality, they responded by saying: "Same sex relationships are not God's plan and sinful. We are all born with sinful, defective desires that manifest themselves in various ways, the goal is to not act on them out of love for Christ." They also pointed to the bible verse 1 Corinthians 6:9-11, which condemns homosexuality in the eyes of God. When asked a question about being transgender, the 'counsellor' replied: "God created you and did not make a mistake."

Nmecha's use of the 'Crowns Down' therefore provoked anger from Dortmund's official fan club, which said in a statement that their ire was "directed at religious networks that, under the guise of faith, promote a worldview in which people are devalued or marginalised because of their sexual orientation, gender identity, lifestyle, or personal choices". The statement added: "The investigations further reveal connections to an evangelical-charismatic environment [within Ballers in God] where, among other things, extremely conservative positions against homosexuality and transgender identity are advocated."

Amid another backlash from his club's own supporters, the player insisted the celebration "is about laying my 'crown' before the soon coming King and pointing to Jesus" and "was never intended to spread intolerance, discrimination, or hatred in any form". However, he was told by new Germany boss Jurgen Klopp to stop performing the gesture when playing for his national team, and Dortmund planned talks with him at club level.

After netting against Monchengladbach following the November international break, he pivoted to a new celebration, signalling to the crowd and apparently mouthing 'Jesus loves you'. Ballers in God posted about the change on social media, notably removing Dortmund's club badge, sponsor and kit manufacturer from the images.

Nmecha is not the only player to have done the 'Crowns Down' celebration recently; in the Premier League, both Nottingham Forest's Jair Cunha and Fabio Carvalho of Brentford have performed it, but strangely there has been no uproar in response.

Nmecha has been defended by Ballers in God, but there are still questions over what his views are

Daniels, who is connected to Bostock and advocates for the work he has done, insists there would not have been any ill intent behind Nmecha's actions. "Felix was straightforwardly part of the network called Ballers in God," he says. "They're great guys. They're not looking to cause trouble. They work in changing rooms all the time. I think Felix was straightforwardly wanting to join in with celebrating a goal and using it to express his faith.

"I'm absolutely certain there was no malign desire on his part in doing it. I don't know him personally, but absolutely not." Daniels adds: "I think it's an obtuse link from a website to another website, perhaps without enough research. Possibly. That's what I'm guessing."

Amid the furore, Ballers in God felt compelled to release their own statement that seemingly defended Nmecha's actions without directly addressing the accusations of discrimination against LGBTQ+ that had been levelled against them. "At the heart of our community is the belief that Jesus Christ is King and that He is the hope of the world," it read. "We believe the hope found in Him is for everyone, and our desire is to share this message by making Him known.

"We celebrate players who live out their faith privately, as well as those who choose to express it publicly. We are encouraged by player-led movements such as The King's Return, where footballers themselves take the initiative to express their faith in Jesus. Our heart is to support and celebrate their witness and believe everyone should be free to express their faith respectfully, without fear of prejudice or exclusion.

"Our desire is not only to share our hope, but to demonstrate love and respect towards everyone, including those who do not share our beliefs. Our focus has always been, and will always be, to point people to Jesus with grace and love."

Ballers in God have been accused of failing to properly respond to the accusations levelled at them

That follows what appears to be a trend in Ballers in God's external communications: a message of acceptance and that Jesus loves everyone, even those who disagree with the network's views - but it's still not entirely clear what those views actually are as they face accusations of homophobia, transphobia and anti-abortionism.

Jon Holmes, founder of Sports Media LGBT+, an advocacy organisation and digital publication focusing on the LGBTQ+ community in sports, has been left unconvinced. "I think there have been some questionable social media posts that the organisation has put out in the past," he tells GOAL. "When it comes to the LGBTQ part of this, I haven't really seen them address that. They did make a statement in the wake of the Nmecha goal celebration controversy, but it wasn't really directly responding to a lot of the key points that were being raised. I feel it's up to them to decide whether or not they want to make their position clear."

Anti-discrimination in football organisation Kick It Out has reported that there was a 24% rise in reports of homophobic incidents at professional level in the UK in 2025-26, as well as a 23% increase in reports of online abuse. However, Holmes insists it's impossible to draw a correlation between that sharp spike and the growing visibility of evangelical Christianity at the highest levels of the game.

"I think it's just too difficult to try to draw connections there. There is no question about trying to implicate people on the basis of their faith, because that would be discriminatory in itself. Nobody that I've encountered in this whole conversation has wanted to potentially ostracise people on the basis of their faith. That's the last thing that anyone wants. But clearly, there are questions to be raised over what Ballers in God have said in the past, and the fact they're not really saying anything now.

"It's not that long ago, only last year during Pride Month, that they were putting out social media posts about rainbow armbands and celebrating the fact that the Premier League was dropping Rainbow Laces. Now, they haven't done that this year, even though the Premier League has moved on to a different campaign. It's not like it's dropped its LGBTQ inclusion values. Ballers in God are not making those kinds of statements on social media this year, from what I've seen. So there does seem to be a change in strategy.

"What we all just need to be conscious of is trying to understand more about the motivations of the organisations. Everybody ultimately should want the same thing: for there to be no form of discrimination, whether that's against people's faith or against people's sexual orientation or gender identity. If we truly believe in creating a game free from discrimination, then we should be sharing the same ambitions."

Daniels argues that the diversification of football, including more vocal Christians in the game, has created the potential for more friction, albeit he does not believe that tension exists in the changing room. "When you work inside a changing room, all that matters to you when you sign a player is whether he's a good character. You want a new left-back or a cover left-back, 'is he a good left-back?'. That's all you care about. You really don't care what he does in his private life, as long as it's legal. You really don't. No manager cares, no director of football cares, no team-mate cares. Not at all. Your private life is your own business.

"I've been around the game all my working life. I've never seen, especially in the more modern era we're discussing now, homophobia inside changing rooms from Christians or non-Christians. That doesn't mean it's true universally, but it's a case study of one person here. In my time in the game, people are just interested in the player."

Daniels also points to the furore surrounding Guehi and Ipswich captain Sam Morsy, a Muslim, during the Rainbow Laces campaign in 2024. The latter refused to wear the rainbow armband altogether on the grounds of his faith. "It brought into the public square something of real significance in a liberal democracy: freedom of speech and expression. That's the wonder of living in a country where you're expected, and the bar is that you respect all faiths, all sexualities and all ethnicities. It's a mutual respect in a democratic setting. That has to be balanced against the freedom of expression to say, 'Well, I don't actually agree with your perspective there, or your philosophical or sociocultural take on that issue'.

"The art of living a truly human, interactive life is to be able to say, 'Well, we can't agree on that, but let's be sure that, as human beings, we may sometimes have to agree to disagree, even on significantly profound and difficult things'. What's happened here is that one incident has blown up the whole conversation around that issue of mutual tolerance, mutual acceptance and the flexibility to have different opinions. That's a democracy, isn't it?

"This would absolutely never have been a conversation 10 or 20 years ago, because there wouldn't have been more than five people who said they had a Christian faith in professional football. Clearly, what's happening here is that the entrance of not just Christian faith, but Muslim faith and other faiths into the game has meant that the equilibrium between a secular perspective and a religious perspective has shifted. There's a greater equilibrium now and therefore more tension, in a way, that simply wouldn't have existed before."

Bostock believes it is Ballers in God members and other Christians who face persecution for voicing their opinions

GOAL contacted Ballers in God for a comment on the 'Crowns Down' controversy and allegations against the group but received no response. Bostock has, though, previously addressed the potential backlash to his movement in his interview with Premier Christianity, suggesting that it is members of his network and other Christians who risk being persecuted.

"Scripture speaks about having zeal, but also wisdom," he said. "Not every player has to reveal 'I belong to Jesus' after every single goal. But at the same time, we need to be unashamed of our faith. Was Jesus politically correct? Absolutely not. But the angle he came from was always love, even in his correction.

"We encourage players to be bold. We don't tell them to wear shirts. We have conversations around Pride month. What are our thoughts about the rainbow laces? We talk about these things and pray about them. There will be persecution when you make a stand for Jesus, but he's always worth it."

For now, Ballers in God continue to fly somewhat under the radar in the British media, but Holmes believes that could change as the movement seems to grow unabated. "I think what's played out in Germany is that, even before some of the key individuals connected with the Ballers in God movement signed for their club, Nmecha was already under a degree of scrutiny because of previous social media posts that he shared in the past. That's something that Dortmund have dealt with over time.

"I think maybe because this Crowns Down celebration is still relatively new to the Premier League, that's something we're going to see play out over the course of the coming weeks and months, perhaps. It would be up to those fan groups particularly and the clubs. I expect maybe there have been conversations being had behind closed doors that we're just not aware of yet. Perhaps we will see more of that in the future."

#2699. Greg Rousseau ties Mario Williams for seventh in Bills history

Buffalo Bills outside linebacker Greg Rousseau moved into a tie for seventh place on the team's all-time sacks list on Thanksgiving night. Rousseau sacked quarterback Patrick Mahomes on a 3rd & 16 midway through the third quarter on Thanksgiving night to bring his career total to 43, catching former Bills defensive end Mario Williams.

Williams spent four seasons (2012-2015) in Buffalo, recording double-digit sacks in each of his first three years with the team. His best season came in 2014 when he recorded 14.5 sacks and earned first-team All-Pro honors.

Rousseau, now in his sixth NFL season, has spent his entire career in Buffalo after the Bills selected him with the 30th overall pick in the 2021 NFL Draft. Having already established a new personal single-season record for sacks this year, the 26 year old is now working his way through some familiar names in Buffalo's history books.

Once Rousseau gets past Mario Williams, there's another Williams waiting for him. Former defensive tackle Kyle Williams (48.5), who spent all 13 of his NFL seasons in Buffalo, sits sixth on the franchise's all-time list.

With six regular-season games remaining, and the way Rousseau has been getting to opposing quarterbacks lately, we might not have to wait until next season to talk about him catching another Williams.

#2685. What are Spurs fans thankful for this Thanksgiving?

The Spurs had a tough loss in Portland before the Thanksgiving break and will face arguably their biggest challenge yet when they face the West-leading Lakers after it. We are getting close to a quarter of the season being on the books, and games are starting to feel more meaningful as most teams round into shape.

As the season progresses, it gets harder to sit back and just enjoy San Antonio basketball without any concerns, but fortunately Thanksgiving offers the perfect opportunity to think about all the good times it has provided already and to reflect on how lucky fans of the Silver and Black really are.

Lee Dressie had a fantastic post about it that you should check out, but it would be interesting to see what you, the readers, are thankful for. Here's my list, as a way to get things started.

This one is self-explanatory. Wembanyama is the most tantalizing talent to hit the league in a generation, and he's a Spur. Luck got him to San Antonio, but he embraced the fanbase and seems to be happy to be in the city. He's lived up to the hype and seems like a perfect fit for the franchise, adapting to its traditions and ways while staying eager to forge his own path.

Watching Wemby is a joy for anyone who loves basketball, but it's extra special to watch him dominate while wearing Silver and Black.

The Spurs will be without Dylan Harper due to a hip injury for a while longer. Fans have not even gotten to see how Tobias Harris looks on this team, as he's been out since before preseason with a calf strain. A dirty play by Jeremiah Fears has forced De'Aaron Fox to sit out a few games. San Antonio has had its share of injuries.

Fortunately, none of those injuries have sidelined anyone for the rest of the year and, if everything goes well (knocks frantically on wood), all three players should be back relatively soon. Other contenders have not been so lucky, so it's important to be thankful for the injury luck the Spurs have had so far.

Sometimes fans are forced to root for players that, while talented, are not particularly likable. Whether because they are out of touch after becoming rich and famous or because of their personalities or bad behaviour, it can occasionally be hard to actually like the guys wearing the jersey. Luckily, that's not a problem with the current Spurs.

Sure, Wembanyama can come off as arrogant, but he also seems to have a good moral compass and is boring in a good way, putting basketball above everything. De'Aaron Fox always has a smile on his face and has adapted to any role asked of him. Harrison Barnes is the ultimate professional and a very charitable person. The young guards are hard workers who are willing to continue to improve instead of relying on talent and athleticism alone. Devin Vassell is soft-spoken but committed to winning, no matter what it takes.

Even the guys who have struggled, like Keldon Johnson and Luke Kornet, have great personalities that make them lovable. It's really hard to find someone to dislike on the roster, which makes watching the Spurs a lot more fun.

This one is important to remember, especially after rough losses. The Spurs have fallen short in four games this season and have had some close calls against inferior opponents. It's completely understandable to have some concerns about the team during the bad times, and occasionally even during the good times. The good news is, while there are some issues, none seem unsolvable.

The Spurs have a ton of talent, so they can overcome some mistakes, which is great. The three-point shooting has been so bad that it's bound to improve. The bench play has been poor, but it shouldn't be impossible to find some lineups that work better. Having Harris back will certainly help the second unit. And if all else fails, a trade or a signing could give the team a boost if it needs one. San Antonio is in a great place already, but things could realistically get even better.

Now let's get to the important part. What are you thankful for as a Spurs fan? Let us know in the comments.

Austin Reaves moved one step closer to making his return to the court on Thursday.

The Lakers star was upgraded to questionable on the team's injury report for Friday's road game against the Spurs in San Antonio.

Reaves was sidelined for the Lakers' previous five games because of a bruised left heel injury he suffered during the third quarter of their Nov. 11 road win over the Bucks in Milwaukee.

Austin Reaves (15) of the Los Angeles Lakers shoots a free throw. NBAE via Getty Images

The team deemed his status day-to-day, but Thursday was the first time he was listed as questionable on one of the team's injury reports since he's been sidelined.

The 6-foot-5 star guard was a full participant in the team's practice on Wednesday.

"It felt good to play basketball again," Reaves said in his first public comments since suffering the injury. "Wind was a little bad, but kind of to be expected being out two weeks. But felt good."

Austin Reaves has been sidelined for five games because of his heel injury. NBAE via Getty Images

He wasn't sure what happened on the play against the Bucks to cause the injury.

"I had no idea," he said. "Tried to play through it, and then I drove baseline, planted on it, and was like, I can't do this. So walked to the back and was in some pretty bad pain. I didn't think I broke my foot, but it sure felt like I broke my foot."

The Lakers went 4-1 after Reaves suffered the injury, but the team clearly missed his offensive production.

They had a 112.9 offensive rating (tied for No. 18) in the five games Reaves missed compared to the 121.6 (No. 1) offensive rating in their first 13 games.

"Who would have thought that not having an elite offensive player, an All-Star level player would hurt your offense," coach JJ Redick quipped. "That's crazy."

Los Angeles Lakers' Austin Reaves suffered his heel injury against the Bucks. AP Photo/Aaron Gash

Reaves is averaging 24.7 points (51.3% shooting from the field, 40.9% on 3-pointers), 4.7 assists and 3.3 rebounds on the season.

"One of those things that just, it sucks," Reaves said. "I was rolling, playing well. We were rolling as a team, wanted to continue to be out there and play games. Hate missing games. #2673. Observations after Sixers' 5-game win streak ends with blowout loss to Blazers

Observations after Sixers' 5-game win streak ends with blowout loss to Blazers originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

The Sixers' five-game winning streak was snapped Monday night by the Trail Blazers.

With a 128-111 defeat at Xfinity Mobile Arena, the Sixers dropped their first game of the year against Western Conference opposition and fell to 14-4. Portland improved to 11-6.

LeBron James had a season-high 23 points and six rebounds. Tyrese Maxey scored 22 points and Jaylen Brown added 20.

Deni Avdija led the Blazers with 31 points and seven assists. Donovan Clingan posted 15 points and 18 rebounds.

The Sixers were missing Joel Embiid (illness). Ja Morant (left hamstring strain) and Shaedon Sharpe (right knee meniscus surgery) were among Portland's sidelined players.

Next on the Sixers' schedule is a Wednesday night game vs. the Heat. Here are observations on their blowout loss to the Blazers:

Jabari Walker, listed at 6-foot-7, defied conventional wisdom by winning the opening tip-off against the 7-2 Cllingan. Maxey then canned a three-pointer.

Brown scored the Sixers' next four points with a pair of free throws and a short jumper. VJ Edgecombe's layup gave the team a 9-2 lead. Brown and Dean Wade both returned Monday after sitting out the last two games with left hamstring injuries.

Avdija got hot in the first quarter. He scored 11 quick points, made his first four field goals and helped the Blazers avoid a serious early deficit.

The Sixers took a 32-30 edge with 9.3 seconds left in the first when Walker jammed in a put-back dunk. The former Portland second-round draft pick played 17 minutes in his second start of the season and continued to look deserving of a rotation spot. He posted 10 points and five rebounds.

Adem Bona was available again following an eight-game absence with a cervical spine sprain. However, Dominick Barlow checked in first to back up Walker.

Barlow had an outstanding start to his night. He scored a clever lefty push shot over Clingan and threw down a dunk in the first quarter. Barlow also made a highlight defensive play in his opening stint, defending Avdija in isolation and rejecting his layup attempt.

Bona then subbed in for Barlow with 3:23 left in the first quarter. He had a positive first possession, grabbing an offensive rebound and driving in for a dunk.

Wade later played at center, too. Barlow logged 16 minutes and had six points. Bona recorded four points and two boards in five minutes. Sixers head coach Nick Nurse ended up using a 10-man rotation and did not play rookie guard Labaron Philon Jr. until fourth-quarter garbage time.

Overall, the Sixers' defense remained considerably worse without Embiid. The team also conceded 15 offensive rebounds, including five to Clingan.

"I think your rim protection and ability to do that with some size is always a focal point of being really good defensively," Nurse said. "And then you've got to do it a little bit by committee (with Embiid out). I thought, for the most part, I was looking at possessions where I liked our help into the paint. They were doing a good job of zinging it out.

"I didn't particularly like our (defense) back out. … There were a couple of times they missed those and still got rebounds. We were compacted in the lane with everybody because we didn't get back out, and then still giving up an offensive rebound as well. That's just playing through the possession, a little bit of energy, all that kind of stuff. … We just didn't do enough pieces well."

Brown delivered tons of efficient offense for the Sixers in the first half and sure didn't appear rusty. His layup late in the second quarter tied the game at 58-all. The five-time All-Star scored 19 first-half points on 8-for-10 shooting.

Avdija exceeded Brown's production, hitting heat-check threes, leaners through contact and just about everything he put up regardless of the defender. He tallied 25 points in the first half and shot 9 for 12 from the field.

James reached 16 points when he capped a high-scoring half by nailing a corner three. The contest was even at 69 apiece heading into halftime.

Monday's game was James' first of the season with three or more made three-pointers. The four-time MVP went 4 for 5 beyond the arc. He'd gone 10 for 46 (21.7 percent) over his first 13 games and was due for a good long-range night.

James was whistled for his third foul early in the third quarter. Brown picked up his fourth with 10:15 to go in the period, forcing him to sit for an extended stretch.

"I wasn't too happy about it. … I think that affected the game," Brown said. "It also affected my rhythm a little bit in the second half. I had to sit (almost) the whole third quarter. Coming back from injury, coming back from a hamstring thing, my body didn't really feel the same after that."

Brown noted postgame that he had "a little bit of soreness and stuff like that."

"I think everything will check out," he said. "The medical staff is on top of everything. Those hamstrings are tricky, so you want to make sure you play it the right way, be safe. I also don't want to miss a lot of games, so I might be out there, but I've also got to be smart. I think I played it the right way today."

Avdija stopped lighting up the Sixers in the third period, but the team still had another unimpressive defensive quarter. Portland posted 32 points in the third and built its lead to double figures in the opening minute of the fourth.

The game devolved into a blowout. An Avdija dunk put the Blazers' advantage at 22 points with 5:15 on the clock and the Sixers didn't have a miracle comeback in store.

Even with all their wins, there's no question the Sixers have been trending downward on defense over the past couple of weeks, allowing regular dribble penetration and plenty of comfortable threes.

They'll aim to raise their level on that side of the floor and expect Embiid's presence to be a major help once he's back in action.

"I think it's just mindset," Walker said. "We're capable when we want to. You need games like this every now and then just to remind you that it's not as easy as it feels sometimes. It takes effort every game.

"I think we can learn a lot from this. It's just part of the growing pains, but I'm confident we'll get back to that (early-season) level of defense. We have what it takes."

#2669. Mourinho considering bold Real Madrid midfield experiment after stunning PSV comeback

Real Madrid played one of their worst halves of football in recent weeks during their 5-1 victory over PSV Eindhoven in the Champions League.

Los Blancos could not get going in the first half, with the Dutch side looking far superior.

However, Jose Mourinho's half-time changes and tactical tweaks saw Real Madrid score five unanswered goals against PSV.

The Portuguese manager is now considering making one of those adjustments a more regular feature of his system.

According to MARCA (h/t Madrid Zone), Mourinho has not ruled out using Arda Guler and Bernardo Silva together in a double pivot.

Jude Bellingham changed the game for Real Madrid against PSV Eindhoven. (Photo by Angel Martinez/Getty Images)

The experiment worked wonders against the Eredivisie side after Mourinho introduced Jude Bellingham in place of Aurelien Tchouameni at half-time.

This saw Guler drop back to form a double pivot alongside Bernardo, and the trio worked very well together.

The transformation was remarkable, with both Bellingham and Guler getting into advanced positions and offering plenty in terms of creativity and goalscoring.

After the game, Mourinho highlighted the midfield adjustment as one of the main reasons for the second-half turnaround.

While neither Guler nor Bernardo is a natural defensive midfielder, they offered Real Madrid much better control of the ball.

With Federico Valverde now permanently playing at right-back, Madrid have four options for defensive midfield.

Tchouameni and Bernardo have proven to be the preferred pairing, with Eduardo Camavinga and Arda Guler providing alternatives.

Arda Guler offers a different level of creativity from deep-lying midfield. (Photo by Florencia Tan Jun/Getty Images)

The former is the only naturally defensive option in that position, but there are games when Los Blancos need more on the ball than his ball-winning prowess.

Deploying Guler deep gives Real Madrid a Toni Kroos-like playmaker in deeper areas, with the Turkish international's vision among the best in the squad.

While pairing him with Bernardo carries some obvious risks, especially in transition, it could prove to be a potent weapon when used correctly.

The PSV Eindhoven game was yet another example of Mourinho's in-game management and ability to take control of a situation.

It remains to be seen whether the Bernardo-Guler experiment was a one-off or something the manager considers using in future games.

#2667. Bills beat Chiefs on deflected punt, Tyler Bass' 57-yard field goal at the buzzer

The Bills overcame a sluggish offensive game in rainy, windy conditions to beat the Chiefs on Thanksgiving in Buffalo, winning 13-10 on Tyler Bass' 57-yard field goal as time expired.

The kick came after a Bills defensive stop deep in the Chiefs' own end and a partial block of Matt Araiza's punt. Local hero Joe Andreesen got a piece of Araiza's punt, and Greg Dortch bravely returned it to the Kansas City 39-yard line, setting up Bass' game-winner in an ugly offensive night.

It was Buffalo's sixth straight regular-season victory over the Chiefs, dating back to 2021.

The Chiefs had a chance to run out the clock in a 10-10 game with less than 30 seconds left, but Patrick Mahomes fumbled the first-down snap, derailing the drive, and Travis Kelce dropped a well-placed pass that likely would have sent the game to overtime. The Bills then deflected Araiza's punt and returned it to the Chiefs' 39-yard line.

The Chiefs also had a huge first-down catch by Rashee Rice controversially wiped out by replay with just under two minutes left that could have tilted the game in Kansas City's favor.

The two teams combined for 471 yards of offense in the poor weather, which kept up for the duration of the game.

The Bills moved to 10-1, maintaining their lead on the rest of the AFC. The Chiefs fell to 8-3, half a game behind the first-place Broncos in the AFC West.

Buffalo increased its probability of winning the conference's No. 1 seed to 63%, according to The Athletic. Kansas City's fell to 3%.

Josh Allen struggled through one of the poorest passing games of his career, throwing for 81 yards and two interceptions. His legs got the Bills out of some jams, but they mainly had to lean on the running of James Cook, who ran for 117 yards and their only touchdown of the game on 32 carries, which tied his career high.

Mahomes, the hotter quarterback coming into the game, had more success Thursday, throwing for 174 yards on 16-of-29 passing. But the Chiefs punted on their first four possessions and came up empty on their final four series, with Harrison Butker's missed field goal with just over six minutes left looming large.

The first half was a mess — cold, rainy, windy — and a stark contrast to the high-scoring first two games on Thanksgiving. Both teams traded a pair of punts in a scoreless first quarter. The Bills struck first, laboring down the field to get in the end zone on Cook's 5-yard run, overcoming an overturned TD and a questionable false-start call at the goal line.

Buffalo's suddenly hot defense took advantage of the elements and KC's four straight punts to open the game. It appeared that the Bills would take a two-score lead as they drove to the Chiefs' 9-yard line, but Allen's pass was tipped by George Karlaftis and intercepted in the end zone by Alohi Gilman to thwart that drive.

The Chiefs finally got going before halftime, driving to the Bills' 8-yard line, but Mahomes' end-zone pass to Rice was incomplete, and the Chiefs settled for a short Butker field goal to cut Buffalo's lead to 7-3.

Kansas City came out of halftime with renewed focus, looking the best they had offensively all game. Emmett Johnson, starting again for an injured Kenneth Walker III, capped the drive with a 1-yard TD run. It was an impressive drive despite the rain continuing to fall, giving the Chiefs a 10-7 lead. It was Johnson's fifth straight game with a touchdown. That score ended a streak of 49 drives without allowing a TD by the Bills' defense.

Allen, who had only 41 first-half passing yards, was working through his issues gripping the ball, and the Bills penetrated the Chiefs' red zone on their opening drive of the third quarter. But Allen's on-target pass to Khalil Shakir deflected off his hands and went down as Allen's second interception, this time by Nohl Williams.

The Bills' defense muscled up again and pushed the Chiefs back, giving Buffalo good field position again. Another labored drive — its fifth of the game of at least four minutes — bogged down, as the Bills had to settle for Bass' 54-yard field goal, tying the game at 10-10.

Mahomes was under fire on the ensuing drive, but he completed a third-and-15 pass under heavy pressure — vintage Mahomes — throwing back against his body for 19 yards and a clutch first down.

But penalties were a problem all game for the Chiefs, and consecutive flags pushed them back 15 yards. The Chiefs settled for a Butker field-goal try from 46 yards, but he pushed it to the right for his eighth miss of the season. That is two more than he's had in any single season in his 10 years as a Chief.

"I'm not going to make any decisions," Reid said when asked about Butker's struggles, according to The Athletic's Nate Taylor.

The Chiefs' defense showed it could flex its muscles, too. After Cook moved the chains, the Chiefs sacked Allen just as the Bills moved into Kansas City territory. It was that kind of night for the offense and for Allen.

Backed up inside his own 10, Mahomes hit Rice with an 11-yard pass on third-and-10, taking a big hit from the Bills' Amani Hooker. But the play was reviewed, and it was determined that the ball came loose and touched the ground, forcing the Chiefs to punt.

Allen got the ball back at his 47-yard line with plenty of time to mount a game-winning drive but had a first-down completion wiped out by penalty and took a massive sack on third down, and the Bills punted with less than 40 seconds left in regulation.

Instead, the Chiefs watched the Bills pull out the ugly game in the waning seconds.

The Bills won a game in which Josh Allen went 10-for-21 for 81 yards, 0 touchdowns and 2 interceptions. It began as a slog, but then every stop began landing like a haymaker.

All three games today were decided in the final three seconds.

Tyler Bass is good from 57 yards out and that will do it. This game seemed destined for overtime, until a catastrophic play put the game in the Bills' hands. That missed 46-yarder by Harrison Butker looms large.

A Chiefs three-and-out, a tipped punt and a quick return has the Bills attempting a 57-yarder for the win.

Patrick Mahomes fumbled the shotgun snap in the Buffalo cold and rain, but he got the ball back before the Bills defense could get there.

The Bills appeared to move into field goal position, but Dalton Kincaid got called for a blatant offensive pass interference, then Josh Allen got sacked on 3rd-and-9. The Bills are punting with 38 seconds left.

It's a short punt for the Chiefs too. Buffalo will get the ball at the Kansas City 37-yard line needing only a field goal with 1:40 left.

The Chiefs were facing 3rd-and-10 deep in their own territory, but Patrick Mahomes found Rashee Rice for 11 yards and a first down. However, replay overturns the catch — Rice didn't have the ball secure when it hit the ground — and that makes this a three-and-out for Kansas City.

The Bills' next drive goes nowhere quickly, with Nick Bolton and Christian Roland-Wallace combining to sack Josh Allen on third down. The Chiefs will get the ball back at their own 9-yard line with two minutes left.

Harrison Butker lined up for the 46-yard attempt, but his kicking woes continued.

He was not able to handle the weather conditions and pushed the kick wide right.

The game remains tied at 10 with 5:56 left in regulation.

Bad weather isn't keeping Patrick Mahomes from pulling some magic.

After scrambling toward the right sideline, he threw across his body, and Cyrus Allen came out of nowhere to pick up 19 yards on third and 15.

The fourth quarter began with Buffalo getting some extra yards, but not being able to sustain the drive.

Even with the bad weather, Tyler Bass lined up for the 54-yard attempt. He nailed it as it hooked right through the uprights to tie the game at 10.

12 minutes to go in a brand new ballgame.

#2666. Observations after Sixers beat Bucks to move to 3-0, Embiid posts triple-double

Observations after Sixers beat Bucks to move to 3-0, Embiid posts triple-double originally appeared on NBC Sports Philadelphia

The Sixers stayed unbeaten Saturday night at Xfinity Mobile Arena, earning a 127-116 win over the Bucks and improving to 3-0 on the season.

Joel Embiid had his 10th career regular-season triple-double, tallying 28 points, 11 rebounds and 10 assists.

On his 30th birthday, Jaylen Brown posted 27 points and five assists. Tyrese Maxey had 26 points. VJ Edgecombe scored 17 and grabbed 13 boards.

The Sixers' absences on the first night of a back-to-back included LeBron James (low back/sciatica management). Sixers head coach Nick Nurse said pregame that he did not know yet who would be available for his team's matchup with the Pistons on Sunday.

Here are observations on the Sixers' victory Saturday:

Dean Wade made his Sixers debut and started in James' place. He'd missed the first two games of the regular season with a left ankle sprain.

The 3-and-D forward scored the night's first points by a sinking a corner three-pointer on the opening possession.

Embiid also had a sharp start. He moved well, made good decisions and served as the main hub of his team's offense in the early going.

The Sixers' seven-time All-Star center has often enjoyed facing Myles Turner. He entered the night with an average of 29.4 points in 18 previous games against the Bucks big man.

Embiid did a little bit of everything in the first quarter, posting eight points, four assists and four rebounds over nine minutes. After snatching an offensive board, Embiid drained a fadeaway jumper to give the Sixers a 10-1 lead.

One of Embiid's assists was quite stylish. He found Edgecombe open beyond the arc with a behind-the-back bounce pass. Edgecombe knocked down the shot and wound up going 3 for 4 from three-point range in the first quarter.

The Sixers added rookie Labaron Philon Jr. to their rotation. Jabari Walker stayed in the mix, though he didn't enter until the 7:36 mark of the second quarter.

Philon played four minutes in his NBA debut and missed his lone shot attempt, a corner three. On defense, Philon allowed a couple of blow-bys off the dribble. He generally looked like he belonged on offense, albeit without any production in his brief run.

Maxey banked in a half-court heave at the first-quarter buzzer to put the Sixers up nine points. The Sixers couldn't carry forward any momentum, however, and began the second quarter poorly.

Adem Bona had another rough stint amid a subpar start to the season. After Anfernee Simons missed a transition layup try, Ryan Rollins' three lifted the Bucks into a 40-37 lead.

The dreadful stretch for the Sixers on both sides of the ball called to mind how they'd fallen into a 29-point deficit Thursday night vs. the Cavaliers before clawing out a comeback win.

The Sixers mustered just seven points in first six minutes of the second quarter and had many stagnant possessions that concluded with contested jumpers. The team's transition defense was dismal for much of the second period. Milwaukee had the game's first 19 fast-break points.

The Sixers regained the lead late in the second quarter. Kentavious Caldwell-Pope made two three-balls in the second and nabbed three first-half steals. Embiid assisted a go-ahead, and-one Walker layup.

Brown hit a three with 11.8 seconds left in the second quarter. Unsurprisingly, his variety of shotmaking skills were useful without James in the lineup.

Even when James or Embiid sit, the Sixers should have a simple advantage in terms of volume of stars over most opponents this year. None of Brown, Embiid or Maxey had the sort of off night that would have improved the Bucks' odds of a road win. They'd all passed the 20-point mark by the end of the third quarter.

Maxey notched another final-possession bucket, this time with a more conventional make. He canned a jumper from the right elbow with 1.7 seconds left in the third to extend the Sixers' lead to 97-87.

The Bucks made a late push in the fourth quarter. Kel'el Ware's put-back, and-one layup cut the Milwaukee's deficit to 117-114.

The Sixers ultimately handled business. Embiid reached his triple-double by assisting a second-chance Brown jumper and and Caldwell-Pope soon drilled a dagger corner three. Embiid even threw down a last-minute dunk for good measure.

For the second consecutive season, the Sixers have a 3-0 start. They got to four wins last year before dropping their first game.

#2664. Nottingham Forest vs Chelsea – Match preview and team news

Nottingham Forest welcome Chelsea to the City Ground on Friday night with both sides under pressure. The buzz that greeted high-profile managerial appointments in the summer has subsided somewhat, as both have struggled to find consistency in their results.

Forest hover just above the Premier League relegation places, while Chelsea have slipped to eighth.

Last meeting: Chelsea 1-3 Nottingham Forest, May 4th 2026, Premier League

Oliver Glasner remains without Callum Hudson-Odoi, Nicolo Savona, and Nicolas Dominguez, whose return dates are all unclear.

Liam Delap will hope to lead the line against the side he left in the summer, having scored three goals in nine Premier League starts since his arrival at the City Ground.

Glasner is expected to continue with a 3-4-2-1 system, featuring Jair Cunha, Nikola Milenkovic, and Murillo in central defence. Cunha's form has kept summer arrival Ousmane Diomande out of the side.

Chelsea will hope to have Joao Pedro available with the Brazilian back in training. The club's joint-leading league goalscorer has missed the last four games with a thigh issue. Jamie Gittens is also back in team training.

Moises Caicedo will be assessed after a heavy knock against Leeds, though Reece James and Maxence Laxcroix are battling to be back before January.

Nottingham Forest were brought back down to Earth with a bump at Bournemouth last weekend, having headed into the international break with optimism.

An impressive win over Manchester City had looked like a potential turning point, only for another setback on the south coast. Oliver Glasner has won just twice in 11 league games, with Forest above the relegation places on goal difference.

Xabi Alonso is facing pressure after Chelsea's heavy loss to Leeds last weekend. The Blues were beaten 4-1 at Stamford Bridge, losing to their fierce rivals for the first time at home since 1999.

Chelsea have now lost three times in their last four games to drop to eighth, and continue to leak goals at an alarming rate. Alonso's side are the third-highest scorers in the Premier League, but have the fifth-worst defence.

Nottingham Forest predicted XI: Sels; Cunha, Milenkovic, Murillo; Munoz, McAtee, Yates, Williams; Ndoye, Gibbs-White; Delap.

Chelsea predicted XI: Martinez; Acheampong, Fofana, Colwill, Chavarria; Lavia, Henderson; Neto, Palmer, Rogers; Emegha.

Nottingham Forest vs Chelsea will be broadcast live in the UK via Sky Sports.

#2663. Jeffery Simmons: I didn't simulate snap count on false starts, Lions are "crying" about a them problem

Long before the Bears beat the Lions on a last-second touchdown catch by wide receiver Rome Odunze, one of the storylines of the game was a run of false start penalties by the Lions.

Center Juice Scruggs was called for back-to-back false starts and then picked up a third later in the half. Left guard Christian Mahogany was flagged for another one before the next snap and there were indications from the Lions that Bears defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons was simulating the snap count to get them to jump.

Mahogany made that accusation explicit after the game that the Bears “find out the snap count of the quarterback and they use it” while adding that Lions linemen were wearing microphones that he believes will back him up. Simmons was not penalized, but was seen speaking to the referee during a break in play. He denied Mahogany’s allegation after the 39-35 win.

“We don’t have to. We don’t have to,” Simmons said, via Dave Birkett of the Detroit Free Press “We line up and play football. They quarterback check. I said, ‘Run.’ I didn’t say, ‘Hut.’ I mean, their cadence, they say, ‘White 80, white 80.’ I mean, when you lose football games, it’s a lot of complaining and a lot of crying. I mean, there was a couple times that they false start, we didn’t say a word. So that’s their problem, not ours. . . . If I say, ‘Run,’ I’m telling my defense, run. Think I care to tell them what they about to do? I’m talking to my guys. So all the crying that they’re doing, that’s a them problem, not me.”

Mahogany was flagged for taunting Simmons during a 70-yard Jahmyr Gibbs touchdown run in the fourth quarter and kicker Jake Bates missed the ensuing extra point to leave the score 35-24. The Lions would not score again and the Bears headed back to Chicago with an improbable victory.
